edits.chapter_key: binding words: oaths, vows, and their atonement
edits.body_md:
If a man says, "If Allah heals my sickness, or returns to me the one who is absent, or grants me wealth or a child, then I owe such and such a vow," and names that vow, he is bound to fulfill it once Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has granted what he longed for — for he laid the vow upon himself in that matter. If, however, he does not name the vow, saying only, "If such a thing comes to pass, I owe a vow to Allah," without specifying what it is, then nothing is required of him. Should he then vow some particular thing, that suffices him and stands as a voluntary act, not an obligation. And if he makes his vow equal in measure to the expiation of an oath, that is good and seemly.

### Concerning the Expiations

> لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِٱللَّغْوِ فِىٓ أَيْمَنِكُمْ وَلَكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا عَقَّدتُّمُ ٱلْأَيْمَنَ ۖ فَكَفَّرَتُهُۥٓ إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَكِينَ مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ أَوْ كِسْوَتُهُمْ أَوْ تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍۢ

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: "Allah will not take you to task for the thoughtless word in your oaths, but He will take you to task for the oaths you have deliberately sworn. Its expiation is the feeding of ten poor persons from the average of that with which you feed your own families, or the clothing of them, or the freeing of a slave. Whoever does not find the means, then a fast of three days. That is the expiation of your oaths when you have sworn. And guard your oaths. Thus does Allah make clear to you His signs, that you may be grateful" (al-Maidah: 89).

So whoever swears by Allah and then breaks his oath with a breach that makes expiation obligatory upon him owes the expiation set down above. If he is able, he feeds ten poor persons, or clothes them, or frees a slave, and he is free to do whichever of these he wishes, for he has the choice among them.

If the one who broke his oath can find no means to feed ten poor persons, and possesses neither the means to free a slave — whether of small or great worth — nor the means to clothe ten poor persons, then he must fast three days. Fasting does not stand in place of the other forms of expiation until none of what has been named — neither food, nor clothing, nor manumission — can be found.

Jafar ibn Muhammad, (ع), said that wherever the Quran states an obligation with "or," giving the choice among options, the one upon whom the obligation falls has that choice freely. But wherever the Quran says "if he does not find" or "if he is not able," the first option must be performed whenever it can be found and carried out; the second does not suffice until the first is beyond both finding and performing.

> لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ ٱللَّهُ بِٱللَّغْوِ فِىٓ أَيْمَنِكُمْ وَلَكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا عَقَّدتُّمُ ٱلْأَيْمَنَ ۖ فَكَفَّرَتُهُۥٓ إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَكِينَ مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ أَوْ كِسْوَتُهُمْ أَوْ تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍۢ

The feeding required by oath expiation is not discharged by a single day's provision given to the poor. The minimum is a mudd of food, together with whatever accompanies it. The idam — the middle grade of seasoning — is vinegar and oil; meat constitutes the highest grade; salt alone is the lowest, and it does not suffice. This rests on the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: "from the average of that with which you feed your families" (al-Maidah: 89). The average is the most balanced measure: whatever the one making expiation feeds his household on most days and in the ordinary run of his circumstances is what he ought to feed in the expiation of his oath. If he feeds them better than that, it is the more excellent course.

As for the clothing in oath expiation, each poor person is to receive two garments.

Regarding the freeing of a slave as oath expiation, a slave born into bondage suffices. A mudabbar — one whose release has been tied to his master's death — may not be freed for this purpose unless the master first revokes that arrangement, the tadbir, returns him to the full condition of a slave, and then frees him. The fast in oath expiation is three consecutive days.

The feeding and clothing of the people of allegiance from oath expiation is an obligation on those commanded to perform it. If such persons cannot be found, those among the weak who bear no enmity are entitled to receive it. Nothing from expiation, nor from charity, nor from anything of that kind, may be given to a Nasib — one known for his hostility toward the family of Muhammad (ع) — even if no one else can be found.

When a person lays a vow upon himself regarding some matter, conditional on its coming to pass, and that matter had in fact already occurred before he bound himself, without his knowledge, nothing is required of him. A man put a case of this kind to Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali. He said: "I have a slave girl by whom I am loath to have a child. Her menses ceased to come at the expected time, and I feared she had conceived, so I bound myself before Allah to free a slave, to fast, and to give charity if she should menstruate. She did menstruate — but before I had made that vow, and I did not know it."

Abu Jafar said: "Nothing is required of you."

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali held that if a man swears he will not give another man dinars, and then gives him goods in their place, he has not broken his oath. If a man swears he will not sell his wares at a named price, and then sells them for goods worth that same price, he has not broken his oath. And if a man is owed dinars and swears he will not receive them except in full, and is then paid part in coin and part in goods of equal value, he has not broken his oath.

He, (ع), was asked about a man who swears to slaughter his son. He said: "There is nothing upon him in that, and it is among the steps of Satan."

He also said that the expiation falls due after the oath is broken.

edits.chapter_key: when a marriage ends: divorce and separation
edits.body_md:
Chapters of Divorce

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ

Allah Almighty has said: ﴿ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا الْعِدَّةَ ﴾ "O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at the onset of their waiting period, and count the iddah." And He, glorified and exalted, has said: ﴿ وَإِن يَتَفَرَّقَا يُغْنِ اللَّهُ كُلًّا مِّن سَعَتِهِ ﴾ "And if the two separate, Allah will enrich each of them out of His abundance."

Allah, mighty and majestic, has permitted divorce in His Book and placed it in the hands of men rather than women. A man may divorce his wife whenever he wishes, whether for a cause or for none. Yet it is reported from Ali, may Allah's prayers be upon him, that he disliked divorce without cause — though he did not forbid it, nor did he invalidate a divorce pronounced without one.

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ

Umm Said, his servant, related that one day she was pouring water over his hands — peace be upon him — when he raised his head toward her and said, "O Umm Said." She said, "At your service, O Commander of the Faithful." He said, "I have longed to be a bridegroom." She said, "And what prevents the Commander of the Faithful from that?" He said, "Woe to you — after four, and in al-Rahbah?" She said, "Then divorce one and bring another in her place." He said, "Woe to you, divorce is an ugly thing, and I dislike it."

Al-Hasan — peace be upon him — was much given to divorce, and he divorced a great number of women without cause. It is said that he once passed by a group of women who sent word to him asking, "Do you know this company of women?" He said, "No." One of them said, "There is not one among us but that you have married her and then divorced her." The most that Ali — may the prayers of Allah be upon him — said concerning this was: "O people of Kufa, do not give your daughters in marriage to al-Hasan, for he is a man much given to divorce."

**The divorce that is forbidden and the divorce that is permitted**

From the Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah — peace and prayers be upon him and upon the Imams of his household — it is narrated that word was brought to him that Abdullah ibn Umar had divorced his wife three times while she was menstruating. He said to Umar: command him to take her back, then divorce her according to the Sunnah — إذا طلقتم النساء فطلقوهن — if he wishes.

So: whoever divorces his wife after consummating the marriage — while she is in a period of purity during which he has been intimate with her, or while she is menstruating, or without calling witnesses as Allah Almighty has commanded, or during her postnatal bleeding, or by swearing a conditional oath of divorce and then breaking it — his divorce is no divorce, and she remains his wife. This is the divorce of innovation, for it runs contrary to what Allah, mighty and majestic, has commanded and to the Sunnah of His Messenger concerning divorce according to the Sunnah. Both forms of divorce are, despite the difference in wording, one in substance.

When a man wishes to divorce his wife — one who menstruates — he waits until she has her period, then becomes pure. Once she has cleansed herself of the blood and bathed after her menses, he divorces her before touching her, in a state of purity in which he has not yet approached her, with a single pronouncement, calling two witnesses of just character, as Allah Almighty has commanded. He retains the stronger right to take her back and may do so if he wishes; she remains with him, with two pronouncements now counted against her, until she has menstruated three full times. When those three periods are complete, she has the stronger right over herself, and he has no path back to her unless both he and she are willing. In that case, he may marry her again by a fresh contract, with a dowry, a guardian, and witnesses, and she remains with him with two pronouncements remaining. This is the Sunnah divorce — the one that is recommended — on account of the words of Allah, mighty and majestic:

﴿ لَا تَدْرِي لَعَلَّ اللَّهَ يُحْدِثُ بَعْدَ ذَٰلِكَ أَمْرًا ﴾

"You do not know; perhaps Allah will bring about, after that, some new matter" — meaning the taking back.

If he divorces her in the manner first described — with a single pronouncement — and then takes her back before her waiting period has elapsed, or after it by a fresh contract, he may not divorce her again until he has been intimate with her. When he then wishes to divorce her a second time, he leaves her until she menstruates and becomes pure, then pronounces the divorce while she is in a state of purity in which he has not touched her, calling two witnesses of upright character. If he wishes to take her back, he does so in the way described earlier, at any point before her waiting period ends. If her waiting period has elapsed, she has the greater right over herself; and if both he and she are willing, he may marry her again by a renewed contract as previously described. Whether he takes her back or marries her anew in this way, she is his wife, and there now remains against her with him a single pronouncement.

If he then wishes to divorce her, he may not do so until he has been intimate with her. He leaves her until she menstruates and becomes pure, then divorces her while she is in a state of purity in which he has not touched her — this time with a third pronouncement. She thereby becomes irrevocably separated from him and is not lawful to him until she has married another husband, as Allah, mighty and majestic, has said.

This is the divorce of the *iddah*: he divorces her, takes her back and is intimate with her, then divorces her across three pronouncements in the manner described. This is the sound and permissible form of divorce, and there is no disagreement on the matter.

If a man divorces his wife twice or three times within a single period of purity, the additional pronouncements are not valid. Once he has pronounced the first divorce, she is divorced; the second pronouncement cannot fall upon her until he has taken her back and she has become his wife again. A divorce pronounced upon a woman who is already divorced does not take effect, just as a divorce pronounced upon a woman who is not one's wife — without the authorization of her husband — would not take effect.

Equally, if he pronounces divorce three times, or names any number of pronouncements, in a single sitting and within a single period of purity, only one divorce falls upon her — provided she was in a period of purity during which he had not been intimate with her.

The following pronouncements are invalid, because each is contrary to what Allah, mighty and majestic, has commanded concerning divorce and contrary to the Sunnah of His Messenger:

- A divorce pronounced while she is menstruating.
- A divorce pronounced during a period of purity in which he has been intimate with her.
- A divorce pronounced without witnesses being called to it.

The same position is held by those who permit this form of divorce and call it a Sunnah of the general body of Muslims, in direct contradiction of the Book and the Sunnah. They concede that the one who pronounces it is a transgressor who has overstepped, yet they maintain that the divorce takes effect and is binding.

The reply put to them is this: what would they say if a man were to contract a marriage contrary to the Book and the Sunnah — marrying a woman while she is still in her waiting period, for instance, or while she already has a husband? Their own position is that such a marriage is impermissible, and they forbid it. When pressed on why they forbid a marriage that contradicts the Book and the Sunnah while permitting a divorce that does the same, they have no proof to offer.

The argument is pressed further. This divorce, which they have permitted despite its being contrary to the Book and the Sunnah, is itself what opens the door to a marriage that is contrary to the Book and the Sunnah — the very marriage they declared impermissible in their own doctrine. For this divorce renders the woman forbidden to the man who divorced her and makes her lawful to another who would marry her. Were the divorce invalid, that subsequent marriage would likewise be invalid, since she would remain a woman with a living husband. Their annulment of her first marriage through this divorce is precisely what, on their own reasoning, establishes the validity of her marriage to the second man. The result is that a marriage has been made lawful by means contrary to the Book and the Sunnah — which is the very outcome they themselves reject.

The arguments that arise in a matter such as this run long, and they pass beyond the bounds of this book.

The testimony of women is not admissible in divorce, for Allah, mighty and majestic, said concerning it: ﴿ وَأَشْهِدُوا ذَوَيْ عَدْلٍ مِّنكُمْ ﴾ "And call to witness two of just character from among you."

Divorce falls upon five kinds of women, who are divorced under any circumstance, with no waiting for a menstrual cycle or a period of purity:

- The pregnant woman whose pregnancy has become apparent.
- The young girl who has not yet reached the age of menstruation.
- The woman past her courses, whose menstruation has ceased entirely.
- The woman whose husband has not consummated the marriage with her.
- The woman whose husband is away on a distant journey.

Whenever any one of these women is divorced, the divorce takes effect immediately, and she observes her waiting period by counting months — each month standing in place of a menstrual cycle. The exception is the woman with whom the marriage was never consummated: if her husband divorces her, she has no waiting period to observe, in accordance with the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿ فَمَا لَكُمْ عَلَيْهِنَّ مِنْ عِدَّةٍ تَعْتَدُّونَهَا ﴾ "You have against them no waiting period that you may count."

**Metaphors for divorce, and the word of divorce**

A husband who intends to divorce his wife may do so by saying to her, "You are divorced," or by naming her and saying, "So-and-so is divorced," or, when she is named to him, by saying, "She is divorced." He may also say to her, "Reckon your waiting period," intending divorce by those words, or convey any of these formulas through a messenger, or direct that "So-and-so should reckon her waiting period." These are the only two vehicles for divorce — the explicit word of divorce and the reference to the waiting period — for they are precisely the two that Allah, mighty and majestic, mentioned in His Book:

﴿ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ ﴾

"O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at the onset of their waiting period."

The verse names nothing beyond the divorce itself and the waiting period. Should a husband say to his wife, "You are set loose," or "a wilderness," or "severed," or "cut off," or "forbidden," or any other expression besides these two, his words effect nothing — just as any other speech he might address to her falls outside the category of divorce. Likewise, if he says, "You are forbidden to me," or "your private part is forbidden to me," or declares any part of her forbidden to himself, no legal consequence follows from those words, and she is not rendered forbidden to him.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, prayers of Allah be upon him, is recorded as having said of a man who said to his wife, "You are forbidden to me": had he authority over such a man, he would have struck him soundly on the head, and said to him that Allah made her lawful, and yet he forbids her? The man has done nothing more than lie, claiming that what Allah made lawful to him is forbidden. No divorce falls upon him by those words, nor is any expiation binding.

It was said to him: but the words of Allah, mighty and majestic — ﴿ يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ مَا أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكَ ﴾ — "O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful to you" — placed an expiation in the matter.

He replied that this very verse confirms the position he had stated. Allah, mighty and majestic, reproached His Prophet, and He made expiation binding upon him only because the Prophet had, alongside that act, sworn an oath. This is made plain by His words: ﴿ قَدْ فَرَضَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ ﴾ — "Allah has ordained for you the absolution of your oaths."

The Master said: that was because the Messenger of Allah had been alone with Mariyah the Copt, his slave woman, before she bore Ibrahim, (ع). Aishah came upon this and it grieved her, and wishing to please her, he forbade Mariyah to himself and swore an oath that he would not approach her again. He confided this to Aishah as a secret and bade her conceal it, but she told it to Hafsah, and the two of them united against the Messenger of Allah. So Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down: "O Prophet, why do you forbid what Allah has made lawful to you, seeking the approval of your wives? And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. Allah has already ordained for you the absolution of your oaths; and Allah is your Protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise. And when the Prophet confided a matter to one of his wives, and she then disclosed it, and Allah made it known to him, he made known part of it and turned away from part; and when he informed her of it, she said, Who told you this? He said, The All-Knowing, the All-Aware told me."

When a man pronounces divorce upon his wife, the only words that carry weight are those Allah Almighty named in His Book, where He said:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ﴾

"O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at the beginning of their waiting period."

He named nothing but the divorce (al-talaq) and the waiting period (al-idda). So if a man says to his wife, "You are loosed," or "You are quit of me," or "You are severed," or "You are cut off," or "You are forbidden," or any such word other than divorce and the waiting period, it counts for nothing. Such speech is no different from any other words he might say to her that fall outside those two terms. And if he says, "You are forbidden to me," or "Your body is forbidden to me," or declares any part of her forbidden to himself, no consequence follows, and she does not become unlawful to him.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said of a man who told his wife, "You are forbidden to me": "Had I any authority over him, I would strike his head and say, Allah made her lawful for you, and then you forbid her? He has done no more than tell a lie, claiming that what Allah made lawful for him is forbidden to him. No divorce enters upon him through that, and no expiation is binding."

It was said to him: "But Allah Almighty says, ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ لِمَ تُحَرِّمُ مَا أَحَلَّ اللَّهُ لَكَ﴾, O Prophet, why do you forbid yourself what Allah has made lawful for you? — and He placed an expiation in it."

He said: "This confirms what we have said, for Allah Almighty was reproaching His Prophet (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family). The expiation was laid upon him only because he had joined an oath to it. The proof of this is His saying, ﴿قَدْ فَرَضَ اللَّهُ لَكُمْ تَحِلَّةَ أَيْمَانِكُمْ﴾, Allah has already ordained for you the absolution of your oaths."

The Master explained that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) had withdrawn in private with Mariya the Copt, his bondwoman, before she gave birth to Ibrahim. Aisha came upon them, and the matter grieved her. Wishing to please her, he forbade Mariya to himself and swore that he would not approach her again. He confided this to Aisha and asked her to keep it secret, but she disclosed it to Hafsa, and the two of them joined against the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family). Allah Almighty then revealed verses concerning the matter, setting things right between the Prophet and his wives. The revelation declared that Jibril, the righteous among the believers, and the angels were his supporters, and that if he were to divorce his wives, his Lord would replace them with wives better than they, as He said:

﴿عَسَىٰ رَبُّهُ إِن طَلَّقَكُنَّ أَن يُبْدِلَهُ أَزْوَاجًا خَيْرًا مِّنكُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٍ مُّؤْمِنَاتٍ قَانِتَاتٍ تَائِبَاتٍ عَابِدَاتٍ سَائِحَاتٍ ثَيِّبَاتٍ وَأَبْكَارًا﴾

"obedient, believing, devoutly worshipping, repentant, given to worship, given to fasting, both previously married and virgins."

Allah then commanded him to expiate the oath he had sworn. He expiated it and returned to Mariya, and Ibrahim was born of her. She thus became the mother of his child (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family).

**The option and the transfer of authority**

> ٱلَّذِينَ يَعْلَمُونَ وَٱلَّذِينَ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ ۗ إِنَّمَا

The traditions transmitted from the Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ record that his wives expressed discontent and pressed him for more of the goods of this world, as women are wont to do, and that the most severe among them in this regard was Hafsa. She said to him, "If you divorced us, we would find among our own people men of equal standing." The Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) bore with them patiently, withdrew from their company, and revelation was withheld for twenty days. Then Allah Almighty revealed:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ قُل لِّأَزْوَاجِكَ إِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ الْحَيَاةَ الدُّنْيَا وَزِينَتَهَا فَتَعَالَيْنَ أُمَتِّعْكُنَّ وَأُسَرِّحْكُنَّ سَرَاحًا جَمِيلًا ۝ وَإِن كُنتُنَّ تُرِدْنَ اللَّهَ وَرَسُولَهُ وَالدَّارَ الْآخِرَةَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ أَعَدَّ لِلْمُحْسِنَاتِ مِنكُنَّ أَجْرًا عَظِيمًا﴾

"O Prophet, say to your wives: If you desire the life of this world and its adornment, then come, I will provide for you and release you graciously. But if you desire Allah, His Messenger, and the abode of the Hereafter, then indeed Allah has prepared for the doers of good among you a great reward."

He withdrew from all of them for twenty-nine nights in the chamber of Umm Ibrahim. Then he called them, recited to them what Allah had revealed concerning them, and gave them the option, and they chose him (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family).

Abu Jafar and Abu Abdillah (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) held that what the Prophet did was not a divorce, but that had the wives chosen themselves, it would have counted as a single, irrevocable divorce. Abu Abdillah further said: when a man wishes to give his wife the option, he should first withdraw from her, as the Messenger of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) did, until she menstruates and then purifies herself. He then presents the option while she is in a state of purity in which he has not been intimate with her, and he calls witnesses.

If she then chooses herself, the divorce is irrevocable and he has no right of return over her. He may court her again, and if both parties wish it, they may contract a new marriage. If she chooses him, no divorce takes place.

The option is exercised by her saying, "I have chosen myself," or "I have chosen you." Two outcomes follow from what she does next:

- If she chooses herself, the matter is settled.
- If she remains silent until one of them rises and they part from where they were sitting, the option lapses.

Likewise, if he withdraws the option before she has exercised it, she retains no right to choose. And if he approaches her — laying his hand upon her, kissing her, or being intimate with her — before she speaks, the option granted to her lapses. If he offers her the option and she says, "I do not accept your option," she has no option.

If he grants her the option while she is menstruating, or during a period of purity in which he has been intimate with her, or without two witnesses present, the option counts for nothing.

The Master said: "No divorce, no khul, no mutual release, and no granting of the option takes effect except by the testimony of two witnesses, during a period of purity untouched by intercourse."

He said: "If a man entrusts the option to his wife, or to her father, or her brother, or her guardian, and she is content that the one entrusted should decide the matter, that is permissible." The transfer of authority carries the same standing as the option itself: it is his saying to her, "I have placed you in command of yourself," or "I have placed your affair in your hands." This stands in the place of his saying to her, "Choose."

**What is binding in divorce and what is not**

Narrated from the Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is that he said, "There is no divorce except after marriage, and no divorce for one who has not married." And Ali (ع) said: "There is no divorce except after marriage, no emancipation except after ownership, no continuous fasting that joins two days without breaking fast, no fasting that is silence from speech from morning until night, no suckling after weaning, and no orphanhood after a child reaches maturity."

A man put a question to Abu Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع): "I have a kinswoman who has been offered to me in marriage. I wished to marry her, but before today I had said, 'The day I marry her, she is divorced.'" Abu Jafar asked whether he had already married her. The man said he had not. Abu Jafar replied that he might marry her if he wished, for divorcing a woman whose marriage bond one does not yet hold is no divorce at all.

Abu Abdillah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man who says, "If I marry such a woman, or marry in such a land, or buy such a slave, or take a concubine, or purchase such-and-such — then the one I marry is divorced, the one I buy or take as concubine is free, and what I buy is given as charity." Abu Abdillah answered that none of this amounted to anything: a man's divorce of a woman not yet bound to him in marriage is invalid, as is his emancipation of one he does not yet own, and his giving as charity what he does not yet possess.

Abu Abdillah was then asked about a man who divorced his wife while ill, where either her waiting period expired or it did not, and one of the two died. He replied that if her waiting period expired — whether while he was still ill or after he had recovered — he inherits nothing from her; yet she inherits from him should he die of that illness, whether her waiting period has expired or not, unless he recovers.

From Ali: "Every divorce is valid" — meaning as duly required — "except the divorce of one bereft of reason." From Abu Jafar and Abu Abdillah alike: the man bereft of reason, whose mind has gone from him, his divorce is not valid, nor is his emancipation.

Ali was asked about a man who saw in a dream that he had divorced his wife. He said: "That is from Satan. The divorce of a sleeping man is nothing, even if his tongue utters it while he sleeps, until he wakes and pronounces divorce as it is required." No divorce stands from one bereft of reason, nor from one who raves, nor from one in delirium, nor from a boy who has not reached puberty, nor from a drunkard who does not comprehend.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad: "Whoever is compelled to divorce his wife, his divorce is not valid. There is no divorce and no emancipation under compulsion."

On the matter of a man who says to his wife, divorce being duly due, "You are divorced one and a half times," the ruling is that she is divorced once, for divorce admits no fractions. The same applies if he says, "You are divorced three quarters, or a quarter, or a sixth of a divorce" — or names any other fraction, or leaves it unnamed: she is divorced once. If a man addresses four wives or fewer, divorce being duly permissible, and says, "I have divorced you, one divorce shared among you," each of them is divorced once. Likewise, if he says, "I have divorced all of you, two divorces shared among you" — or three, or four — each of them is divorced once. And if he says, "I have divorced you, five divorces shared among you," each of them is still bound by only a single divorce. This rests upon the principle already established: within a single period of purity, only one divorce is binding, and whatever exceeds it counts for nothing.

**Khul and mutual release (mubarat)**

Allah Almighty said:

﴿وَلَا يَحِلُّ لَكُمْ أَن تَأْخُذُوا مِمَّا آتَيْتُمُوهُنَّ شَيْئًا إِلَّا أَن يَخَافَا أَلَّا يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ اللَّهِ ۖ فَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ أَلَّا يُقِيمَا حُدُودَ اللَّهِ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا فِيمَا افْتَدَتْ بِهِ﴾

The Imams of the household of the Prophet of Allah (may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family) — among them Ali and the Imams of his line — are reported to have held that khul' is permissible when the man places it in its proper context: that is, when his wife says to him, "I fear that I will not maintain the limits of Allah toward you, so I give you such-and-such — set me free," or when her husband says something to the same effect. In either case, it is permissible for them to act on what they have agreed.

Jafar ibn Muhammad said that the husband has no right to take anything from her unless she transgresses in her speech. The transgression consists in her saying to him:

- "I will not obey any command of yours."
- "I will not honor any oath to you."
- "I will not purify myself from impurity for you."
- "I will not let you share my bed."
- "I will admit to your house one whom you dislike."
- "I will enter upon you without your leave."

Or she says, "I will not maintain the limits of Allah toward you," and makes that plain. When she says such a thing, it becomes lawful for him to take whatever she ransoms herself with, even if it exceeds what he originally gave her. But if she says no such thing, he ought not to take from her more than what he gave her.

The Master said: "Khul' and mutual release take effect only as divorce does — in a state of purity during which he has not touched her, and before witnesses." When he releases her in this way, he divorces her with a single divorce, as described above. She thereby becomes clearly separated from him, and he has no right of return unless she too consents, so that they reconcile through a fresh marriage. She remains with him according to whatever is left of her divorce count, and he may marry her again — if both parties wish it — whether before her waiting period expires or after.

As for the words of Allah Almighty:

﴿وَإِنْ خِفْتُمْ شِقَاقَ بَيْنِهِمَا فَابْعَثُوا حَكَمًا مِّنْ أَهْلِهِ وَحَكَمًا مِّنْ أَهْلِهَا إِن يُرِيدَا إِصْلَاحًا يُوَفِّقِ اللَّهُ بَيْنَهُمَا ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيمًا خَبِيرًا﴾

"And if you fear a breach between the two, appoint an arbitrator from his family and an arbitrator from her family. If they both desire reconciliation, Allah will bring about agreement between them. Indeed, Allah is All-Knowing, All-Aware."

It has come from Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abdillah that this verse applies to a husband and wife who fall into discord, cannot reach agreement, and whose quarrel is prolonged until they bring the matter before the ruler. He then appoints an arbitrator from the man's family and an arbitrator from the woman's family. If the two arbitrators are able to reconcile the couple, they do so. If reconciliation proves impossible and they move toward separating the couple, they may not do so until both the man and the woman are first consulted. If the couple do not consent to separation, the two are not parted.

**Al-Ila (the oath of abstention)**

Allah Almighty said:

﴿لِّلَّذِينَ يُؤْلُونَ مِن نِّسَائِهِمْ تَرَبُّصُ أَرْبَعَةِ أَشْهُرٍ ۖ فَإِن فَاءُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ ۝ وَإِنْ عَزَمُوا الطَّلَاقَ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ سَمِيعٌ عَلِيمٌ﴾

"For those who swear off their wives there is a waiting of four months. Then if they return, Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. But if they are resolved on divorce, then Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing."

The Imams of the household of the Messenger — may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family — transmit this teaching through Ali and the Imams of his line: al-Ila is when a man swears to his wife that he will not have intercourse with her, then keeps apart from her until four months have passed.

Abu Abdillah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: "It is not for the woman to bring her husband to account before four months have passed from the day of his oath. Once four months or more have elapsed, she may bring him to account whenever she wishes, taking the matter to the ruler. When she does so, he gives the husband the choice between returning to her — that is, resuming relations with her in the proper manner — or divorcing her. He must do one of the two. If he merely keeps apart from her without an oath, abstaining for as long as he wishes, that is not al-Ila and is not counted a divorce, until the woman takes the matter to the ruler and the ruler compels him: either he returns or he divorces then and there. Al-Ila takes effect only in a state of purity untouched by intercourse, and with witnesses, as divorce does. It falls only upon a wife whose marriage has been consummated; it does not fall upon one with whom he has not yet been intimate."

A man is at liberty if he swears off his wife for four months or less. Once four months pass and she brings him to account, nothing is lawful for him but to return to her in the proper manner or to divorce her. The return is intercourse. If he is unable to it through illness, a chronic complaint, or travel, and he affirms his return with his tongue and calls witnesses, that suffices and is permissible. When he is able, he returns to her in the proper manner.

From Ali: "When the one bound by al-Ila is halted and resolves upon divorce, let him leave her until she menstruates and purifies herself. When she is pure, he divorces her and calls two upright witnesses. He is then the more entitled to take her back so long as three menstrual cycles have not elapsed. Once they have elapsed, he is but one suitor among others, and she is in command of herself. If he wishes and she wishes, he may marry her afresh, and she remains with him according to what is left of her divorce count."

A man asked Abu Jafar, saying, "My wife bore a boy, and I feared that if I were intimate with her she would conceive and the child would perish, so I swore by Allah that I would not approach her until she had weaned him." Ali said, "There is no al-Ila upon you in seeking the child's welfare."

By this he meant that whoever swears to his wife that he will not approach her for a month, or for less than four months, that is not al-Ila. Equally, if he approaches her before four months have passed, no al-Ila applies, for al-Ila exists only by oath — the oath is its binding force. Even if he persists until four months have elapsed, it still does not constitute al-Ila, for there is no al-Ila without the swearing, and al-Ila is the swearing itself.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad: "If the one bound by al-Ila says, I have already had intercourse with her, his word is accepted along with his oath" — meaning, if he had been intimate with her prior to that. When a man has been intimate with his wife and later becomes incapable of intimacy, no separation is made between them. But if he has not been intimate with her, or is incapable at the outset, he is given a term, after which separation may be made between them. He said: "And if he swears off her for more than four months, he is one bound by al-Ila."

**Al-Dhihar**

Allah, exalted be His remembrance, said:

﴿الَّذِينَ يُظَاهِرُونَ مِنكُم مِّن نِّسَائِهِم﴾

"Those among you who pronounce dhihar against their wives," to the end of the passage on al-Dhihar.

The narration transmitted from the Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah — may Allah's blessings be upon him and his family — relates that a man came to him and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I have pronounced dhihar against my wife." He said, "Go and free a slave." The man said, "I have none." He said, "Then fast two consecutive months." He said, "I am not able." He said, "Then go and feed sixty poor persons."

Ali said: "When the one who has pronounced dhihar possesses the means to free a slave, he frees one, and fasting does not suffice for him. If he is able to fast, he fasts, and feeding does not suffice for him. And if he finds nothing to free and is unable to fast, he feeds."

Abu Abdillah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: "Everything in the Quran that uses أو or leaves its doer free to choose whichever of them he wishes, as in the saying of Him who is the Speaker:

﴿لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ ۖ فَكَفَّارَتُهُ إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَاكِينَ مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ أَوْ كِسْوَتُهُمْ أَوْ تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ﴾

The one performing expiation is free to choose whichever of those options he wishes. Where the divine words specify *if he does not find such-and-such* or *if he is unable to do such-and-such*, the latter option is not lawful until he has genuinely failed to find or is genuinely unable to perform the former.

The Master said: "Al-Dhihar takes effect only when the wife is in a state of purity untouched by intercourse, and in the presence of two witnesses — as is the case with divorce. If either condition is absent, it counts for nothing. Al-Dhihar does not occur within an oath, just as divorce does not. It occurs only when a man intends it and says to his wife, while she is in a state of purity and before two upright witnesses, *You are to me as my mother's back* — without adding any conditional such as *if you do such-and-such*.

"Al-Dhihar cannot be pronounced more than once within a single period of purity, in a single sitting; if that happens, only one expiation is due. If he pronounces it on separate, duly completed occasions, each instance carries its own expiation. If he pronounces dhihar against four wives, each wife incurs a separate expiation. Al-Dhihar is binding with respect to every woman within the forbidden degrees, as when he says, *You are to me as my mother's back.*"

When a man has pronounced zihar (ظِهَار) against his wife and seeks a way to discharge its consequence, the order of expiation is fixed. If he owns a slave he is able to free, he must free that slave; fasting is not open to him while emancipation remains within his power. If he is capable of fasting, he fasts; feeding the poor is not open to him while fasting remains within his power. Only when he can neither free a slave nor fast does he feed the poor.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: "Everything in the Quran in which there is an *or* — offering a choice — its owner may do whichever of them he wishes." This is like the saying of Allah, exalted be His mention:

﴿ لَا يُؤَاخِذُكُمُ اللَّهُ بِاللَّغْوِ فِي أَيْمَانِكُمْ وَلَٰكِن يُؤَاخِذُكُم بِمَا عَقَّدتُّمُ الْأَيْمَانَ ۖ فَكَفَّارَتُهُ إِطْعَامُ عَشَرَةِ مَسَاكِينَ مِنْ أَوْسَطِ مَا تُطْعِمُونَ أَهْلِيكُمْ أَوْ كِسْوَتُهُمْ أَوْ تَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ ﴾

"Allah will not take you to task for what is unintended in your oaths, but He will take you to task for the oaths you have deliberately sworn. Its expiation is the feeding of ten of the poor with the average of what you feed your own families, or clothing them, or freeing a slave" (al-Maidah: 89). Here the one expiating may choose whichever of the three he wishes. But where the wording runs, "and whoever does not find such-and-such, or is unable," the second option is not opened to him until he has first failed to find, or been unable to perform, the option that precedes it.

The Master said: "Zihar is valid only in a state of purity in which he has not touched her, and with the testimony of two witnesses, just as is required for divorce. If it is otherwise, it counts for nothing. There is no zihar within an oath, just as there is no divorce within one."

Zihar comes about only when the man intends it and speaks to her while she is in a state of purity and in the presence of two upright witnesses, saying, "You are to me as my mother's back," أنتِ عليَّ كظهر أمي, without adding any conditional such as "if I do such-and-such."

Zihar does not occur more than once in a single sitting within one period of purity, and a single expiation suffices even if the man repeats the pronouncement several times within that sitting. If, however, he pronounces it on separate occasions, an expiation falls due for each occasion. Likewise, if he pronounces it against four wives, an expiation is owed for each one of them.

Zihar binds a man with respect to every woman who is permanently unmarriageable to him — as when he says, "You are to me as my mother's back," or names his sister, his paternal aunt, his maternal aunt, or any other of his unmarriageable kin.

The zihar remains binding until he has intercourse with her, and zihar does not apply between a man and his slave-woman. If he wishes to approach his wife after pronouncing it, he must first make expiation and may not draw near her until he has done so. Should he approach her before that, he has acted wrongly; he then expiates afterward, seeks forgiveness from Allah, and turns to Him in repentance. If he divorces her after pronouncing zihar but before approaching her, no expiation is required of him. If he takes her back after that divorce, he may not approach her until he has performed the expiation for zihar. If, however, he leaves her until the separation is complete and then marries her anew, no zihar attaches to the new marriage, for she had already become fully separated from him.

A slave incurs zihar just as a free man does when he pronounces it against his wife, yet he owes no freeing of a slave and no feeding of the poor unless his master grants him the means to do so. If the master does not, the slave fasts one month — half of what the free man fasts. The free man's fast for zihar is two consecutive months, as Allah, exalted be His mention, has commanded. If the slave fasts a month or less and then breaks his fast, he must begin again from the start, and what he has already fasted does not count. If, however, he fasts a full month and then breaks off a day or two — or more — into the second month before completing it, he makes up only what remains, because he has already joined the two months in succession.

As for the freeing of a slave as expiation for zihar, any slave suffices — young or old, Muslim or non-Muslim, male or female — because Allah, mighty and majestic, said ﴿ فَتَحْرِيرُ رَقَبَةٍ ﴾, "then the freeing of a slave," and placed no condition upon it. It is not permitted in zihar to free an insane slave, nor one with a corrupting defect, nor a mudabbar, since his manumission may be revoked, nor a mukatab who is still paying off his installments.

According to a report from Ali, if the one who has pronounced zihar cannot find a slave to free and so begins fasting, but then acquires the means to free a slave before his fast is complete, he frees the slave and the fast is thereby annulled. If, however, he completes the fast and only afterward finds himself able to free a slave, nothing further is required of him.

A further report from Ali states that the expiation by feeding consists of providing sixty poor persons each with half a sa. Jafar ibn Muhammad held that feeding each poor person a mudd is sufficient. What Ali said is the obligation upon one who is able, while what Jafar ibn Muhammad said applies to one who is unable — his ruling entering by way of the latitude that the law extends in cases of hardship. What Ali said is the commanded measure, yet whoever feeds each poor person a mudd has discharged the duty, as Jafar ibn Muhammad affirmed.

Neither zihar nor its expiation becomes binding except where there has been intercourse with the wife — and this remains the case even if the man has not approached any of his wives. If a man approaches his wife without first having expiated, he has done wrong and committed a grave sin; he must seek the forgiveness of Allah and turn to Him in repentance.

**Mention of Lian**

Allah, exalted be His mention, said:

﴿ وَالَّذِينَ يَرْمُونَ أَزْوَاجَهُمْ وَلَمْ يَكُن لَّهُمْ شُهَدَاءُ إِلَّا أَنفُسُهُمْ فَشَهَادَةُ أَحَدِهِمْ أَرْبَعُ شَهَادَاتٍ بِاللَّهِ ۙ إِنَّهُ لَمِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ ۝ وَالْخَامِسَةُ أَنَّ لَعْنَتَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهِ إِن كَانَ مِنَ الْكَاذِبِينَ ۝ وَيَدْرَأُ عَنْهَا الْعَذَابَ أَن تَشْهَدَ أَرْبَعَ شَهَادَاتٍ بِاللَّهِ ۙ إِنَّهُ لَمِنَ الْكَاذِبِينَ ۝ وَالْخَامِسَةَ أَنَّ غَضَبَ اللَّهِ عَلَيْهَا إِن كَانَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ ۝ وَلَوْلَا فَضْلُ اللَّهِ عَلَيْكُمْ وَرَحْمَتُهُ وَأَنَّ اللَّهَ تَوَّابٌ حَكِيمٌ ﴾

These verses establish the procedure of *li'ān* — the oath of condemnation — for a husband who accuses his wife of adultery but has no witnesses to support the charge. He testifies four times, swearing by God that he speaks the truth, and a fifth time calling God's curse upon himself if he is lying. She, in turn, may avert punishment by testifying four times that he is lying, and a fifth time calling God's wrath upon herself if he speaks the truth. The passage closes by reminding that, were it not for God's grace, mercy, and His willingness to accept repentance, the consequences of such accusations would be far graver still.

According to Ali, no *li'an* arises between a husband and wife unless he either claims to have witnessed the act directly — saying, "I saw a man between her legs committing adultery with her" — or disavows her child. In the account transmitted from Jafar ibn Muhammad, the procedure takes place only before a judge, and only after the husband has held firmly to his statement without retracting it and she has denied his charge. At that point the judge orders him to perform *li'an*.

The husband's *li'an* is as follows: he declares, "I bear witness by Allah that I have indeed seen a man committing adultery with her," or, "I bear witness that this child is not mine." He repeats this four times, then says on the fifth, "If I am lying, then the curse of Allah be upon me." The judge says, "Amin."

The judge then turns to the woman. If she affirms what her husband said, she is stoned. If she denies it, she declares, "I bear witness by Allah that he is among the liars in what he has accused me of," repeating this four times, then says on the fifth, "If he is truthful, then the wrath of Allah be upon me." The judge again says, "Amin."

Once this has been completed, the judge separates the two, and she is never again lawful to him. As for the child whose paternity was disavowed, he is not attributed to the one who disavowed him; rather, he is ascribed to his mother and her maternal kin, and his inheritance passes to them. The woman's dowry falls upon the one who performed *li'an* against her.

*Li'an* may only be performed before a judge. It is not valid between a husband and wife unless he has consummated the marriage, even if he accuses her of adultery or disavows the child she bore. If he refuses to perform *li'an* and she brings the matter before the authority, he receives the *hadd* lashing for slander, unless he can produce proof of his accusation. If he does produce proof, and four upright men testify to her adultery, she is stoned and *li'an* is no longer applicable. Likewise, if he disavows the child she bore and refuses to perform *li'an*, he receives the *hadd* lashing once she brings the matter forward, and she remains his wife unless he divorces her.

If he performs *li'an* and then retracts his accusation, declaring himself a liar, he receives the *hadd* lashing. She does not return to him, yet the child inherits from him, though he inherits nothing from the child.

*Li'an* is valid in the following pairings:

- A Muslim man and a *dhimmi* woman
- A free man and a slave-woman
- Two slaves
- Any married couple, provided both are of age

*Li'an* is not valid between two minors; once they reach maturity, the husband may not perform *li'an* against his wife for an accusation he made while both were still minors. Nor is it valid between a mute husband and a mute wife, since *li'an* is enacted by spoken words alone. If a man accuses a mute wife, the two are separated, and no *li'an* is performed. A husband may not perform *li'an* against a pregnant wife; he waits until she has given birth, and only then proceeds.

If a man impugns his wife only through insinuation, *li'an* does not apply. If he says to her, "I did not find you a virgin," nothing is required of him and no *li'an* is performed, because virginity may be lost through means other than intercourse. If he accuses her before the marriage has been consummated, he receives the *hadd* lashing and she remains his wife.

The two parties perform *li'an* standing, not seated.

If a man accuses his wife and then divorces her, and she raises the matter while still within her *iddah*, he performs *li'an*. If she raises it after the *iddah* has elapsed, he receives the *hadd* lashing unless he produces proof of his accusation.

If he accuses her and she dies before *li'an* is performed, and one of her guardians steps forward to pursue *li'an* against the husband on her behalf, the husband takes no inheritance from her. If no guardian steps forward, he inherits from her.

If a man divorces his wife before consummation and she then claims to be pregnant by him while he denies it, the following applies: if she establishes that he had drawn a veil over her in seclusion, he performs *li'an*; otherwise, he swears that he never drew a veil over her nor approached her, and her claim is set aside. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ).

---

**Mention of the *Iddah*, the Maintenance Within It, and the Mourning**

Allah, mighty and majestic, said:

﴿ وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجًا يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنفُسِهِنَّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْرًا ﴾

"And those of you who die and leave wives behind, they shall wait by themselves four months and ten days" (al-Baqarah: 234). And He said:

﴿ وَالْمُطَلَّقَاتُ يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنفُسِهِنَّ ثَلَاثَةَ قُرُوءٍ ﴾

"And divorced women shall wait by themselves three menstrual cycles" (al-Baqarah: 228). And He said:

﴿ وَأُولَاتُ الْأَحْمَالِ أَجَلُهُنَّ أَن يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ ﴾

"And as for those who are pregnant, their term is that they deliver their burden" (al-Talaq: 4). And He said:

﴿ ثُمَّ طَلَّقْتُمُوهُنَّ مِن قَبْلِ أَن تَمَسُّوهُنَّ فَمَا لَكُمْ عَلَيْهِنَّ مِنْ عِدَّةٍ تَعْتَدُّونَهَا ﴾

"Then you divorce them before you have touched them, you have no waiting period over them to count" (al-Ahzab: 49).

When a man dies leaving a wife, she observes a waiting period of four months and ten nights — whether he had consummated the marriage with her or not, and whether she is an adult or a child — because Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجًا يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنفُسِهِنَّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْرًا ﴾, drawing no distinction between a wife whose marriage was consummated and one whose was not, nor between a child and an adult. She may observe this waiting period wherever she wishes, whether in her late husband's house or elsewhere.

If a man divorces his wife while she is menstruating, her iddah is three menstrual cycles, and she observes it only in her husband's house. A pregnant woman whose husband dies observes the longer of the two terms. If she gives birth before the four months and ten nights have passed, she completes the four months and ten; if the four months and ten pass and she has not yet given birth, she waits until she gives birth, because Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ وَأُولَاتُ الْأَحْمَالِ أَجَلُهُنَّ أَن يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ ﴾, and said: ﴿ وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجًا ﴾, making no exception in either verse. If he divorces her while she is pregnant, her term ends when she delivers her burden; whenever she delivers, the separation from him is complete. Everything she brings forth that is recognizably a child effects that separation. If her womb holds two children or more, however, she is not separated until she delivers the last of them.

If a man divorces his wife with one or two revocable pronouncements and then dies while she remains in that state, she observes the waiting period of death, for she had not yet become separate from him — he died while she was still within his bond. Allah, mighty and majestic, says: ﴿ وَالَّذِينَ يُتَوَفَّوْنَ مِنكُمْ وَيَذَرُونَ أَزْوَاجًا يَتَرَبَّصْنَ بِأَنفُسِهِنَّ أَرْبَعَةَ أَشْهُرٍ وَعَشْرًا ﴾.

If a man divorces his wife while he is absent, her waiting period is reckoned from the day he pronounced the divorce, even if the news reaches her only some time afterward; once the period has run its course, she becomes lawful for other husbands. If, however, he dies while absent, she must begin her waiting period from the moment the news of his death reaches her, and whatever time elapsed before that is not counted. The reason lies in a distinction between the two cases: mourning is obligatory upon a widow, whereas no mourning falls upon a divorced woman.

A woman divorced before consummation has no waiting period and may remarry whenever she wishes. A divorced woman suffering from istihaḍa counts her waiting period by the onset of menstruation. The distinction between the two kinds of blood has already been set out: menstrual blood is thick, dark, foul-smelling, and warm, while the blood of istihaḍa is thin and clear, neither warm nor foul. When she recognizes the blood of istihaḍa, she reckons her waiting period accordingly. If she does not know how to tell one from the other, she counts by months instead. The same applies to a woman who is divorced and menstruates once or twice before her menstruation stops: she begins her waiting period again from scratch, counting by months, and the menstrual cycles already passed are not carried forward. God, mighty and majestic, has imposed three complete cycles upon the woman who menstruates and three months upon the woman who has despaired of menstruation. Because this woman did not complete three cycles before her menstruation ceased, she is required to observe a waiting period of three months.

Beyond the reckoning of the waiting period itself lies the question of what a woman is owed once the marriage has come apart. Here the law weighs carefully the different ways in which a marriage may end:

- A divorced pregnant woman is entitled to both maintenance and accommodation.
- A widowed pregnant woman whose husband has died has no entitlement to maintenance.
- A woman divorced revocably, while passing her waiting period, is entitled to maintenance and accommodation until that period is complete.
- A woman divorced irrevocably has neither maintenance nor accommodation.

Mourning belongs to the widow whose husband has died. It is not required of the divorced woman, nor of the woman parted from her husband by khul, nor of the woman parted by mubarah, nor of the woman parted by lian. Mourning means that the widow, throughout her waiting period, does not comb her hair or dye it, does not perfume herself or apply kohl, does not adorn herself or wear a dyed garment — unless that garment is black. She does not leave her house during the day, nor does she pass the night away from it. She may, if she wishes, go out in the final part of the night, provided she returns before evening. This is the essence of mourning.

### On the Provision of Divorce and Making the Divorced Woman Lawful Again

Allah, mighty and majestic, said:

> لَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِنْ طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ مَا لَمْ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ أَوْ تَفْرِضُوا لَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةً ۚ وَمَتِّعُوهُنَّ عَلَى الْمُوسِعِ قَدَرُهُ وَعَلَى الْمُقْتِرِ قَدَرُهُ مَتَاعًا بِالْمَعْرُوفِ ۖ حَقًّا عَلَى الْمُحْسِنِينَ
>
> "There is no blame upon you if you divorce women whom you have not touched, or for whom you have not specified an obligation.

The provision is therefore obligatory. He also said:

> وَلِلْمُطَلَّقَاتِ مَتَاعٌ بِالْمَعْرُوفِ ۖ حَقًّا عَلَى الْمُتَّقِينَ
>
> "And for divorced women there is a provision in kindness, a duty upon the God-fearing." (Al-Baqarah 241)

> لَّا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِن طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ مَا لَمْ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ أَوْ تَفْرِضُوا۟ لَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةًۭ

The provision of muta is owed to the woman divorced according to the Sunnah and to the woman passing her iddah, whether or not the marriage was consummated. No muta is owed to the woman separated by khul, nor to the woman separated by mubarah. No fixed amount is prescribed. The obligation falls upon the man according to his means, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "upon the wealthy according to his means and upon the straitened according to his means." Whatever the divorcing husband provides fulfills the obligation. When a man has means, it is recommended that he be generous in what he provides — whether dinars or dirhams, a slave or a slave-girl, goods or food — all of which has been narrated from the Imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ). The provision is not given until after the iddah has ended and the separation has become complete. For as long as he still holds hope of her return, and she of his, the provision is not yet given.

If a man divorces his wife — whether the iddah divorce or the Sunnah divorce, with three pronouncements — she does not become lawful to him again, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said, except after another husband has married her and consummated the marriage with her.

That second husband may then divorce her, or he may die. Once her waiting period from the second husband has expired, the first husband may marry her again if both parties wish it — a fresh and renewed marriage — and she stands before him with the full count of divorce beginning anew. If he divorces her three times in this new marriage, and she then marries another man, and he afterward seeks to take her back, she does not become lawful to him again on the strength of those three, no matter how many times she remarries. She becomes lawful to him only through a marriage of genuine desire — nikah ghibta — with an adult man who consummates the marriage and has intercourse with her. A castrated man does not make her lawful to him. Nor does a boy who has not yet reached puberty, unless he has intercourse with her after reaching puberty. A marriage of muta does not make her lawful to him either. It is likewise unlawful for him to collude with a man so that the man will marry her and thereby make her lawful for him, or to arrange for any other man to serve that purpose.

If he divorces her once or twice, so that she becomes separated from him, and she then marries another man who either dies or divorces her, and the first husband marries her again after her waiting period from the second husband has expired, she stands with him for whatever remained of her count of divorces, up to the full three, as set out above. She does not become lawful to him except through a husband. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt.

### On the Return, the Status of Slaves, and the Dowries Binding upon Husbands

When a man divorces his wife, he may take her back so long as her waiting period has not ended. Once it has ended, he is but one suitor among suitors. If both parties are willing, he marries her in a fresh and renewed marriage, and she stands with him for whatever remains of her count of divorces. If he takes her back before her waiting period expires, that is his right whether she consents or refuses, and she stands with him for whatever remains of her count of divorces. The return must be witnessed by two just witnesses. When he takes her back before her waiting period has ended, he does so without any compensation and without a new dowry. If her waiting period has passed and both parties agree upon a return, he may not take her back except with a new dowry that he names for her.

A man does not need his wife's permission to return to her so long as he retains the right of return. If he divorces her a third time, no return is possible. A divorce pronounced by a slave against a free woman counts as three; a divorce pronounced by a free man or a slave against a slave-woman counts as two.

If a man divorces his wife before consummating the marriage, she receives half the dowry, as Allah said. Where he had given her an animal as her dowry and that animal bore young while in her keeping, and he then divorced her before consummation, the matter is examined:

- If the animal was already pregnant at the time it was given as dowry, he takes back half of it and half of its offspring.
- If the pregnancy occurred while the animal was in her keeping, the offspring belong entirely to her, and she returns half of the mother-animals.

If he had given her a dowry and she afterward returned it to him as a gift or bestowed it upon him as charity, and he then divorced her before consummation, he takes back half of it from her.

If the dowry was her own freedom — that is, she was his slave-woman and he had made her manumission her dowry, as described earlier — and he divorced her before consummation, he takes back half of her assessed value as calculated on the day of the marriage.

If he dies without having named a dowry for her and without having consummated the marriage, she has no claim to a dowry, yet she inherits from him.

### Gifts, Bequests, and the Shares of Inheritance

### On Gifts and Generosity

Gifts, good works, and acts of beneficence offered for the sake of God Almighty and in pursuit of His reward carry within them virtue, righteousness, and recompense. The Messenger of God — peace be upon him and his family — said: "All of creation are the children of God, and the most beloved of creation to God Almighty is the one who benefits His children, who brings joy to a household, and who walks with a Muslim brother in his time of need." Such a person, he said, is more beloved to God Almighty than two months of itikaf in the Sacred Mosque.

Ali, prayers of God be upon him, said that the people of goodness stand in greater need of having their goodness accepted than the needy stand in need of them, because through that goodness come praise, reward, and remembrance for them from God. Whoever performs a kind act toward one of God's creatures has in truth ennobled himself by it and adorned his own honor.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, prayers of God be upon him, said: "When God raises the believer from his grave, a beautiful figure goes forth with him. As he passes through those terrors, it says to him, *Do not fear, no harm shall come to you,* and it does not cease to reassure him and give him glad tidings until it brings him before God, who calls him to an easy reckoning and then commands that he be taken to Paradise. The believer says to it, *Who are you, may God have mercy upon you? You promised me and were truthful to me and gave me security.* It replies, *I am a creation your Lord fashioned out of the joy you used to bring to the believers. Today it is I who gladden you.*"

Jafar ibn Muhammad, prayers of God be upon him, said: "There is nothing more excellent than beneficence except its reward, and beneficence is a gift from God Almighty to His believing servant. Not everyone who loves to do good to people is opened to it; not everyone who desires it is able to do it; not everyone who is able to do it is given leave to do it. When God Almighty bestows His grace upon a servant, He gathers together for him three things:

- the desire for beneficence,
- the ability to perform it,
- and the leave to act upon it.

There, happiness and honor are complete — both for the one who seeks the good and for the one to whom it is directed."

The Master said, peace be upon him: "Beneficence is not made complete except by three qualities: making little of it, making it easy, and hastening it. When you make little of it, you have made it great in the eyes of the one to whom you do it; when you make it easy, you have rendered it complete for him; and when you hasten it, you have made it a cause of joy for him. But if you do not do these things, you have spoiled it and rendered it thankless."

He said: "The best of Muslims is the one who joins, helps, and gives." And he said: "I heard my father say: the doing of good wards off the calamities of evil. Every kindness is a charity, and the people of goodness in this world are the people of goodness in the Hereafter. The first to enter Paradise are the people of goodness."

The Messenger of God and his family said: "Whoever has a kindness done to him, let him repay it; if he is unable, let him praise the one who did it; and if he does not, then he has been ungrateful for the blessing."

The Imams of the People of the House of the Messenger of God, prayers of God be upon them, permitted a man to favor some of his children over others in wealth and gifts, if he chose to do so. A gift or a charity is valid whether or not possession has been transferred to the recipient. Whoever gives a gift for the sake of God Almighty, or to a blood relative or kinsman, has no right to take it back. If, however, he gives a gift or grant expecting compensation in return, that is disliked, and he may reclaim it if no compensation is given. Whoever gives a gift or charity to a blood relative or kinsman who then dies — so that it returns to him through inheritance — there is no harm in that.

The *umra*, the *ruqba*, and the *sukna* are among those arrangements that carry merit and reward. The *umra* is a grant by which a man gives another man the use of a house, an estate, or any other property for the duration of that other man's life. The *ruqba* carries the same general meaning, but with one distinguishing condition: whichever of the two parties dies first, the property reverts to the original grantor or to his heirs.

The terms of such a grant determine where the property rests:

- If a man grants something for his own lifetime, it remains his for as long as he lives.
- If the condition is tied to the grantor's life and he dies, the property returns to his heirs.
- If the condition is tied to the recipient's life, the property belongs to the recipient for the duration of his life; should the grantor die in the interim, the grantor's heirs have no claim over it — the recipient may continue to dwell in it and make use of it until his own death.
- If the grantor made the grant for the recipient and his heirs, then it belongs to the recipient and passes to his heirs after him, in accordance with whatever the grantor originally settled.

Presents are commended when they are given for the sake of God Almighty and for His pleasure alone. No good attaches to a present given to curry favor in something false, to obtain a like return, to secure the fulfillment of a need, or to win the attention of the recipient. Attending to a believer's needs and caring for him in what is right is an obligation upon his believing brother; if he takes payment for that, what he takes is unlawful gain. The same applies to whatever he receives in exchange for collusion in falsehood.

> إِن تُبْدُوا۟ ٱلصَّدَقَتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِىَ ۖ وَإِن تُخْفُوهَا وَتُؤْتُوهَا ٱلْفُقَرَآءَ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌۭ لَّكُمْ

Obligatory giving — zakat and its like — is best given openly and announced. Voluntary charity is best kept secret, though announcing it carries no harm. God, exalted be He, has said: ﴿إِنْ تُبْدُوا الصَّدَقَاتِ فَنِعِمَّا هِيَ وَإِنْ تُخْفُوهَا وَتُؤْتُوهَا الْفُقَرَاءَ فَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَكُمْ﴾ — "If you disclose your charities, that is good; but if you conceal them and give them to the poor, that is better for you." (Al-Baqarah: 271)

The same principle governs every act of righteousness. Obligatory portions are finer when disclosed and mentioned; voluntary portions are finer when concealed. The obligatory prayer is best performed in the mosque and in congregation; the voluntary prayer is best performed in seclusion. A man who says, "I have prayed the noon prayer" — or the afternoon prayer, or whatever obligatory prayer he names — says nothing wrong; and the same holds if he says, "I have fasted the month of Ramadan." But if he says, "I have risen for the night prayer," or "I have fasted such-and-such" of the voluntary acts, that declaration is disliked, because it opens a door to ostentation. All deeds run on this principle.

Whoever owns something not yet taken into his possession may still give it in charity or as a gift. Whoever gives something in charity may not take it back.

Whoever sets something aside as an endowment for his child, his freed clients, or particular named individuals — removing it from his own possession and delivering it to them — that endowment is valid. It stands according to whatever conditions he stipulates and the terms by which he restricts it. If those beneficiaries later fall into dispute and corruption among them is feared, they may sell the endowment and divide the proceeds in proportion to each person's assigned share, provided the endowment was made to them by name. If, however, he set it aside for them and their descendants, or declared, "When they die out, it becomes a charity," then it is a charity, and they may not sell it. If he designated its final destination as a charity, then when those for whom it was set aside die out, it passes to the poor and the needy. If he made no such final designation and those for whom it was endowed die out, it returns to him if he is still living, or to whoever is entitled to his inheritance if he has died.

If he stipulated that any woman among the beneficiaries who marries forfeits her right in the endowment — and those women are later widowed and return — the condition holds and their right is restored. If, on the other hand, he said, "If I am in need, I have the better right to it," then the endowment is void. In that case it forms part of his estate for his heirs at his death, and he may reclaim it whenever he wishes.

### On Bequests

> كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ ٱلْمَوْتُ إِن تَرَكَ خَيْرًا ٱلْوَصِيَّةُ

God, exalted be He, has said: ﴿كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ إِنْ تَرَكَ خَيْرًا الْوَصِيَّةُ﴾ — "It is prescribed for you, when death approaches one of you and he leaves wealth behind, that he make a bequest." (Al-Baqarah: 180) Death stands present for every living soul, and no one knows when it will come. He also said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا شَهَادَةُ بَيْنِكُمْ إِذَا حَضَرَ أَحَدَكُمُ الْمَوْتُ حِينَ الْوَصِيَّةِ﴾ — "O you who believe, let there be testimony among you when death approaches one of you, at the time of the bequest." (Al-Maidah: 106)

The Messenger of God, upon him and his family be peace, said: "It does not befit a Muslim to let two nights pass without his will written and kept at his head." He also said: "Whoever fails to make his bequest well at the hour of death has fallen short in his manliness and his reason." They asked, "O Messenger of God, how does the dying man make his bequest?" He said that when death comes to him, the people are to be gathered, and he bears witness and makes his bequest — and on this he spoke at length.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, prayers of God be upon him, said: "The bequest is a duty upon every Muslim." And Jafar ibn Muhammad, prayers of God be upon him, said: "The bequest is obligatory upon every Muslim, and it does not befit anyone to let two nights pass without his will written. No dying person meets death except that God Almighty restores to him his reason, his hearing, and his sight before death so that he may make his bequest — whether he takes that opportunity or leaves it."

The Imams of the House of the Messenger of God permitted a bequest of up to one-third of what the testator leaves, and no more, and they did not allow anything beyond that third except with the consent of the heirs.

Where a testator frames a set of bequests directing that the Hajj be performed on his behalf, that a slave be freed, and that expiation be made for his oaths, the following order applies — provided he had not performed the Hajj and was unable to, and the bequest falls within the third:

1. The Hajj is discharged first.
2. The expiation is discharged second.
3. The manumission is discharged third.
4. Whatever shortfall remains is met from what is left.

This order governs when the testator has framed the bequest with words such as "Let my third be brought out and spent on such-and-such." If, however, he made a bequest without naming a third or any fixed sum, and simply directed that the Hajj be performed for him when he had not yet performed it, then the cost of the Hajj is drawn from the whole of the estate. Equally, if he declares that he owes zakat or any other binding obligation and directs that it be discharged on his behalf, it too is drawn from the entire estate. Whatever is voluntary, by contrast, is drawn only from the third. Accordingly, if he had already performed the Hajj and then directs that a further Hajj be performed for him, that direction is voluntary in nature and is met from the third alone.

No bequest may be made to an heir unless the remaining heirs consent to it, for God Almighty has already fixed each heir's share, and nothing may be added to it. An exception arises when the testator makes a bequest for a parent or relative who does not inherit from him — as when his parents are enslaved or non-Muslim, or related to him through nursing, or are foster parents.

When a man, during the illness from which he dies, acknowledges a debt in the presence of his heirs or some of them, his situation is examined. If he is under suspicion, his acknowledgment carries no weight unless clear proof establishes the origin of the debt he has acknowledged — unless the remaining heirs consent to it. If, however, he is sick yet known to be upright and trustworthy, his acknowledgment is accepted without further proof.

Once a man has made his bequest, he may revoke it. He may also add to it or subtract from it at any point while he is alive and of sound understanding. If his bequests exceed the third and his heirs learn of this during his lifetime and give their approval, they have no right to withdraw that approval after his death.

### On the Obligatory Shares of Inheritance

What follows concerns the shares of the child, the parents, the spouses, the grandfather, the grandmother, and the brothers.

God, mighty and majestic, has said: ﴿يُوصِيكُمُ اللَّهُ فِي أَوْلَادِكُمْ لِلذَّكَرِ مِثْلُ حَظِّ الْأُنْثَيَيْنِ فَإِنْ كُنَّ نِسَاءً فَوْقَ اثْنَتَيْنِ فَلَهُنَّ ثُلُثَا مَا تَرَكَ وَإِنْ كَانَتْ وَاحِدَةً فَلَهَا النِّصْفُ وَلِأَبَوَيْهِ لِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمَا السُّدُسُ مِمَّا تَرَكَ إِنْ كَانَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ فَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ وَلَدٌ وَوَرِثَهُ أَبَوَاهُ فَلِأُمِّهِ الثُّلُثُ فَإِنْ كَانَ لَهُ إِخْوَةٌ فَلِأُمِّهِ السُّدُسُ مِنْ بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍ يُوصِي بِهَا أَوْ دَيْنٍ﴾ — "God charges you concerning your children: to the male the like of the share of two females.

The narration from the People of the House, prayers of God be upon them, continues: when a man dies leaving children — sons and daughters, with no other heir — his estate is divided among them so that each son receives the equivalent of two daughters' shares. The same rule applies when he leaves a single son and a single daughter: the son takes two-thirds and the daughter one-third. If he leaves only a single son with no other heir, the entire estate passes to that son. If he leaves two sons, or more, the estate is divided equally among them.

> وَٱلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا۟ مِنۢ بَعْدُ وَهَاجَرُوا۟ وَجَهَدُوا۟ مَعَكُمْ فَأُو۟لَٓئِكَ مِنكُمْ ۚ وَأُو۟لُوا۟ ٱلْأَرْحَامِ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلَىٰ بِبَعْضٍۢ فِى كِتَبِ ٱللَّهِ ۗ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَىْءٍ عَلِيمٌۢ

If he leaves a single daughter with no other heir, she takes one half by the share God Almighty has named for her in the verses already recited, and the remaining half is returned to her by the tie of kinship, in accordance with the word of God, mighty and majestic: ﴿وَالَّذِينَ آمَنُوا مِنْ بَعْدُ وَهَاجَرُوا وَجَاهَدُوا مَعَكُمْ فَأُولَئِكَ مِنْكُمْ وَأُولُو الْأَرْحَامِ بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلَى بِبَعْضٍ فِي كِتَابِ اللَّهِ إِنَّ اللَّهَ بِكُلِّ شَيْءٍ عَلِيمٌ﴾ — "And those who believed afterward and emigrated and struggled along with you, they are of you; and those who are bound by blood are nearer to one another in the Book of God. Truly God has knowledge of all things." (Al-Anfal: 75) If there are two daughters, or more, two-thirds is theirs, divided equally among them by the named share, and the remaining third is returned to them by the tie of kinship.

When children are present alongside those entitled to fixed shares — the husband, the wife, the grandmother, and the parents — those fixed-share heirs receive what God Almighty has named for them, and whatever remains passes to the child or children as already described. If there is no child but there is a grandchild, the grandchild stands in the child's place: males among them as males, females as females, however far the descent extends, provided no one nearer to the deceased exists among them — for whoever is nearer screens out whoever is more remote.

Every heir for whom God Almighty has named a share in the Book holds a stronger claim than one He has not named. When something remains beyond what He named for a given heir, it is returned to that heir, and to sons and the broader group in proportion to their respective inheritance shares — with one exception: nothing is returned to the husband or the wife unless a tie of kinship independently qualifies them for the return.
