To illustrate: a man dies leaving both parents and a daughter. The parents receive two sixths, and the daughter receives the half — her named share. One sixth remains. Since the two sixths assigned to the parents account for two shares, and the half assigned to the daughter amounts to three sixths, five shares have been distributed in total, leaving one share over. That remaining share is returned to the heirs in proportion to their shares, so the estate reverts to five parts: three-fifths to the daughter and two-fifths to the parents.

If instead the man leaves a daughter, a father, and a mother, the daughter again takes the half, and the father or the mother takes the sixth. The estate then reverts, on the same principle, to fourths: one quarter to the father or the mother, and three-quarters to the daughter. Whatever cases follow this pattern are resolved by the same method.

### When a Marriage Ends: Divorce and Separation

When only the parents survive and no other heir is present, the father receives two thirds and the mother receives one third. If a child is also present, the rule proceeds as already described — even when the children are many, and whether they are male or female: they take what remains after the fixed shares are satisfied, with each male receiving the equivalent of two female shares, regardless of how few or how many there are. If two sons survive, they divide what remains equally between them. If two children survive alongside the parents, the children together receive two thirds. What falls to a single child has already been set out above.

When a person leaves behind both parents together with brothers — whether full brothers or brothers through the father — those brothers receive nothing. The mother receives one sixth, and the father takes the remainder, as Allah, mighty and majestic, has stated in His Book. Brothers through the mother do not deprive the mother of her third by inheriting for themselves; they only reduce her share, so that the father receives two thirds and the mother one third. The father inherits alongside the child and alongside the parents, and none inherits together with the child and the parents except the husband, the wife, and the grandmother.

It is narrated from the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, that he assigned an inheritance to the grandmother and fixed one sixth for her, looking to her children as they divided among themselves. The grandmother therefore inherits one sixth alongside both parents, and one sixth alongside either parent alone. If she stands alone with no one to exclude her and no other heir survives, she takes one sixth by the naming of her share, and the remainder is then returned to her, so that she gathers the whole inheritance. If two grandmothers survive — one on the father's side and one on the mother's side — the father's mother and the mother's mother share two thirds between them, while the mother's mother alone takes one third. Among the grandmothers, whichever is closer in degree excludes the one more remote.

The paternal grandfather stands in the position of the full brothers, and the brothers through the father inherit as they inherit. He is counted as one of them, and whoever excludes them excludes him. The maternal grandfather stands in the position of the uterine brother, inheriting as they inherit and excluded as they are excluded. This is because the grandfather's kinship to the deceased mirrors the brother's kinship to the deceased: each is connected to the deceased through his father, and that connection through the father is a single bond — the grandfather being that father's father, and the brother being that father's son.

> وَلَدٌۭ ۚ فَإِن كَانَ لَكُمْ وَلَدٌۭ فَلَهُنَّ ٱلثُّمُنُ مِمَّا تَرَكْتُم ۚ مِّنۢ بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍۢ تُوصُونَ بِهَآ أَوْ دَيْنٍۢ ۗ وَإِن كَانَ رَجُلٌۭ يُورَثُ كَلَلَةً أَوِ ٱمْرَأَةٌۭ وَلَهُۥٓ أَخٌ أَوْ أُخْتٌۭ فَلِكُلِّ وَحِدٍۢ مِّنْهُمَا ٱلسُّدُسُ ۚ فَإِن كَانُوٓا۟ أَكْثَرَ مِن ذَلِكَ فَهُمْ شُرَكَآءُ فِى ٱلثُّلُثِ ۚ مِنۢ بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍۢ يُوصَىٰ بِهَآ أَوْ دَيْنٍ غَيْرَ مُضَآرٍّۢ ۚ وَصِيَّةًۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَلِيمٌۭ

Where the deceased leaves behind no father, no mother, and no other ascendant, but is survived by brothers, the inheritance belongs to those brothers. Full brothers exclude brothers through the father; where there are no full brothers, the paternal brothers stand in their place. When both full brothers and paternal brothers are present together, the estate is divided among them according to the male and female shares. Where the brothers are through the mother alone, the inheritance is divided equally between male and female, as Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿وَإِن كَانَ رَجُلٌ يُورَثُ كَلَالَةً أَوِ امْرَأَةٌ وَلَهُ أَخٌ أَوْ أُخْتٌ فَلِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِّنْهُمَا السُّدُسُ فَإِن كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِن ذَٰلِكَ فَهُمْ شُرَكَاءُ فِي الثُّلُثِ﴾ "If a man dies leaving no children, and he has a brother or a sister, each of them receives one sixth; but if there are more than that, they share one third" (al-Nisa 12). It is narrated that this verse was revealed concerning a brother and a sister through the mother.

When full brothers and brothers through the father are present together, the full brothers receive two thirds divided among them, the male taking the equivalent of two females' shares, whether they are few or many. If maternal siblings are also present — male or female, two or more, whether two sisters, a brother and sister, or brothers and sisters — one third belongs to those maternal siblings, divided equally among them regardless of sex and however many they may be, while the brothers through the father are set aside. Likewise, if a person leaves behind one maternal brother or one maternal sister, that single one receives one sixth; if there are several, they receive one third together. If there is a full sister, she receives one half, and the remainder returns to her through kinship.

Brothers and sisters inherit alongside the spouses. The spouse's share is given first, and what remains goes to the brothers as described. The husband receives half of his wife's estate if she has no child, and a quarter if she has a child, whether male, female, or several. The wife receives a quarter of her husband's estate if he has no child, and one eighth if he has a child, whether male, female, or several — as the explicit text of the Book prescribes. Two, three, or four wives share equally in that same portion: one eighth where there is a child, and a quarter where there is none, dividing it equally among them with nothing added to it.

When a man dies leaving two parents and a wife, the husband receives half his wife's estate, the wife receives a quarter of her husband's estate, the mother receives one third, and the father takes the remainder — as the text of the Book prescribes. By the same principle that gives the father precedence over the mother when brothers are present, the deficiency here falls upon him, for Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿فَإِن كَانَ لَهُ إِخْوَةٌ فَلِأُمِّهِ السُّدُسُ﴾ — "If he has brothers, his mother receives one sixth" (al-Nisa 11). Since brothers do not inherit alongside the parents, whatever remains passes to the parents. The mother therefore receives one third when there are no brothers, and one sixth when there are brothers. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them all.

### On the inheritance of kindred and connections, and on the apportioning of shares without awl and without exclusion

The Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them, have transmitted the following: whoever dies leaving behind those who hold fixed shares named in the Book, they inherit according to the shares Allah, mighty and majestic, has named therein. If he leaves behind none of those named sharers, his estate passes to whichever of his kindred stand nearest to him; where two or more stand at equal distance, the estate is divided among them. A relative who draws near through someone who holds a named share takes precedence over one who draws near through someone who holds no named share. Those who are nearer exclude those who are more remote. The line of succession then runs as follows:

- Whoever is related through the deceased's father inherits the father's share, as though the father were alive.
- Whoever is related through the mother inherits the mother's share.
- Whoever is related through a brother inherits that brother's share.
- Whoever is related through a sister inherits her share.

A man dies leaving a son's son and a son's daughter. The estate is divided between them with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares.

If he leaves a daughter's son and a son's daughter, the son's daughter receives two thirds — her father's share — and the daughter's son receives one third, which is his mother's share.

If he leaves sons and daughters of a predeceased son together with a son or daughter of a predeceased daughter, the division runs as follows:

- One third goes to the single son or single daughter of the daughter, or to all the daughter's children however many they are.
- Two thirds go to the children of the son, divided among them with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares, whether few or many.

The children of the son inherit their father's share as though he were alive, and the children of the daughter inherit their mother's share as though she were alive, whether each group is few or many.

Those who draw near through the mother's kinship inherit as brothers through the mother inherit — male and female alike. Those who draw near through the father's kinship inherit with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares.

The sons of brothers and their daughters, and the sisters, inherit in the manner already described when there is no direct child or grandchild, just as the grandchildren inherit as explained earlier. Where they descend from one father or one mother, the sons of the brother divide the wealth among themselves with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares.

The same principle governs the sons of paternal uncles and the sons of maternal uncles: the sons of maternal uncles divide equally between male and female, each group inheriting what would have belonged to its father or mother had that parent been alive, whether they are few or many.

- The maternal uncle and the maternal aunt share the wealth equally between them.
- The paternal uncle and the paternal aunt share it with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares.
- Their children divide on the same basis respectively.

Of the total estate:

- One third goes to the sons of the maternal uncle and the sons of the maternal aunt, shared among them, their males and females alike.
- Two thirds go to the sons of the paternal uncle and the paternal aunt, divided among them with the male receiving the equivalent of two female shares.

Among the kindred and the connections, the nearer relative excludes the more remote. The paternal uncle excludes the cousin; the son of the maternal uncle and the maternal aunt excludes the cousin and the son of the maternal uncle; the paternal aunt excludes the cousin and the son of the maternal uncle; and the maternal aunt excludes the cousin and the son of the maternal aunt — each of these standing one degree closer to the deceased than the one excluded. Whoever draws near through a full brother is more deserving than one who draws near through a half-brother on the father's side. To the kindred through the mother belongs their portion of the sixth that was the share of the person through whom they are related, divided among them, males and females alike. Whoever draws near through one who holds a fixed share excludes whoever draws near through one who does not. When several groups each draw near through a different shareholder, each group receives the share of the person through whom they are related, as has already been established.

There is no proportional reduction — no *awl* — in any fixed apportionment. The reckoning begins with the one whom Allah, mighty and majestic, has placed first. Whoever Allah, mighty and majestic, has assigned a fixed share when alone, and whose share is then reduced by the presence of another, suffers no deduction from that second named portion. This holds for the husband, the wife, the mother, and the father: nothing is deducted from the husband's quarter, nothing from the wife's eighth, and nothing from either parent's sixth. The deficiency falls upon the residuary heir, and to that heir likewise belongs any increase.

> وَلَدٌۭ ۚ فَإِن كَانَ لَكُمْ وَلَدٌۭ فَلَهُنَّ ٱلثُّمُنُ مِمَّا تَرَكْتُم ۚ مِّنۢ بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍۢ تُوصُونَ بِهَآ أَوْ دَيْنٍۢ ۗ وَإِن كَانَ رَجُلٌۭ يُورَثُ كَلَلَةً أَوِ ٱمْرَأَةٌۭ وَلَهُۥٓ أَخٌ أَوْ أُخْتٌۭ فَلِكُلِّ وَحِدٍۢ مِّنْهُمَا ٱلسُّدُسُ ۚ فَإِن كَانُوٓا۟ أَكْثَرَ مِن ذَلِكَ فَهُمْ شُرَكَآءُ فِى ٱلثُّلُثِ ۚ مِنۢ بَعْدِ وَصِيَّةٍۢ يُوصَىٰ بِهَآ أَوْ دَيْنٍ غَيْرَ مُضَآرٍّۢ ۚ وَصِيَّةًۭ مِّنَ ٱللَّهِ ۗ وَٱللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ حَلِيمٌۭ

An example is a woman who dies leaving behind her husband, her maternal brothers, and her paternal sister. God, mighty and majestic, assigned one half to the husband — she having no child — one half to the sister, and one third to the two maternal brothers, according to the plain reading of what He prescribed. When the highest fixed shares in this case were examined, the calculation proved bewildering, and some inflated the denominator, expanding six shares into eight. Yet God, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿إِنِ امْرُؤٌ هَلَكَ لَيْسَ لَهُ وَلَدٌ وَلَهُ أُخْتٌ فَلَهَا نِصْفُ مَا تَرَكَ وَهُوَ يَرِثُهَا إِن لَّمْ يَكُن لَّهَا وَلَدٌ﴾ "If a man dies having no child, and he has a sister, she receives half of what he left; and he inherits from her if she has no child" (al-Nisa 176). The Almighty thereby made plain that this ruling applies to the sister alone — not when others share the estate alongside her.

The Master also said: ﴿وَإِن كَانَ رَجُلٌ يُورَثُ كَلَالَةً أَوِ امْرَأَةٌ وَلَهُ أَخٌ أَوْ أُخْتٌ فَلِكُلِّ وَاحِدٍ مِّنْهُمَا السُّدُسُ فَإِن كَانُوا أَكْثَرَ مِن ذَٰلِكَ فَهُمْ شُرَكَاءُ فِي الثُّلُثِ﴾ "If a man dies leaving no children, and he has a brother or a sister, each of them receives one sixth; but if there are more than that, they are partners in one third" (al-Nisa 12). Those scholars themselves hold that the brother for whom God named the whole share, were he to stand in the sister's place, would receive only one sixth. In that case, therefore, the husband receives one half, the maternal brothers receive one third, and the paternal sister receives one sixth.

Likewise, if a woman leaves a husband, two parents, and a daughter, the husband receives a quarter, the two parents receive two sixths, and whatever remains goes to the daughter — for were she a son, she would receive no more than this. The deficiency falls upon the one to whom the surplus belongs. All the questions of *ʿawl* proceed on this basis. As for those questions that mention brothers and sisters alongside the mother, it has already been established that they inherit nothing in her presence; any questions of *ʿawl* reported in such cases rest on that meaning. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them all.

### On the inheritance of the son repudiated by lian, the child of adultery, the foundling, the captive of unknown kin, the fetus, the Muslim, the disbeliever, the Magian, the apostate, and the bondservant

The *liʿān* and its procedure have been discussed earlier, along with the ruling that when a man disavows a child his wife has borne and carries out the *liʿān* against her on that account, the child is no longer attributed to him. The child's lineage runs through his mother, and his inheritance belongs to her kindred. The man who disavowed him does not inherit from him, nor does anyone inherit through that man — unless he acknowledged the child after the *liʿān*. For it has been established that if a man carries out the *liʿān* against a child and then subsequently acknowledges him, the child inherits from him; however, the one who carried out the *liʿān* against the child's mother does not inherit from the child, nor does anyone inherit through that man. Rather, the child inherits, and those who are close to him through his own kinship inherit alongside him.

The child of adultery is not joined to the adulterer who lay with his mother and fathered him. He is not attributed to that man, and neither inherits from the other, whether the man acknowledges him or denies him. His mother inherits from him and he from her; kinship flows through her in both directions. No kinship flows through his father — he draws near to no one through his father, and no one draws near to him by that path. As for the foundling who has neither known mother nor known father, he neither inherits nor is inherited from, and no one draws near to him through parents.

The captive of unknown kin is a person taken from the land of disbelief while another is taken alongside him — or before him, or after him. The two come to recognize each other in the abode of Islam and affirm their kinship. They continue in that affirmation for the remainder of their lives, until one of them dies. The survivor then inherits from the deceased by virtue of the kinship they affirmed while both were living; they inherit from one another and stand in relation to one another through that kinship.

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, is reported to have said, "The people of two different faiths do not inherit from one another." On this basis, no two people of differing faiths inherit from each other. Mutual inheritance, by its nature, means that each party inherits from the other. In Arabic, this form is reciprocal, and reciprocal action in the speech of the Arabs requires two agents, even though the simple act may proceed from one. One says that two men struck one another when each struck his companion, and that a man struck another when only one struck the other.

Accordingly, the Jew does not inherit from the Christian, nor the Christian from the Jew; and the Christian, the Jew, and the Magian do not inherit from the Muslim. The Muslim, however, does inherit from them by virtue of kinship — as has come down from the Imams, may the prayers of Allah be upon them — and the disbelief of the non-Muslim relative does not bar the Muslim from that inheritance. The narration supporting this is sound: the polytheists do not inherit from the Muslims, while the Muslims do inherit from them. The two directions are not equal.

Among themselves, the people of each faith inherit according to the fixed shares their own religion prescribes, and that is what is adjudicated between them. If they bring an inheritance dispute before the Muslim authorities, it is judged in accordance with what their own religion and faith prescribe. If they do not raise the matter to the Muslim authorities, they are left to themselves and not interfered with.

A bondservant does not inherit from a free person, nor does a free person inherit from a bondservant through kinship; the bondservant's wealth belongs to his master. If a person embraces Islam after disbelief, or is freed from bondage, before the one from whom he would inherit has died and before the estate has been divided, he receives his share. If he is freed after the division, he receives nothing. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them all.

### On the inheritance of the killer, the blood money, the intersexed person, those who drown together, the freed bondservant and his patron, the divorced woman, and the one who has no heir

Further questions concern the fixed shares and the matter of one heir acknowledging another. Whoever kills another person — whether deliberately or by mistake — does not inherit from him, nor from his descendants, even if he would otherwise have been entitled to that inheritance. As for the parents, if they did not cause the death, they inherit from him according to the shares Allah, mighty and majestic, has fixed. A man inherits from his wife's blood money, and a woman inherits from her husband's blood money — with the exception of brothers through the mother, who take nothing from the blood money.

The intersexed person is one who possesses both a male organ and a female organ. Such a person inherits and is inherited from, marries and is given in marriage, and is judged according to the passage of urine. If urine passes from the male organ, the person is a man: the rulings governing men apply to him, he marries women, no man may marry him, and he inherits and is inherited from according to a man's share. If urine passes from the female organ, the rulings governing women apply: she follows the course of women in all things and the course of men in nothing. If urine passes from both organs, one looks to which it passes from first. If it precedes from the male organ, the ruling is that of men; if it precedes from the female organ, the ruling is that of women. If it passes from both at once, or if the person has neither organ, the matter is uncertain, and the judge determines it by lot. He writes on one card "the servant of Allah" and on another "the handmaid of Allah," sets each card inside a pellet of clay, turns them about in his hand, and says, "O Allah, You know best this naming and how You created it; so bring forth the lot."

The lot is then drawn. The one casting it holds the piece in his hand and says: "O Allah, You know best about this person and how You created them, so bring out the arrow for the one You have made heir among them and the one You have appointed as ruler over the rulings." He then draws one of the two clay pieces, neither of which has been seen, and the contents of neither are known. Whatever emerges determines the ruling that is applied.

After this, the urine is examined. The person is made to stand facing a wall with both hands extended and is directed to step back from it as far as possible. If the urine reaches the wall, it is known to have issued from the male organ; if it runs down between the legs, it is known to have issued from the female organ. Neither men nor women look upon the person beforehand, so that no prior judgment is formed about what the person is before the test has been completed.

When a group of people perish together — drowned in a shipwreck, buried under a collapsed building, consumed by fire, or killed together in battle — and it cannot be determined which of them died before his companion, while they stood in a relationship of kinship to one another, each of them inherits from the other according to what he would have inherited, and the other inherits from him in turn according to his own portion. They inherit from one another whatever each has left behind.

An illustration of this is two brothers who die together in such a manner, one the freed client (mawla) of one people and the other the freed client of another, having no heir besides their respective patrons. One leaves a thousand dinars, the other a hundred. The owner of the hundred is treated as though he had remained alive and his brother had died before him, and his share of the thousand is taken accordingly; the owner of the thousand is treated in the same way, and his share of the hundred is taken on that basis. The result is that the patron of the one who left the thousand receives a hundred, and the patron of the one who left the hundred receives a thousand. In this manner the like of it proceeds: each patron inherits from his deceased client, is himself then inherited from in turn, and thereafter the heirs of each inherit from him.

As for a man who pronounces an irrevocable divorce upon his wife — one that leaves him no right of return — there is no inheritance between them. The one exception is a man who divorces his wife while he is ill: she inherits from him for as long as that same illness persists, unless he recovers or she remarries. Should he regain his health, or should she take another husband, her right to inherit from him is extinguished. As for a man who divorces his wife with a revocable divorce — one in which he retains the right of return — each inherits from the other, provided her waiting period has not yet expired.

Whoever dies leaving no heir other than the patrons (*mawali*) who freed him — or those who became patrons through their agency — his inheritance belongs to those patrons. If he has a blood relative, however, the inheritance passes to that relative by right of kinship, not by right of patronage.

The bond of patronage (*al-wala*) is inherited by men and women alike. Its closeness is established through the father who freed the slave, just as kinship among men is generally established through the father. Whoever stands nearer in the degree of patronage has the stronger claim over one who stands more remote — the same principle already noted regarding the one who frees a slave.

The application runs as follows. A man frees a slave, and that freed man later dies leaving two sons. One of those sons dies, leaving a son of his own. The patron then dies with no close relative surviving him. His inheritance passes to the son of his patron's son — who stands one degree nearer — rather than to the more remote son still living. The rule of inheritance by kinship follows the same logic.

Whoever leaves no heir at the level of an inheritor except a slave he himself had freed is inherited by that freed slave, just as he would have inherited from the freed slave had their positions been reversed. If, however, he leaves both a slave he had freed and a patron who had freed him, his inheritance goes to the patron who freed him rather than to the slave whom he freed.

When some heirs acknowledge a claimant whom the remaining heirs deny, and no attested proof establishes his standing, the one who is nearer inherits according to what he would have inherited. Those who acknowledge the claimant hand over to him whatever remains in excess of their own shares — that is, of what has come to them — while those who do not acknowledge him owe him nothing, and their own inheritance remains complete.

An illustration is a man who dies leaving two sons. One of them acknowledges a third brother; the other denies him. The son who denies inherits one half from his father. The son who acknowledges inherits one third, and pays over one sixth to the one he has acknowledged, corresponding to what that one would have inherited had all three brothers shared the estate in equal thirds.

The shroud of the deceased is drawn from the principal of the estate — from whatever he has left — before any division takes place. His debts, if any lie against him, are settled in the same way. A bequest, if he made one, is taken from a third of the estate or less; beyond that limit it cannot be carried out without the consent of the heirs, unless they choose to discharge it in full. Whatever remains is then divided according to the ordained obligations of inheritance.

As for the mukatab — the slave bound by a written contract of manumission (kitabah) — and the one of whom only a part has been set free: such persons inherit and are inherited from in proportion to the degree of freedom they have attained, as has already been established. The ruling on the validity of the kitabah, and how the intention of manumission takes effect, has been set out in the chapter on the mukatab. Whoever has no known heir, his estate passes to the treasury of the Muslims.

If some of the heirs acknowledge a debt, each one who does so is bound to pay it from his own share of the inheritance, in proportion to what he has acknowledged. If he bears witness to it, being a man of upright standing, his testimony is admitted on behalf of all the heirs. If a man acknowledges a child borne by his slave-woman and his wife, and afterward disowns that child, the disavowal is not permitted: the child remains his son. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt, may.

God's peace be upon him and his family, said: "There is no execution except by the sword" (لَا قَوَدَ إِلَّا بِحَدِيدَةٍ). The condemned is to be struck upon the neck with the sword; he is neither to be tortured nor to be mutilated.

When the heirs of a slain man are of differing condition — some present and some absent, some grown and some still children — the right of retribution belongs to those who have reached maturity. The killer is not held back until the young ones come of age, nor until the absent return. It was on this basis that al-Hasan ibn Ali, peace be upon him, put to death the enemy of Allah, Ibn Muljam — may Allah curse him — the man who struck Ali, peace be upon him, even though Ali's own children had not yet reached puberty.

As for one who is slain, whether by an iron weapon or by any other means: if the killer intended his victim's death and struck him deliberately with whatever he used, and the victim died from that blow, the guardians of the slain may demand retaliation. Retaliation, however, is carried out by no means other than the sword, for the Messenger of Allah, may God's peace and blessings be upon him and his family, said: "There is no execution except by the sword" (لَا قَوَدَ إِلَّا بِحَدِيدَةٍ). The condemned is to be struck upon the neck with the sword; he is neither to be tortured nor to be mutilated.

The accused may be questioned and his confession drawn out by gentle means, but not by beating. A confession extracted under compulsion carries no legal force and does not bind him. If, however, two upright witnesses testify that he committed the killing, or if he confesses freely and of his own will, the killing is established against him. The testimony of women is not admitted in cases of bloodshed, nor in any of the prescribed punishments (hudud) or in retaliation (qisas), though it is admitted in matters where wealth is owed.

When a single man is slain by two people, or by a group who acted together against him — each of them striking him until he died from their combined blows — the guardians of the slain may single out one of those killers and put him to death for their kinsman, for Allah Almighty has said: *"A soul for a soul"* (النَّفْسَ بِالنَّفْسِ). They may not put more than one man to death in return for one. They then turn to the remaining killers and take from each of them blood money proportionate to his share:

- If there were three killers and one was executed, his guardians take two-thirds of the blood money from the remaining two.
- If there were two killers and one was executed, his guardians take half the blood money from the other.
- If there were more than three, the shares are reckoned accordingly.

In every such case, those who were not executed are further subjected to a disciplinary punishment.

If one man restrains another while a third kills him, the killer is put to death and the one who held the victim is imprisoned until he dies, having first been flogged. If a man kills his own slave, he receives a severe punishment. If the victim's guardians pardon the killer, no further claim lies against him, and whoever kills him after that pardon is himself put to death in retaliation. Likewise, if the guardians accept blood money, they are entitled to nothing beyond it, for Allah Almighty has said: *"And whoever transgresses after that, for him is a painful punishment"* (فَمَنِ اعْتَدَى بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ فَلَهُ عَذَابٌ أَلِيمٌ).

Every wound for which retaliation can be carried out without risk of excess and without harm to the one from whom it is taken — such as the surface wound (al-mudihah) and what lies below it — is subject to retaliation. The wound is measured along its length upon the skin, a mark is set, and the one taking retaliation cuts at the corresponding place to the same length and to the same depth in the flesh.

Retaliation likewise extends to a tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye, a nose for a nose, an ear for an ear, and to whatever portion of these has been severed — in accordance with the word of Allah Almighty: *"And the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth, and for wounds is retaliation"* (وَالْعَيْنَ بِالْعَيْنِ وَالْأَنْفَ بِالْأَنْفِ وَالْأُذُنَ بِالْأُذُنِ وَالسِّنَّ بِالسِّنِّ وَالْجُرُوحَ قِصَاصٌ). This applies when the act was deliberate. Where the wound was inflicted in error, however, or where its nature is such that retaliation would risk further harm to the offender, or where the wound has dried and healed, or where a bone has been broken, or where the injury is graver than the surface wound — in all such cases blood money is owed, and its rules will be set out in their proper place. One who inflicts such wounds deliberately is also subject to punishment, so that a man of means does not find it a simple matter to wound and merely pay the blood money in discharge.

In wounds, retaliation is taken from a woman for a man and from a man for a woman in respect of the surface wound and what lies below it. As for retaliation in the eye: the eye not subject to retaliation is bound, an iron or a mirror is heated and brought close to the eye from which retaliation is to be taken, and that eye is held open until it flows. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them all.

### On Blood Money and Its Categories

The blood money for a free Muslim man — whether young or old — is one thousand dinars, owed by those who deal in gold, or its equivalent value from people whose wealth takes another form. They are not compelled to sell their possessions in order to pay in gold; rather, the equivalent of one thousand dinars is taken from them in the currency of their land:

- from the people of silver: the value of one thousand dinars in silver
- from the people of camels: one hundred camels
- from the people of cattle: two hundred cows
- from the people of sheep: one thousand sheep
- from the people of cloth: two hundred garments of like value

This is how the Sunnah has run, and this is the blood money for the soul.

Blood money is owed only in cases of error — that is, where the killer did not intend the death of the one he killed, as when he meant to strike another and hit this man instead. If, however, he acted deliberately with whatever he used, that is intentional killing, and he is subject to retaliation, unless the guardians of the slain accept blood money from him or pardon him altogether. The one who killed in error must, after paying the blood money, expiate his act by freeing a believing slave; if he cannot find one, then by fasting two consecutive months; and if he is unable to do that, then by feeding sixty poor persons.

The blood money is borne by the aqila — the heirs who would inherit from the offender were he to die — with the exception of his maternal aunts, who neither carry this responsibility nor receive any share of the blood money. The deliberate acts of children and of the insane are treated as error, and their blood money likewise falls upon the aqila; yet nothing is laid upon those among the aqila who are poor, nor upon anyone who possesses nothing. The aqila is not bound except where liability is established through clear evidence. Where a person of good standing confesses and acts upon that confession, or where the matter concerns a slave, the aqila bears nothing. Nor does the aqila bear unintentional offenses unless the amount reaches one third of the full blood money or more; whatever falls below that third is paid from the offender's own wealth. As for the people of the dhimma, whatever they incur comes from their own wealth, and their aqila bears none of it. Whoever offends alone bears the consequence alone.

Whoever strikes a pregnant woman so that she expels the seed after it has settled in the womb owes twenty dinars. If she expels a clot — that is, the blood (عَلَقَة) — the liability is forty dinars. For the morsel of flesh (مُضْغَة), once it has taken on the form of flesh, the amount is sixty dinars. If bone has formed within it, eighty dinars are due. If she expels a fully formed child before the spirit has been breathed into it, the liability is one hundred dinars; and once the spirit has been breathed into it, the full blood money is due.

Whoever offends against one already dead — severing his head, or doing to him what would have killed him had he been alive — owes one hundred dinars. For any wound or injury done to him, the offender owes the proportionate share of his blood money. That sum is spent on his behalf in works of piety; the Hajj is performed for him if he had not yet performed it; and his heirs inherit none of it.

Offenses against beasts are reckoned by their value. Whoever kills a beast is fined its worth. Whoever wounds it or breaks one of its limbs owes the amount by which its value has diminished. If a beast breaks loose and causes harm, that harm is without redress — and likewise if one enters upon it in its own place. But if its owners loose it, or station it where they have no right to do so, they are answerable for whatever harm it causes.

When a thief seeks a man's wealth and fights him, and the man so threatened kills the thief, the thief's blood is forfeit. Whoever is slain in defense of his wealth dies a martyr; and if he yields his wealth without fighting for it, no blame rests upon him. Whoever seeks to overcome a woman against her will, and she repels him and kills or wounds him in doing so, whatever she inflicts is without redress. Whoever dies under a prescribed punishment (*hadd*) or under lawful retaliation, no claim arises on his behalf. Whoever peers into the private quarters of a people and they put out his eye, his claim is forfeit.

The Messenger of Allah ruled by al-Qasamah, which applies when a man is killed and his killer is unknown. If, before he dies, the slain man says, "So-and-so killed me," or if his guardians come forward bearing a mark of accusation against the one they charge with his death — declaring, "He killed him" — then fifty men among them swear oaths that he killed him, and the accused is handed over to them. If they do not number fifty, those present repeat their oaths until fifty oaths are completed. If they prefer, they may have the accused swear oaths instead. And if the accused bring proof of their innocence, it is accepted from them.

When a slain man is found in a village and it is not known who killed him, and its people are the people of that one village with no others mixing among them, they swear that they did not kill him and do not know his killer, and they are then made to pay his blood money. If he is found between two villages, the responsibility falls upon whichever of them is nearer to the place where he lay. But if the place where he was struck down is a great city, or a village in which all manner of people mix, or a road along which travelers pass between villages, then the burden of proof falls upon whoever is accused — provided no mark of accusation is found against them — and al-Qasamah is established.

If two horsemen ride toward each other and collide, and one of them dies, half the blood money is due — for his death resulted from his own action combined with that of his companion. If only one of them was moving while the other stood still or walked, and the one who charged was killed, nothing is owed by the one who stood still. But if the one who was struck died, the full blood money falls upon the one who charged, provided he did not intend it; if he did intend it, retaliation is due from him.

A physician or veterinarian is answerable for harm caused by ignorance of their craft; and if they were knowledgeable yet intended harm, they are answerable on that ground as well. A circumciser is answerable for whatever flesh he cuts beyond the proper place of cutting, and a woman who performs the equivalent procedure on girls is held to the same standard when she exceeds the proper limit. Whoever digs a well or pit in a public road, or places an obstruction in it, is answerable for whatever harm results; but if the road lies within his own property, nothing is owed.

A rider is answerable for whatever his mount strikes with its foreleg or chest, but not for what it strikes with its hind leg, since that is beyond his control. When a wall begins to lean and its owner is made aware of it — whether he discovers this himself or is informed — yet he neither rights it nor pulls it down, and it falls, he is answerable for whatever damage it causes. When a man hires a laborer who then dies in the course of his work, nothing is owed on account of that death. When a dog is kept within someone's dwelling or within their property, and a person enters without their permission and is bitten, nothing falls upon them; but if they granted him leave to enter, they are answerable.

When a woman severs a man's organ, or a man severs a woman's part, there is no retaliation between them, for the offense has no true like that can be taken from the offender. Instead, the full blood money falls upon him, and if he acted deliberately, he is severely punished. When a man forces himself upon a woman who is not fit to be approached in that way, or uses violence against her and tears her — leaving her unable to bear children, or causing her to lose control of her water or her bowels, or killing her outright — the full blood money is upon him in every one of these cases. Whoever is found dead bearing no mark of injury, and it is not known that anyone killed him, nothing is owed on his account beyond the oath of the one accused of the killing. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt, may the prayers of Allah be upon them.

### On Offenses Against the Limbs and Wounds of the Head

It has been established that retaliation is taken for a deliberate act in every case where it can be reached exactly, where excess in its execution is guarded against, and where no harm to the offender is feared in the taking of it. Where true retaliation cannot be achieved, however, or where the safety of the offender cannot be assured, the blood money falls upon the offender if the act was deliberate, and upon the *aqila* if it was done in error.

For every part of the body of which a person has only one, the full blood money is owed. For every part of which there are two, half the blood money is owed for each.

For the hair of the head — if it is plucked, falls out as a result of injury, or is burned and does not grow back — the full blood money is owed. The same applies to the skin of the head if it is flayed. If the forehead is struck and the bone is reset, one hundred dinars are owed. If the nose or the tongue is severed, or an offense is committed against the beard such that it does not grow back, the full blood money is owed in each of these cases.

For each of the following, half the blood money is owed individually, and the full blood money when both are taken together:

- the eyebrow
- the eye
- the ear
- the hand
- the foot
- one of the two organs of generation

For the eye of a one-eyed man, the full blood money is owed. For hearing, if it is lost entirely, the full blood money is owed. For speech, if it is lost entirely, the full blood money is owed. For sight, the full blood money is owed even when the pupils themselves remain intact.

For any partial diminishment of these faculties or members, the compensation is reckoned in proportion to what has been lost.

When a man strikes another and causes a partial loss of sight in one eye, the following procedure determines the compensation owed. The sound eye is covered and the injured eye left open. An egg is emptied of its contents and hung by a hair. The injured man is asked to look at it, and it is drawn away from him until he says he can no longer see the hair. That point is marked. The measurement is then taken — without the injured man knowing what is being measured — and repeated from four directions. If all four measurements agree, his truthfulness is established.

The process is then reversed: the injured eye is covered and the sound eye left open, and the same procedure is carried out again from four directions. If that account agrees as well, the matter is settled. If it does not, he is told:

"You have lied; return to the truth."

If his account holds consistent across all four directions for both eyes, the examiner compares what the injured eye has lost against what the sound eye sees. The blood money is awarded in proportion to that loss:

- If the injured eye has lost half its sight, half the blood money is due.
- If it has lost a third, a third is due.
- Whatever fraction has been lost — whether greater or smaller — the compensation is reckoned accordingly.

Where the loss of sight affects both eyes together, the injured man is measured against the sight of an upright man of middling vision — then against two such men, then three. When they agree, or come near to agreement, his own sight is tested against that standard from all four directions, as already described. When the measurements are consistent and his truthfulness is established, he receives blood money in proportion to what has been lost, as set out above.

Where the loss is in hearing, the same procedure applies: a dirham is struck near him until he says, "I do not hear it," and he is then measured by the same method described for the eyes — whether the injury is to one ear or to both.

Where the loss is in the sense of smell, something bearing a scent is brought close and then drawn away by the same reckoning used for sight and hearing, and he is compensated according to his share of the loss.

Where the loss is in speech, what has fallen away is measured against the full count of the letters.

Speech injuries are assessed against the full Arabic alphabet, which numbers twenty-eight letters; blood money is owed in proportion to the letters lost. For the lips, half the blood money is due for the upper lip and two-thirds for the lower — that is, a half and a sixth — reckoned by its role in eating and in the softness of speech.

For the teeth, the assessment divides by position:

- **Front teeth** — four incisors, four lateral incisors, and four canines — each carries fifty dinars.
- **Back teeth** — the molars — each carries twenty-five dinars, and together they complete the full blood money.

The molars number four in each jaw, four above and four below, making up the complete count of teeth as natural creation intends. Some people have five molars in each jaw, the fifth being superfluous. Blood money is apportioned according to the perfect original count, and whatever is lost — superfluous or not — carries twenty-five dinars per tooth.

If part of a tooth is broken, blood money is owed in proportion to the portion broken. If a tooth turns black, its full blood money is due, for it has been ruined.

For a child's tooth knocked out before its natural time to fall: ten dinars are owed for an incisor and five for a molar, provided it grows back afterward. If it does not grow back, the full blood money for that tooth is due.

For the shoulder, the upper arm, and the elbow: if any one of them is broken or dislocated and then heals without defect, one hundred dinars are owed for each. For the forearm and the wrist, one-third of the blood money applies to each. For every finger of the hands and the feet, one hundred dinars. For the shoulder blade, forty dinars. For the ribs joined to the chest, twenty-five dinars per rib; for the ribs not joined to it and not meeting the breastbone, ten dinars per rib. For the hip, the thigh, and the knee, one-fifth of the blood money for each. For the *jaifa* — a blow that penetrates into the inner cavity of the body — one-third of the blood money is due. For a blow to the face that leaves it red without drawing blood and without turning black or green, two and a half dinars; if it turns black or green, three dinars. If the blow falls around the eye and turns it green, three dinars are owed; if it turns black, six dinars.

For the *damiya* — the wound from which blood flows — ten dinars are owed. For the *faqira*, which breaks the skin and reaches the flesh without cutting into it, twelve dinars. For the *badia*, which cuts the skin and enters the flesh, severing part of it, twenty dinars. For the *mutalahima*, which cuts deep into the flesh, thirty dinars. For the *mishaq* — also called the *miltat* — which cuts through the skin and all the flesh down to the membrane over the bone without cutting that membrane, forty dinars. For the *mudiha*, which cuts through all of that and lays the bone bare, fifty dinars. For the *hashima*, which does all of that and breaks the bone, one hundred dinars. For the *munaqqila*, which breaks the bone and draws out a fragment of it, one hundred and fifty dinars. For the *mamuma*, in which the membrane of the brain becomes visible and is reached without any injury beyond it, one-third of the blood money is due.

All of this applies to wounds of the head and face. For wounds to the rest of the body, half these amounts apply. Where a limb is injured — the fingers and the like — blood money is owed in proportion to that limb's share of the full blood money, as already set out. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt, may.

### On the Establishment of the Hudud

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: "And whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has wronged himself." (Surah al-Talaq, 65:1)

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, forbade the neglect of the prescribed limits. He said: "The Children of Israel perished only because, when a man of noble standing among them committed an offense that incurred a limit, they would not carry it out against him, but when a lowly man committed it, they would establish it upon him."

A woman of Quraysh stole a garment during the time of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, and he ordered her hand to be cut off. A group of Quraysh came to him and said: "O Messenger of Allah, she is a woman of ours who holds honor among her people, and what she has stolen is a trifle."

The Messenger of Allah said: "It was by the like of this that those before you were destroyed: they would establish the limit upon their weak and leave their strong and their nobles, and so they perished."

The Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family, also forbade intercession in the prescribed limits, declaring: "Whoever intercedes to nullify one of the limits of Allah has been insolent toward Allah and has striven to undo His limits; and whoever is insolent toward Allah and strives to undo His limits, Allah, Mighty and Majestic, will punish him on the Day of Resurrection." Safwan ibn Umayyah brought before the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, a man who had stolen a cloak of his, and the Messenger of Allah ordered the man's hand to be cut off. Safwan said: "O Messenger of Allah, is his hand to be cut off for the sake of a cloak? I have given it to him." The Messenger of Allah replied: "Why was that not before you brought him to me? Once the limit has been raised to the ruler, it is not fitting for him to leave it unenforced." And he gave the order, and the hand was cut off.

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ

It is related from him, may Allah bless him and his family, that he said: "The back of the believer is inviolable, except for a limit that is due." He forbade anyone from exceeding one of the limits of Allah, whether by falling short or by going beyond what has been prescribed, and he said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has made the limits clear, so whoever transgresses them has wronged himself, as He, exalted be His remembrance, has said." And he set a limit upon whoever transgresses a limit. He, may Allah bless him and his family, said: "The most hateful of creation to Allah is one who bares the back of a Muslim without right." He forbade the carrying out of prescribed limits inside the mosques. It is also related from him that he said: "Whoever commits a sin and is punished for it in this world — Allah is more just than to repeat that punishment upon His servant in the Hereafter; and whoever commits a sin and Allah conceals it for him in this world — He is more generous than to return to something He has already pardoned and concealed."

Ali, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, wrote to Rifaa ibn Shaddad, his judge over al-Ahwaz, a letter in which he said: "Establish the limits upon the near, that the distant may shun them; do not let blood be shed in vain, and do not let the limits be neglected."

When Uthman was brought al-Waleed ibn Utbah, and witnesses testified against him, and the offense he had committed against the Muslims was made plain, the Muslims declared that the limits of Allah had been neglected. Al-Waleed was placed in a room at the side of the house, and it was announced: "Let whoever holds that the limit is due upon him rise and carry it out." Yet whenever a man came in to flog him, al-Waleed would say: "I adjure you by Allah not to sever my kinship, and not to expose me before the Commander of the Faithful" — and the man would turn back from him.

When Ali, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, saw that a limit from among the limits of Allah was being neglected, he took up the whip and went in to him. Al-Waleed said the like to him. Al-Husayn ibn Ali, may both be blessed, followed him in and said: "O my father, what is between you and him? Leave him be; you see what the people have made of his case." But Ali, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, pressed against the chest of al-Husayn (ع) and spoke sharply to him, so that he withdrew. Then Ali took the whip and flogged al-Waleed until the limit was carried out in full.

It is related from him that he said: "Three things, if you do them, no affliction will descend upon you: that you wage struggle against your enemy; that you raise your limits to your imams and let them judge in them with justice; and that you submit to their command."

Umar said to him: "Counsel me, O Abu al-Hasan."

He said: "I counsel you to judge by the Book of Allah in contentment and in anger, to apportion with justice between the red and the black, and to establish the limits upon the distant and the near alike."

Umar said to him: "You have been brief and you have reached the heart of it."

Every Friday, Ali — may the blessings of Allah be upon him — reviewed the prisons, and whenever a prescribed punishment was found to be due against anyone, he carried it out without delay. On one occasion, three men came before him to testify against a man for adultery. He asked: "Where is the fourth?" The fourth witness was absent. They replied: "We will bring him shortly, O Commander of the Faithful." He said: "There is no waiting even an hour in the prescribed limits" — and he flogged the three for false accusation.

A delegation came to him and said: "O Commander of the Faithful, we have come to ask you for something." He said: "Ask me for nothing that I possess but that I will give it to you." They had come on behalf of a man of the Banu Asad against whom a prescribed punishment was due, and they said: "Grant us so-and-so." He brought the man out and carried out the punishment. They said: "Did you not promise us, O Commander of the Faithful, to release him?" He said: "I promised you what I possess; but this belongs to Allah, and I do not possess it."

He once ordered his servant Qanbar to flog a man the prescribed number of lashes. Qanbar, carried away by anger, gave three lashes more than the limit. When this was brought to Ali's attention, he granted the man retaliation against Qanbar and had Qanbar flogged three lashes in return.

He also wrote to Rifaa: "Shield the believer as much as you are able, for his back is a sanctuary of Allah, his soul is honored before Allah, and to him belongs the reward of Allah."

It is related from him that he said, concerning a people who had held out in enemy territory and asked for a covenant exempting them from accountability for what had passed: "Do not grant a covenant that would set aside one of the limits of Allah. How can the limits be lifted from those to whom they apply, when it is the friends of Allah and those who strive in His path who go forth to establish them?"

It is related from Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, that he said: "Pardon nothing of the limits that belong to Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Whoever comes to know of one of them has no fitting course but to raise it to the Imam. As for the rights of people that fall within the limits, there is no harm in pardoning those before the matter reaches the ruler — as with the thief before he is brought before the Imam — but pardon is not permissible once the matter has reached him. And whoever pardons a limit that is his own right, then later wishes to enforce it, has no standing to do so."

It is related from Jafar ibn Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, that he said: "Whoever seizes a thief and pardons him, there is no harm in it. But once the thief has been raised to the Sultan, his hand is to be cut off."

If the one from whom the theft was made says he pardons the thief, the prescribed penalty is not averted, for pardon would have been effective only before the matter was raised to the ruler. Once it has been raised, the limit is not set aside — by the word of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: *and those who keep the limits of Allah.* Once the limit has been raised to the Imam, no one has the standing to abandon it.

### On the Hadd Punishment for Zina

Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: "And do not approach adultery; indeed it is an indecency and an evil way." (Surah al-Isra, 17:32) And He said: "And those who do not call upon another god alongside Allah, nor kill the soul that Allah has forbidden except in truth, nor commit adultery; and whoever does that will meet a penalty. The punishment will be multiplied for him on the Day of Resurrection, and he will abide in it humiliated, except for whoever repents." (Surah al-Furqan, 25:68–70)

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family, said: "The wrath of Allah grows severe against a woman who brings into a people one who is not of them, so that he gazes upon what is sacred to them and treads upon their beds. And the most severely punished of people on the Day of Resurrection is the one who plants his seed in a womb forbidden to him."

He, may Allah bless him and his family, also said: "The adulterer will stand on the Day of Resurrection above the people of the Fire, and a drop will fall from his private part by which the people of Hell will be tormented, and they will say to the keepers, What is this foul stench? and it will be said to them, This is the smell of an adulterer. And an adulteress will be brought, and a drop will fall from her, and the people of the Fire will be tormented by her stench."

He, may Allah bless him and his family, said: "There is no sin greater before Allah, Mighty and Majestic, after associating partners with Him, than unlawful seed that a man places in a womb not lawful to him."

And he said: "Adultery and goodness do not gather in a single house."

He also delivered a sermon, may Allah bless him and his family, in which he said: "Three whom Allah will not speak to on the Day of Resurrection, nor purify, and for whom there is a painful punishment: an adulterous old man, a tyrant king, and a proud pauper."

And he said: "The adulterer does not commit adultery while he is a believer."

Jafar ibn Muhammad, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, said: "When he lies upon her belly, the spirit of faith departs from him; and when he rises and seeks the forgiveness of Allah, it returns to him."

Adultery is the placing of the private part in one who is neither a spouse nor lawfully possessed by a man's right hand. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has said: "And those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or those whom their right hands possess, for then they are not to be blamed; but whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors." (Surah al-Muminun, 23:5–7)

When an adulterer is found, the legal proof against him may be established in one of three ways:

- Four men of just standing testify that they witnessed him commit adultery with a woman — having seen the organ enter her private part — while he held a lawful wife with whom he had consummated marriage and the woman held a lawful husband.
- Both the man and the woman confess.
- One of them confesses and witness testimony is established against the other.

In any of these cases, each party — whether the one who confessed or the one against whom proof was given — receives one hundred lashes. They are then brought out, and a pit is dug for each to the depth of the navel; each is placed upright within it and packed in. Where the matter rested on confession, the judge before whom the confession was made begins the stoning and then directs the people to continue, using stones of moderate size — such as fill the palm or less — until death. The condemned are then brought out, washed, prayed over, and buried.

The confession of an adulterer is not established unless it is made on four separate occasions, while the person is of sound mind, willing, and free from coercion. Where the matter rests on the testimony of witnesses, the witnesses cast the first stones, then the judge, then the people.

A man is not counted as protected until he has consummated marriage with his wife and she is in his keeping; a bondwoman does not render a free man protected, nor does a bondman render a free woman protected. If one party is protected and the other is not, the protected one is stoned after being flogged, and the unprotected one receives a hundred lashes.

The floggings are ranked by severity:

1. The flogging of the adulterer
2. The flogging of the false accuser
3. The flogging of the drinker
4. The flogging of discretionary punishment

A pregnant woman is not flogged until she has delivered and is purified of her postnatal bleeding. No limit falls upon a child, whether boy or girl; yet if an adult commits this sin with a child, the limit is established upon the adult.

When a single child is claimed by more than one man, the elder of the claimants takes precedence, and whoever withheld the child from one of them bears the responsibility for what was done. As for the act of the people of Lot, the one who performs the act upon another is stoned just as two who commit adultery are stoned. If the act is intercrural, the hadd falls due upon both parties. For the act committed between women, each receives a hundred lashes.

Whoever commits adultery with a relative whom it is unlawful for him to marry is put to death, and she too is put to death if she consented, provided neither of them is bound by marriage. If both are married, the hadd is applied and they are stoned. Whoever forces a woman against her will is put to death if he is unmarried, and is flogged the hadd and stoned if he is married. No hadd falls upon the coerced woman, and if he has taken her virginity she is owed a dowry equal to that of her peers. If she is a slave girl, she is owed a tenth of her price; if she is a non-virgin, half a tenth of her price.

No hadd falls upon one who has lost his reason, nor upon one who enters an unlawful union that nevertheless bears the outward form of a marriage — such as a man who marries a woman during her waiting period, or upon a contract that does not meet the requirements of a valid marriage. If two men are found together under a single cover, or a man and a woman in like circumstance, the hadd is applied. If two women are found together in like manner, they are flogged with a punishment short of the hadd of stoning. If a slave or a slave girl commits adultery, each receives fifty lashes, whether or not they are married.

When the adulterer is brought forward to be flogged, the believers are commanded to attend the punishment as witnesses, as Allah Almighty says:

> ﴿وَلْيَشْهَدْ عَذَابَهُمَا طَائِفَةٌ مِّنَ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ﴾
>
> "And let a group of the believers witness their punishment." (al-Nur 2)

The adulterer is flogged in the condition in which he is found. If he is naked, he remains naked; if he is clothed, he remains clothed and is struck through his garments. Anything that would shield him from the effect of the blows — a thick fur or the like — is removed. The woman is seated and kept covered, and every limb is struck except the face, the private parts, and the vital organs. If striking the back alone is the practice, that is permissible, and it is what is customarily done. The blows must not be of a severity that kills. Neither a woman in her post-natal bleeding nor a menstruating woman is flogged until she has been purified.

If the adulterer and the adulteress confess and then retract, they are left alone until they have confessed four times; a retraction made after that is not accepted. Whoever commits adultery with his wife's mother is subject to the hadd. If a man has intercourse with a slave woman in whom he holds a partial share, he is flogged in proportion to the share that is not his, and the hadd is averted from him in proportion to his own share. Likewise, if she is his slave woman who has contracted to purchase her freedom, he is struck in proportion to the part of her that has been freed, and the hadd is averted from him in proportion to the part still owned.

A man who imitates women in his manner is disciplined; if he persists, he is banished from inhabited dwellings. Whoever commits an act with an animal is punished, and the price of the animal is paid to its owner. If the animal is of a kind that is eaten, it is slaughtered and buried, and eating it is not lawful. If it is not of a kind that is eaten, it is sold and removed to a place where it will not be recognized, and the one who committed the act is publicly reproached.

A slave under a contract of manumission is flogged with the hadd of a free man in proportion to the part of him that has been freed, and with the hadd of a slave in proportion to the part still in bondage. All of this is the unanimous teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt, may.

### The Hadd Punishment for Slander

Allah Almighty said:

> ﴿إِنَّ الَّذِينَ يَرْمُونَ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْغَافِلَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ لُعِنُوا فِي الدُّنْيَا وَالْآخِرَةِ وَلَهُمْ عَذَابٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾
>
> "Indeed, those who accuse chaste, heedless, believing women are cursed in this world and the Hereafter, and for them is a great punishment." (al-Nur 23)

And He said:

> ﴿وَالَّذِينَ يَرْمُونَ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ ثُمَّ لَمْ يَأْتُوا بِأَرْبَعَةِ شُهَدَاءَ فَاجْلِدُوهُمْ ثَمَانِينَ جَلْدَةً وَلَا تَقْبَلُوا لَهُمْ شَهَادَةً أَبَدًا وَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ ۝ إِلَّا الَّذِينَ تَابُوا مِن بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ وَأَصْلَحُوا فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾
>
> "And those who accuse chaste women and then do not produce four witnesses, flog them with eighty lashes and never accept their testimony thereafter; it is they who are the defiantly disobedient, except those who repent after that and make amends, for indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful." (al-Nur 4 to 5)

It is narrated from Ali that he said: "The major sins are associating partners with Allah Almighty, killing a believer while under covenant, fleeing from the battle line except as one wheeling to fight or withdrawing to rejoin his own troop, consuming usury after the proof of its prohibition has been established, devouring the wealth of the orphan unjustly, reverting to the life of the desert after the Emigration, and accusing chaste, heedless, believing women."

It is narrated from Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad, (ع), that he said: "Whoever falsely accuses a believing man or a believing woman of something that is not in them, Allah Almighty casts him into the clay of corruption until he comes forth from what he said." He was asked about a man who slanders a chaste Muslim woman, and he said: "The hadd is established against him once it is proven, and his repentance consists in his declaring himself a liar before the people and turning back from what he did. If he does this, his testimony is accepted thereafter."

The slanderer is flogged eighty lashes. If he slanders a group and they bring their claims against him together, he receives a single hadd covering all of them; but if they come forward one after another, he receives a separate hadd for each. If the one slandered — man or woman — confesses to what was said of them, or the evidence of it is established against them as Allah Almighty has indicated, then no hadd falls upon the slanderer. Whoever slanders a polytheist incurs no hadd, unless the polytheist has a Muslim child, in which case the hadd is applied out of regard for the sanctity of Islam. It does not befit a Muslim to slander a polytheist, nor anyone else.

If a free man slanders a slave, he receives a disciplinary punishment but not the full hadd. If a slave slanders a free man, the full hadd is applied. If a dhimmi slanders a Muslim, the hadd is applied and he is made a public example. If a man slanders another man and that man slanders him in return, and both bring the matter before the authority, each receives a discretionary punishment. Whoever says to his wife, "I did not find you a virgin," incurs no hadd.

Whoever has already incurred one hadd and is then falsely accused of another offense, the slanderer is flogged the hadd for that accusation. Whoever acknowledges a child as his own and then disavows him is flogged the hadd, the child's lineage is fixed to him, and a mere insinuation — falling short of an explicit claim — carries no hadd. Whoever insults the Prophet, may the, is put to death. Whoever insults any of the Imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) is likewise put to death. Whoever commits slander in any language has the hadd imposed upon him.

Whoever slanders another and then pardons the one he accused before raising the matter to the authority, that pardon is valid; the right to pursue the claim is extinguished. If, however, he has already raised the matter to the authority and lodged a petition against the accused, no pardon is accepted after that point.

If someone slanders a child or a person who has lost his reason, no hadd falls upon them, though the child is disciplined so that he does not grow bold in slander. If a man or a woman slanders their own child, no hadd is imposed upon them; but if the child slanders them, the hadd is applied on their behalf. If a man says to another, "O sodomite," no hadd falls upon him, because he has only ascribed the man to Lot (ع); but if he says, "O you who do the work of the people of Lot," the hadd becomes obligatory. If a man slanders an absent or a deceased woman, her guardian may rise against him on her behalf, and the hadd belongs to him.

Whoever denies a man his lineage incurs the hadd. Whoever reviles a man or a woman receives a discretionary punishment on their behalf — as when he says, "O immoral one," "O malicious one," "son of a Christian," "son of a Zoroastrian," and the like among curses and insults. All of this is the teaching of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ).

### The Punishment for Intoxicants and Wine, and Related Rulings of the Hudud

Allah Almighty said:

> ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِنَّمَا الْخَمْرُ وَالْمَيْسِرُ وَالْأَنْصَابُ وَالْأَزْلَامُ رِجْسٌ مِّنْ عَمَلِ الشَّيْطَانِ فَاجْتَنِبُوهُ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾
>
> "O you who believe, wine, gambling, idols, and divining arrows are only a defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it, that you may be successful." (al-Maidah 90)

The Messenger of Allah said: "May Allah curse wine, the one who presses it, the one who has it pressed, its seller, its buyer, the one who pours it, the one who consumes its price, its drinker, the one who carries it, and the one to whom it is carried." He also said: "There is no one who drinks wine in this world and then drinks it in the Enclosure of Holiness."

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (ع) said: "One addicted to wine meets Allah Almighty, when he meets Him, as one who worships an idol." And whoever drinks a single draft of it, Allah does not accept a prayer from him for forty nights.

The Messenger of Allah said: "Every intoxicant is forbidden, and whatever intoxicates in a large quantity, a small quantity of it is forbidden as well."

Whoever drinks wine, whether little or much, has the hadd applied to him. If he confesses to drinking it a second time, he is struck again; and if he drinks it a third time, he is put to death — though not until the hadd has been administered upon him twice.

Whoever drinks an intoxicant and becomes so intoxicated that he does not know his own state is flogged the hadd of eighty lashes. If he returns to it after being struck once, he is struck again; and if he returns after being struck twice, he is put to death on the third occasion. If he drinks but does not become intoxicated, he receives a discretionary punishment; and if he returns to it, he is punished with a severe chastisement.

Whoever drinks wine or an intoxicant without knowing it is forbidden incurs no hadd. Whoever acknowledges drinking wine and then denies it is still given the hadd, and no regard is paid to his denial.

The hadd for a slave in the matter of wine is eighty lashes — the same as the hadd for a free man.

If the people of the dhimma openly drink wine or an intoxicant, they are struck just as Muslims are struck, for their covenant was granted to them only on the condition that they not openly display anything forbidden in the religion of Islam.

When doubt arises concerning a hadd, it is suspended. There is no surety in a hadd, no testimony built upon testimony, no oath, and no letter from one judge to another taken as a basis for it. No hadd is carried out on the strength of intimidation, nor on a confession extracted under duress; for that reason, a man is neither imprisoned nor beaten to produce one. If several hadd punishments fall due upon a single person, all of them are carried out; and where death is among them, the lesser penalties are applied first, and he is then put to death. A man may not carry out a hadd upon his own slave except by permission of the authority. If a hadd becomes due upon someone and its prescribed measure is unspecified, he is beaten until the one striking him desists. Whoever is testified against for a hadd is held until the evidence is duly established; once it is established and the hadd is applied, he is not held in further detention.

### The Rulings Concerning Thieves and Brigands

Allah Almighty said:

> ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِالْبَاطِلِ﴾
>
> "And do not consume one another's wealth among yourselves through falsehood." (al-Baqarah 188)

And He said:

> ﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ فَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا﴾
>
> "As for the thief, male and female, cut off their hands." (al-Maidah 38)

The Messenger of Allah, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said: "I have seen in the Fire the man with the crooked staff who used to steal from the pilgrims with it." And he said: "The thief does not steal while he is a believer."

Whoever enters another's home without permission and steals from their property — or removes from a secured place goods worth five dinars — and either confesses or is convicted by evidence, has his right hand cut off at the joint where the four fingers meet the palm; the thumb and palm are left to him for his use. Should he steal a second time, his left foot is cut off at mid-foot, the heel and what adjoins it being left to him so that he may still walk. A third offense results in life imprisonment, and if he steals while imprisoned, he is put to death. When amputation is carried out, the site is cauterized with fire to hasten healing and to protect him from mortal harm. If the one performing the amputation errs — cutting the left hand or the right foot instead — that suffices, and nothing further is taken from him. Whatever of the stolen goods is found still in his possession is returned to its owners, and he is held liable for whatever he has destroyed. After the amputation is carried out, he is banished to a land other than the one in which the sentence was executed.

No cutting applies to a guest who steals from his hosts, to a hired man who steals from the household that employed him and admitted him, or to anyone who entered the premises with the household's permission. Snatching carries no cutting, nor does open robbery committed within a town — such as seizing an item and overpowering its owner in plain sight. The one who grabs openly and flees is not subject to amputation, nor is the pickpocket; both are punished by public example instead.

When such acts are committed on the road, however, the perpetrator is a brigand. Once he is brought before the Imam, the ruler holds discretion in the matter:

- He may put him to death.
- He may crucify him and leave him alive until he dies.
- He may cut off his hand and his foot from opposite sides.
- He may banish him from one land to another.

This is the treatment applied when the brigand has terrorized the road and waylaid Muslims. If he repents before he is seized, he is pardoned. Whoever fights such an aggressor in defense of himself and kills or wounds him bears no liability for that.

If the brigand is captured and wealth is found with him, it is returned to its owners, provided they are known. If its owners are not known, and he confesses or witnesses testify that the wealth belongs to what he plundered, it is placed in the treasury of the Muslims until a rightful claimant comes forward.

A thief who holds a share in what he steals is not subject to the cutting penalty. Nor is cutting imposed on one who bores a hole or forces open a door but carries nothing away. There is no cutting for an ordinary stone, however valuable its appearance — only a precious gem crosses that threshold — nor for fruit stolen from the tree, nor for the pith of the palm, nor for any bird. What is taken from places open to the public likewise falls outside the penalty: mosques, inns, bathhouses, open courtyards, and every place a person may enter without permission. The exception is when stolen goods are removed from a secured enclosure within such a place; that changes the judgment. Sheep stolen from open pasture carry no cutting penalty either.

When a thief steals repeatedly and evades capture, then is finally caught, his hand is cut and he is held liable for everything he took across all those offenses. When a man is found in possession of stolen property but neither confesses nor has the theft proven against him, he is not subject to cutting; the property is simply taken from him and restored to its rightful owner.

A madman who steals is not subject to cutting, nor is a boy who has not yet reached puberty, nor a minor — though the child is disciplined so that he does not grow bold in stealing. A grave robber has his hand cut when he removes the shroud from the grave, for the grave is a secured place. If someone whose hand has been cut dies as a result of the cutting, no liability follows. The thief ought to be admonished after the cutting.
