It is narrated that Ali cut the hands of a group who had stolen, then brought fire, then fed them and gave them drink until they had recovered, then clothed them, and commanded them to take their severed hands in their sound hands.

He then said to them, "Raise your hands toward the sky and say: O Allah, Ali has cut off our hands according to Your Book and the Sunnah of Your Messenger." When they had said it, he replied, "Yes, O Lord, upon Your Book and the Sunnah of Your Messenger." Then he said to them, "These are your hands. They have gone ahead of you to the Fire. Whoever among you repents, his hand will drag him to Paradise, and whoever does not repent, it will drag him to Hell."

There are cases in which no hand is cut at all. If a slave steals the property of his master, his hand is not cut off, though if he steals from anyone other than his master, it is. If a father steals from his son's property, or a child from his father's, or a wife from her husband's, or a husband from his wife's, or a sister from her brother's, or a brother from his sister's, no cutting applies in any of these cases. Nor is a thief's hand to be cut if he stole during a year of famine and hardship. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt.

---

**Mention of the rulings on apostates and innovators**

Allah the Almighty said: "How shall Allah guide a people who disbelieved after their faith?" And He said: "Whoever of you turns back from his religion and dies while he is a disbeliever, those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter." And He said: "It has been revealed to you and to those before you: if you associate partners with Allah, your deeds will surely become worthless, and you will surely be among the losers."

The Messenger of Allah said: "It is not permissible to kill a believing man except for one of three things: disbelief after faith, fornication after the establishment of marriage, or the taking of a life for no life." And he said: "Every innovation is misguidance, and every misguidance is in the Fire." And he said: "Whoever changes his religion, kill him."

Whoever is born into Islam and then departs from it into any form of disbelief is killed and is not invited to repent. If the apostate is a woman, however, she is imprisoned until she repents.

As for the heretic — one who denies the resurrection and the reckoning, or who denies the prophethood of the Prophets — or one who held a religion other than Islam, then submitted, and afterward reverted, Islam and repentance are presented to him over three days. If he repents, he is left alone. If he persists in his position, he is killed on the fourth day and is not invited to repent at that point. If he repents of his own accord before then, he is left; if he does not, he is killed.

A male slave is likewise killed if his case is such.

As for a female slave who apostatizes, the terms imposed upon her are harsher. She is put to the most demanding service, clothed only with what covers her nakedness, and fed only with what sustains her life, until she repents or dies. She is not killed outright, so that her family is not deprived of her through destruction. The same ruling applies to the mother of a child.

When an apostate apostatizes, whatever property he leaves behind passes as inheritance to his heirs, since his apostasy is treated as his death. His wife observes her waiting period and may remarry if she wishes. His children remain Muslims. Whichever parent submits to Islam, that parent's minor children — and any children born thereafter — are Muslims by virtue of that parent's Islam. If they grow up and refuse Islam, they stand in the position of apostates, and what is done to apostates is done to them.

Whoever works sorcery against the Muslims has disbelieved, for Allah, exalted is He, says concerning the two angels: "And they taught no one until they said: We are only a trial, so do not disbelieve." And He says: "And they followed what the devils recited during the reign of Solomon, and Solomon did not disbelieve, but the devils disbelieved." The Messenger of Allah said: "The sorcerer among the Muslims is killed, but the sorcerer among the polytheists is not killed." It was asked, "O Messenger of Allah, and why is that?" He said, "Because the shirk he is upon is greater than the sorcery." Sorcery and shirk are thus bound together upon one tether. Whoever embraces Islam and then partakes of anything forbidden in Islam is beaten; and if that act carries a prescribed penalty, the penalty is carried out upon him. All of this is the saying of the Ahl al-Bayt.

**Mention of usurpation and transgression**

Allah, the most truthful of all who speak, said: "And do not transgress; indeed, Allah does not love those who transgress." And He said: "And do not consume your wealth among yourselves through falsehood." The Messenger of Allah said: "The sanctity of your wealth among you is like the sanctity of this sacred day, in this sacred month, in this sacred land."

Whoever comes into unlawful wealth is therefore obligated to repent and to free himself of it. Repentance admits of no other form than this: he must rid himself of that wealth and return it to its owners, if he knows who they are. If he does not know them, he places it in the treasury of the Muslims until the one entitled to it comes forward. If no path to that exists, he gives it in charity — and if its owners later make themselves known to him, he makes restitution to them. He may neither keep that wealth nor draw any benefit from it.

As for the one who has been wronged — who has had something usurped from him, or stolen — he must not himself transgress, usurp, or steal from the one who wronged him, even if he has the power to do so. Usurpation, betrayal, theft, and transgression are all forbidden, without exception. That a forbidden act has been done to a person does not permit him to do the like of it in return. Rather, he must hold to his trust: he must not betray, and he must not steal. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad said: "Render up your trusts, and do not betray the one who betrayed you."

Whoever usurps a slave woman and she bears him a child must return her to the one from whom she was taken, and his child by her belongs as a slave to that same person. If he usurped her and then sold her to a man who, knowing she was usurped, fathered a child by her, she is returned to her original owner, the buyer pays the value of the child, and he then has recourse against the usurping seller for her price and for the value of the child he surrendered.

Whoever usurps a slave, a beast, or anything whatever, and it perishes in his possession, owes its value or its like-in-kind. If the usurped property increased in his hands, the increase belongs to its rightful owner. If it diminished, the usurper is liable for what was lost. If he hired it out, the hire belongs to its owner. If what he seized were sheep or other animals that bred, then the animals and their offspring alike belong to the one from whom they were taken.

Whoever assaults something belonging to the instruments of frivolity and breaks it, or pours out wine or any intoxicant, bears no liability for that.

Whoever has wealth stolen or usurped from him and then comes upon the very thing itself may take it back, but it is not lawful for him to take some substitute in its place.

---

**On loans and deposits**

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "And do not forget generosity among yourselves." The Messenger of Allah said: "A loan of use is an act of affection." Jafar ibn Muhammad said: "The loan, the lending of an article, and the hosting of the guest are obligations within the Sunnah." And Ali said: "Whoever guards the property of an orphan, Allah, mighty and majestic, makes Paradise obligatory for him, just as He has made the Fire obligatory for the one who devours it." As sin falls upon the one who betrays a trust, so the reward belongs to the one who receives a trust and renders it faithfully.

Whoever borrows an article and stands surety for it to the lender, and it then perishes or is lost in his keeping, is liable to make it good — whether or not any fault on his part caused the loss. If he did not stand surety for it but then wronged it, transgressed against it, or wasted it, he is likewise liable. If, however, it perished or was damaged through no wrongdoing and no neglect of his, no liability falls upon him, and his word is accepted if he is a man of trust. If he borrows dinars or dirhams and they perish

edits.chapter_key: the marketplace: honest earning, trade, and property
edits.body_md:
God has commanded the believer to seek what He has set aside of His bounty. He says, ﴿وَاسْأَلُوا اللَّهَ مِن فَضْلِهِ﴾, "And ask Allah of His bounty," and He says, ﴿فَإِذَا قُضِيَتِ الصَّلَاةُ فَانتَشِرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَابْتَغُوا مِن فَضْلِ اللَّهِ﴾, "When the prayer is concluded, spread out in the land and seek the bounty of Allah." The pursuit of provision is therefore not a lapse from religion but something religion itself enjoins, provided it is pursued in the manner God has prescribed.

A man came to the Prophet ﷺ and said, "O Messenger of Allah, my soul has not been content with anything of this world, nor is it satisfied by it." The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to him, "Say: O Allah, please me with Your decree, bless me in what You have given me, and make me content with what You have apportioned for me, so that I may not wish to hasten what You have delayed, nor to delay what You have hastened." Contentment, then, is the first discipline of the one who earns, for the soul that cannot be satisfied will not be steadied by any increase of wealth.

It is narrated through the Imams of his household, from al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad, upon him be the prayers of Allah, from his father, from his forefathers, upon them be the prayers of Allah, from the Messenger of Allah, that he said, "The faithful spirit breathed into my heart that no soul shall die until it has completed its provision. So be measured and at ease in seeking sustenance. There is no servant of Allah but that he has a provision, and between him and it there is a veil. If he is patient with restraint, Allah brings it to him lawfully; and if he is not patient, he tears the veil and so consumes it unlawfully." The same provision reaches a man either way, but his patience decides whether it reaches him as a blessing or as a sin.

He said, upon him be peace, "Do not let the slowness of any provision drive you to seek it through disobedience to Allah, and be gracious in your seeking, for what is with Allah is not attained by disobedience." He also said, "If one of you becomes destitute, let him go out and seek his provision, strike out into the earth, and seek the bounty of Allah. Let him not sit in his house, grieving himself and his family and becoming a burden upon others." And he said, "Beneath the shade of the Throne, on the Day when there is no shade but His, will be a man who went out striking the earth, seeking the bounty of Allah, to restrain himself from begging and to provide for his dependents."

A man came and said, "O Messenger of Allah, I am skilled in no trade that I take up without finding it goes badly for me." The Messenger said, "Look at something you have once managed to earn from, and hold fast to it." The man said, "The cutting and selling of acacia for tanning." He said, "Then keep to the acacia trade."

The Messenger of Allah once passed through one of the markets and said, "O company of merchants, the merchant is a licentious man, and the licentious are in the Fire." When they heard this, they shut the doors of their shops and abandoned trade. The next day he passed through the market and found no one there, and asked, "What is the matter with them?" It was said, "They abandoned trade, O Messenger of Allah, when they heard what you said yesterday." He said, "I say the same again today, except for the one who takes what is rightfully his and gives others their right." The condemnation, then, fell not upon trade itself but upon the dishonesty that so often accompanies it.

He said, "I was sent as a mercy to people; I was not sent as a merchant, nor as a farmer. The worst of this nation are its merchants and its cultivators, except for those among them who guard their religion jealously." And he said, "Verily Allah loves the servant who is easy in selling, easy in buying, easy in settling what he owes, and easy in seeking what is owed to him."

The Messenger of Allah once saw a strong young man driving fat, well-laden camels. Someone said to him, "O Messenger of Allah, how excellent is this man's strength, and the strength of his camels — if only it were in the way of Allah." The Messenger of Allah turned to the youth and asked, "What do you do with these camels of yours?" The boy said, "I labor with them and earn my living from them." He asked, "And what do you do with your earnings?" The boy said, "I have a wife and children whom I support, sparing them from having to ask of others, and I pay off a debt I owe." He said, "If he speaks truthfully, he has a reward like the reward of the one who fights in the way of Allah, and of the one who performs the Hajj and the Umrah." And Ali, upon him be the prayers of Allah, said, "The setting out of one of you in the way of Allah is no greater than his setting out to seek for his children and dependents that which will sustain them."

The Prophet, upon him be peace, said to a man who asked his permission to take up trade, "Have you gained understanding in religion?" The man said, "Some of it." He said, "Woe to you. Understanding first, then the marketplace; for whoever buys and sells without understanding falls into usury" — and by usury here he meant that which is deferred. Knowledge of what is lawful must precede the transaction, or the trader sinks unknowingly into what is forbidden.

Muhammad ibn al-Munkadir said, "I saw Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, upon him be peace, on a day of severe heat. He had come in from a farm, and being a heavy man, he was worn out with fatigue. I said to myself: I shall counsel a man of his nobility. I said, 'May I be your ransom. With your standing of honor, you exert yourself like this in seeking the world? Tell me — if your appointed hour came upon you in this state, what would you say of it?' He said, 'Were my hour to come upon me in this state, it would find me in an act of obedience to Allah. By it I restrain myself from needing others and prepare provision for my Hereafter, striving to earn from what is lawful. What I would truly fear is that my hour should come upon me while I was in disobedience to Allah Almighty — and I seek refuge in Allah from that.' So I said to him, 'May I be your ransom. I meant to counsel you, and you have counseled me.'"

A man said to Jafar ibn Muhammad, upon him be the prayers of Allah, "O son of the Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah to grant me provision in ease, without effort." He replied, "I will not pray to Allah for that. Seek as Allah Almighty has commanded you." And he said, upon him be peace, "It befits the Muslim to seek his provision until the heat of the sun reaches him."

Among the supplications of the Ahl al-Bayt, upon them be peace, is this: "O Allah, do not burden me with seeking what You have not apportioned for me, lest my occupation with it draw me away from obeying You and I be unable to attain any of it. O Allah, whatever You have apportioned for me of this, bring it to me in chastity and ease, and set me right by that which You have set right the righteous, for the righteousness of the righteous comes from You." It is reported, in the words of Abu Muhammad ibn Ali — (رضي الله عنه) and may mercy and blessing be upon him — that this was among the supplications of Dawud, upon him be peace.

Jafar ibn Muhammad, upon him be peace, said to Sufyan, who had come to ask him, "O Sufyan, when a blessing appears upon you, praise Allah; and when something of your provision is slow in coming, seek the forgiveness of Allah." Then he recited, "Ask forgiveness of your Lord; verily He is ever Forgiving. He will send the sky upon you in abundant rain," up to His words, "and will make for you rivers." He continued, "And when something of the terrors of this world befalls you, say: There is no power and no strength save with Allah, the Most High, the Most Great."

Sufyan said, "Grant me these three — and what are the three?"

He, upon him be peace, also addressed one of his Shia, counseling him: "When you go out, morning or evening, in search of your provision and you desire success in it, pray two units of prayer. When you have finished the tashahhud, say:

*O Allah, I have gone forth — if I am one going forth — or set out — if I am one setting out — seeking of Your bounty as You commanded me. So grant me of Your bounty a lawful and wholesome provision as You commanded me, and grant me well-being in what You have provided for me.*

Say that three times. Then pray two more units, and after the tashahhud say:

*I have gone forth — if I am one going forth — or set out — if I am one setting out — by the power of Allah and His strength, with no power or strength of my own, but by Your power, O my Lord, and Your strength. I declare myself free, O my Lord, before You, of all power and strength. O Allah, I ask You for the good of this day, if it is day, or the good of this night, if it is night, and I ask You to provide me from Your bounty a lawful and wholesome provision, driven to me by Your power and Your strength, while I remain at ease, in chastity.*

Say that three times, then rise to your purpose."

The Prophet said, upon him be peace, "Allah Almighty has divided provision among His servants, and He has reserved beyond it a great surplus that He did not divide among them; so ask Allah of His bounty." He also said, "The one who sets out in pursuit of lawful provision is like the one who strives in the way of Allah." And to a man of his Shia who was engaged in trade, he said, "When you seek something of this world and it escapes you, remember what Allah Almighty has singled you out for from His religion, and the favor He has shown you in turning others away from it. That is more fitting to lift your soul above the loss."

Ali ibn al-Husayn, upon him be the prayers of Allah, said, "Allah Almighty has made provision ten parts: nine of them in trade and one part in all other things."

A man said to Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad, upon him be the prayers of Allah, to whom he was devoted, "O son of the Messenger of Allah, I have abandoned trade, waiting for the appearance of your cause." The Imam said to him, "Do not do so. Open your door, spread out your mat, and seek provision from your Lord, for that is better for you. If you hold back from seeking your provision, your wealth will dwindle. So seek of the bounty of Allah, your Lord."

**On What Is Forbidden to Sell**

The Messenger of Allah forbade the sale of free persons and declared such transactions void. He likewise forbade the sale of carrion and of wine. Transmitted from the Imams of his household, upon them be the prayers of Allah, is the ruling that everything unlawful may neither be sold nor earned from, nor may its price be received. This covers filth, carrion, blood, swine, wine, every intoxicant, and all instruments of idle amusement. The Imams forbade the making of such things, earning from them, buying and selling them, learning them, and lending any assistance toward them.

They permitted, however, the sale of:

- Grapes, pressed juice, raisins, honey, dates, and figs — even to one who will turn them into wine or another intoxicant — because the sale of these goods is itself lawful, and the sin falls only upon the one who renders them unlawful.

They likewise permitted the taking of payment in every case where the sale of a thing is forbidden, when it is sold to one who will use it for himself — though it remains forbidden for that buyer to do so. As for the price received by one into whose hands a thing has passed by lawful means, there is no harm in it.

There is no harm, either, in dealing with polytheists and accepting payment for what they purchase from Muslims, nor in receiving what they hold from the proceeds of things they have sold that were not lawful to sell. Most of their wealth derives from usury and unlawful gain, yet it may be taken from them as the jizya or as payment for what they purchase from Muslims, and it becomes lawful for the one who receives it through its rightful means.

They — upon them be peace — disliked the price of the biting dog, yet permitted the price of the hunting dog, and the sale of the herding dog is allowed. They disliked the price of the cat. They forbade buying what one knows to be stolen or taken by treachery until it has been returned to its rightful owners, who may then sell it. They permitted the sale of copies of the Quran.

From the Messenger of Allah, upon him be peace, comes a general prohibition against the sale of water, of pasture (al-kala), and of fire. This prohibition bears upon the sale of what no one owns: water lying open in the wilderness, rainwater gathered there, and all such waters that belong to nobody, as well as the flame of a fire from which a man lights his lamp or takes a brand without diminishing it. However, if a man has dug a well on his own land, or possesses a flowing spring, a developed river, a cistern, or anything similar — including rainwater that has settled on his property, water stored in a vessel, or water carried on his back, his mount, or by any other means — then its sale is permitted. Likewise, if he has gathered pasture grass from the wild, uprooted it, or tended and watered it on land he owns, the sale of it is permitted. The same principle applies to fire: when it resides in something owned — firewood, charcoal, or any other material in which fire is kindled — its sale is permitted, for it becomes property among the recognized kinds of property.

Buying from or selling to someone known for treachery, theft, or other wrongdoing carries no prohibition in itself — unless one knows that the specific item being purchased was itself stolen or taken by treachery. Where that knowledge is absent, the transaction is permissible. As has already been established, trade with polytheists is likewise permitted, provided one does not know that their goods were acquired by treachery or theft; the Muslim, however, bears the greater obligation to inquire.

---

**On the Prohibition of the Sale of Gharar**

Allah Almighty has said: ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِالْبَاطِلِ﴾ — "And do not consume one another's wealth among yourselves unjustly." The Messenger of Allah, as transmitted by the pure Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt — upon them all be the prayers of Allah — prohibited the sale of gharar in general terms. The sale of gharar is every sale concluded over something unknown. The Messenger of Allah then specified several of its forms.

Among them, he forbade the sale of habal al-habalah — the offspring of an offspring. This was a transaction practiced in the time of ignorance: a man would sell a commodity against the price of the offspring of a she-camel, to be paid once she had given birth and her young had itself produced young. Of the same kind is the sale of an animal's offspring before it is born, for people of that era traded in what still lay in the wombs of camels and other beasts.

Among the forbidden transactions, the Prophet also prohibited the sale of al-madamin and al-malaqih. The malaqih are the embryos already described — sold while still in their mothers' wombs. The madamin are what lies in the loins of stallions: people traded in whatever a stallion would sire over a stated period, whether once or a fixed number of times.

Also forbidden was the sale of al-mulamasah — the sale by touch. This occurs when a man sells a garment or some article that is folded so its inside cannot be seen, or when the mere touching of it with the hand is made to stand in for a proper inspection, on the condition that the buyer has no right to reconsider once he sees, unfolds, or spreads out the item. It also occurs when a seller says, "When you touch this commodity, the transaction between us is binding." The contract of sale, however, is made binding only by spoken agreement and by the parting of the two parties in mutual consent. Of the same kind is the touching of goods from behind a curtain, where the sale is concluded on that contact alone.

Also forbidden was the sale of al-munabadhah. This occurs when a man looks at a folded garment in another man's hand and says, "I buy this from you, and when you throw it to me the sale between us is complete, with no right of withdrawal for either party" — or when each of the two throws a garment or some article to the other.

Among the sales the Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family) nullified were those in which a man concluded a bargain by saying simply, "This for this," without turning the goods over or examining them. Also nullified was the sale of pebbles — a practice of the pre-Islamic era in which the two parties sealed a contract by each throwing his pebble, making that throw the binding act of sale. He nullified all such sales.

He also prohibited the sale of al-wala and the giving of it as a gift, declaring that al-wala belongs only to those who hold it by lineage and is neither to be sold nor given away. He prohibited the sale of a slave on condition of keeping him before the slave had come into one's possession, and likewise the sale of a stray camel or similar animal before it is found.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) said: If such a stray animal — or anything like it among absent goods — is sold together with something present, such as a slave, a beast, a garment, or any other permissible item that is at hand, then the sale of that combination is permissible, provided that both seller and buyer know the stray or absent item. Upon its arrival, the price falls upon the present item that both parties have seen. Such a sale does not fall under the words of Allah Almighty, ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُمْ بَيْنَكُمْ بِالْبَاطِلِ﴾, "And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly" (Al-Baqarah 188).

Likewise, if a man sells the milk still in the udder of his sheep together with a quantity already drawn from it that is lawful to sell, the sale is permissible, because the price falls upon the present portion that both parties have seen. Most sales are of this kind: the price rests upon what is seen, or upon the part that is seen and purchased while the greater portion remains concealed — as with houses, dwellings, garments, and animals. Only what is apparent is visible; what lies hidden is not. Yet the sale covers both the visible and the hidden, both what has been examined and what has not.

It is permissible to buy the dust of mines with gold or silver, hand to hand, even if upon extraction it yields more or less than the price paid — because at the moment of purchase it was neither silver nor gold but merely dust. Selling it on deferred terms, however, is disliked.

It is narrated from Ali that he disliked the sale of fish still in the water when they can be reached only by fishing. If a catch is already secured and can be had without hunting, however, selling it is permissible. The Prophet forbade the sale of wool upon the backs of sheep, and of their hides likewise, until the wool is shorn and the hide flayed. He forbade a man to sell his share of the spoils before he has received it, because he does not know what will come to him from it. The sale of sukuk — that is, written certificates of debt — is also forbidden.

### The Sale of Fruits

The Imams of the Prophet's household narrated that he forbade, in general terms, the sale of fruits until their goodness becomes apparent. Jafar ibn Muhammad said that the ripening of fruits begins when they turn red or yellow. What the Prophet meant was their coming to soundness: if some portion of the fruit has reached that condition, the whole of it may be sold; if nothing has yet ripened, the sale falls under the principle already established concerning present and absent goods. If nothing has appeared that is free of what is objectionable, the sale is not permissible unless both parties agree to it — and if either of them moves to annul it, the sale is annulled. If one variety among several shows ripeness, that variety may be sold together with the others even where nothing of them has yet ripened, provided the whole is sold in a single transaction, all according to the principle already named.

The Imams (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said: when the fruit blooms, or part of it does, it may be sold together with whatever the same trees will bear of such fruit for a year or two afterward, so long as that is named and stated. If nothing comes forth in the future, the price falls upon what was present at the time of sale. This too rests upon the principle already mentioned.

The generality of scholars do not permit selling fruit for years in advance, on the grounds that such a sale constitutes gharar — an uncertain and deceptive transaction — yet they do permit selling fruit once part of it has shown soundness. The position is not consistent. Whatever soundness appears while the sale still encompasses the remainder falls under the same ruling, and that is precisely the point they denied: they objected that part of the price would rest upon fruit whose soundness had not yet begun, while they themselves allowed selling such fruit together with what had already become sound, with the price resting upon the sound portion. Their own concession reopens the very door they claimed to shut. Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad said accordingly: it is permissible to sell fruit once its soundness, or the soundness of part of it, has begun — for a year or two afterward; if it does not come forth in that year, it comes forth in the next.

The people's duty is to follow the teaching of the Imams and to abandon dispute with them, for what issues from the Imams is itself a proof — whoever holds to it is spared any further search for evidence or witness.

The strongest argument those who reject the multi-year sale of fruit have been able to advance is an unspecified hadith they claim to narrate from the Prophet (may Allah bless him and his family), in which he forbade "the sale of years," without mentioning fruit or anything else. Even if that hadith is established, it is unspecified in its scope, and the Imams' interpretation makes plain that its intent is not what the generality have supposed.

If the hadith is taken as general, those who invoke it are bound to apply it to everything that falls within its scope — and it admits many meanings. Among them:

- In Arabic usage, "years" denotes times of hardship and adversity. The Arabs say, "The years have come upon us," meaning trials and distress have descended; and a year of drought and affliction is itself called "a year." On this reading, the prohibition would fall upon whatever is sold during times of hardship, rendering every transaction concluded in such a period void.
- In the figurative usage of the language, "the sale of years" may mean selling by the year and for years to come — which itself opens onto further meanings.

Given this range of possible interpretations, following what has come from the Imams with clear explanation is more deserving of acceptance — all the more so when the foundational principles attest to it and upon which the subsidiary rulings are built.

When fruit is sold before its soundness has become apparent, and the buyer accepts the terms, and neither party moves to cancel but both proceed, the sale is permissible — not forbidden — despite the reports of prohibition. Jafar ibn Muhammad said: The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade the sale of fruits before their soundness appeared only because people were buying them while the fruit was still liable to perish. Blight might strike before the crop was complete and sound, and the disputes this caused were brought before the Messenger of Allah. When such disputes multiplied, he forbade the practice until soundness became clear; he did not declare it unlawful for them.

He said: Whoever sells his fruit and reserves from it a known portion, that sale is permissible. Whoever makes a sale reserving an unknown portion, that sale is not permissible, because it was concluded over something unknown.

He said: If the buyer sells the fruit before he gathers it, the sale is permissible.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade al-muzabana: the sale of dates still on the heads of the palms for a measured quantity of dates, and of grapes still on the vine for raisins. He ruled that grain may not be sold before it can be reaped in the customary manner. If it is sold for wheat, or on the condition that it be left standing, and the buyer then reaps it or leaves it until it ripens fully, there is no harm in that. Likewise, if it is bought for something other than wheat and then reaped or left to ripen, there is no harm in that either. It is therefore permissible to sell standing crops and fresh herbage when the quantity is known, the buyer taking one cutting or several where the plant grows back, while the root remains the seller's once the cuttings are spent.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) said: Whoever buys palm trees already bearing fruit that has appeared, that fruit belongs to the seller unless the buyer stipulates otherwise. The same ruling applies to the sale of trees bearing fruit that has reached the stage the fruit of the palm reaches at the time of pollination: if the buyer does not stipulate it, the fruit belongs to the seller.

### The Prohibition of Cheating and Deception

The Imams from the household of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and them all) narrated that he said, "مَنْ غَشَّنَا فَلَيْسَ مِنَّا" — that is, "Whoever cheats us is not one of us." He forbade cheating, treachery, deception, and beguilement in selling, and the breaking of pledges, and he commanded the fulfillment of contracts in selling, buying, marriage, and covenant.

The words "Whoever cheats us is not one of us" mean that such a person is not among those who follow the command of the Prophet and belong to his company. They do not mean that the act of cheating causes a person to leave Islam and fall into apostasy — for were that the case, the cheater would incur what the apostate incurs, namely death. Allah Almighty said, reporting the words of Ibrahim (ع): ﴿فَمَن تَبِعَنِي فَإِنَّهُ مِنِّي وَمَنْ عَصَانِي فَإِنَّكَ غَفُورٌ رَحِيمٌ﴾ — "Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, then You are Forgiving and Merciful." The one who cheats has likewise not followed the command of the Messenger of Allah and is therefore not of those who followed his command. Yet if he is a Muslim, he remains among those who followed the Prophet but disobeyed him in some of what he commanded, and his affair is referred to Allah Almighty: if He wills, He forgives him, and if He wills, He punishes him, as with other disobedient Muslims.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad said that mixing two grades of food — or similar goods — the superior with the inferior, when done for the purpose of sale, constitutes cheating. His meaning was that cheating occurs when the superior grade is what is displayed to the buyer while the inferior is concealed. If both grades are shown together, however, or the inferior is displayed while the superior is kept back, that does not amount to cheating. Ali used to move through the markets of Kufa warning the people against this practice, saying, "Show the poorer part of your wares just as you show the good part of them."

He forbade blowing into meat and said, "إِنَّمَا النَّفْخُ مِنَ الشَّيْطَانِ فَلَا تَنْفُخُوا فِي طَعَامٍ وَلَا شَرَابٍ" — that is, "Blowing is from the devil, so do not blow into food or drink." He permitted blowing to separate the hide from the flesh in skinning, but forbade blowing into the flesh itself for the reason already given: it is a form of cheating, since the blown air works into the sinews and the thin membranes beneath the skin, making the flesh appear fat when it is not. He likewise forbade mixing milk with water when the intention is to sell it, though for one who means to drink it himself there is no harm in doing so.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade *tatfif* — the giving of short measure and short weight, taking more than one's due while giving less than is owed. Whoever gives full measure, or more, to the one he sells to, or accepts less than his due from that person, has done well. Whoever takes exactly his right and renders the like has acted justly. Allah, exalted be His mention, said:

﴿وَيْلٌ لِلْمُطَفِّفِينَ * الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ * وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَو وَزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ﴾

"Woe to the defrauders, who, when they take measure from people, take in full, but when they measure or weigh for them, give less" (Al-Mutaffifin 1–3). The meaning is that when they receive they claim their full due, and when they give they fall short. This applies to matters of sale and exchange. As for the gift and voluntary charity, whoever renders it in full earns the greater reward, and if he falls short in it nothing is held against him; but where it is an obligation, he must render it in full.

Ali instructed that care be taken in buying and selling with dinars and dirhams, and he ordered that no debased coin enter his treasury. The concern is with coin whose defect is concealed — detectable only by those with a practiced eye — while it passes freely among others. Debased coin that is widely recognized and openly known, however, traded at its proper rate, presents no difficulty; nor do known mintings that differ in value, nor coins of pure copper, nor any other currency that is familiar and free of obscurity. There is no harm in buying and selling with any of these. It is narrated from Jafar ibn Muhammad that he forbade the use of differing measures and weights within a single town, on account of the doubt and confusion such variation invites.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade tasriyah: the practice of leaving a ewe or a milking camel unmilked for a day or two before a sale, so that milk accumulates in the udder and the animal appears to the buyer to be a generous producer. The buyer is deceived and harmed by the sight of the swollen udder.

The buyer therefore has three days — reckoned from the time he first milks the animal — in which to decide. If he wishes, he may keep it; if he wishes, he may return it, together with a sa of dates as compensation for the milk he drew from it. If he found little milk in the udder, nothing beyond that is owed.

This right of return belongs to the option that attaches to the sale of animals, khiyar al-hayawan. The musarrat is returnable even when the buyer has already relinquished the three-day option, provided the seller knew of the defect before the sale and concealed it. If, however, the seller disclosed the matter before the sale — stating plainly how many days the milking had been withheld — and the buyer accepted those terms, then no right of return on account of the tasriyah remains. It remains only if the buyer discovers some separate defect beyond it.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade najsh in transactions, saying, "لَا تَدَابَرُوا وَلَا تَنَاجَشُوا" — that is, "Do not turn your backs upon one another, and do not drive up bids against one another." Those who turn their backs fall into severance, enmity, harshness, and estrangement; the prohibition carries the sense that no one should turn his back upon his brother in this way. Najsh is the practice whereby a person who has no intention of buying approaches a commodity and raises its stated price, not because he wishes to purchase it, but so that others nearby will hear him and raise their own bids in turn — inflating the price against the genuine buyer. It is a form of deception: the false bidder is taken as a reliable guide, and others follow his lead upward. On that ground, the practice was forbidden.

The Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade a townsman from selling on behalf of a Bedouin. The meaning is this: the Bedouin brings a commodity, entrusts it to the townsman to sell, and the townsman sells it without ever offering it openly in the market. That much is plain from the wording of the prohibition itself.

The prohibition does not apply, however, when the townsman cries the goods publicly, announces their price, makes that price known, and offers his counsel — then reports back to the owner what he has learned, whereupon the owner either directs him to sell or comes and sells the goods himself. In that case the prohibition is not engaged, because a command issued for an act ascribes that act to the one who commanded it.

The principle is well established. It is said of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) that he cut off the hand of a thief, stoned the married adulterer, and put to death those upon whom death was due — yet all of this was carried out by his command, not by his own hand. Likewise it is said, "The prince killed so-and-so" or "struck so-and-so," even when another performed the deed on his order.

By the same reasoning, when the Bedouin orders the townsman to sell his goods, it is the Bedouin who has sold them. But if the townsman, or any other party, sells those goods without having been ordered to do so and without the owner's leave, the sale is not permissible unless the owner afterward authorizes it. That is the scope of what the prohibition addressed.

The Prophet ﷺ forbade going out to meet the *rukban* — the caravans and traders arriving with their goods — before they reach the city or marketplace where they intend to sell. The prohibition guards against two harms:

- The arriving merchants are wronged, since whoever rides out to meet them knows the prevailing prices and market values of which those sellers are themselves unaware.
- The townspeople who could not ride out are shut out from buying.

There is also an element of deception in the practice, since the one who goes out holds knowledge of price and worth that the seller does not.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad fixed its measure: whoever goes out to meet incoming goods at a distance of a day's journey or less falls within the prohibition; beyond that distance, the act is no longer counted as meeting them. And whenever goods are dressed up so that their price is raised with no benefit to the buyer, that is deceit (*ghishsh*), and it is forbidden.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man who buys food and then sells the same measure of it in return. He said: "If he does not add to its price, there is no harm in it; but if he uses it to deceive the Muslims, there is no good in it, and it is not sound." He was also asked about a man who buys food by weight and finds in it more than he had paid for. He replied: "If the surplus is of the kind that people do not haggle over — the sort of variance that may ordinarily occur between two measurings — there is no harm in it. But if it is excessive, it is an error and must be returned to the seller, unless the seller is content to leave it with him."

From Ali: he permitted the buyer to ask the seller for a little more — to tip the balance in the buyer's favor or to add to the measure — but only after the seller has already given the buyer his full due, and only as a request from the buyer. If the seller's heart is content with it, he may do so, and it is wholesome for the buyer; if his heart is not content, the buyer has no right to compel him. Should the buyer stipulate such an increase as a condition within the contract of sale while it remains unspecified, the sale is void; if it is specified, however, the sale stands, and the known increase enters into the contract of measure and weight. Justice in this matter is what keeps to the truth, neither adding nor subtracting — and that is the fulfillment (*al-wafa*) that Allah Almighty commanded, where He says, and He is the most truthful of speakers:

﴿أَوْفُوا الْكَيْلَ وَلَا تَكُونُوا مِنَ الْمُخْسِرِينَ ۝ وَزِنُوا بِالْقِسْطَاسِ الْمُسْتَقِيمِ ۝ وَلَا تَبْخَسُوا النَّاسَ أَشْيَاءَهُمْ وَلَا تَعْثَوْا فِي الْأَرْضِ مُفْسِدِينَ﴾

"Give full measure and be not of those who cause loss. Weigh with the straight balance (*al-qistas*). And do not defraud people of their things, nor go about the earth spreading corruption." (al-Shuara 181–183)

Fulfillment is justice and truth, without increase or decrease. Shortchanging (*al-bakhs*) is to give less than is due, and skimping (*al-tatfif*) is to receive one's full due yet give short to others, as Allah Almighty has said, and He is the most truthful of speakers:

﴿وَيْلٌ لِّلْمُطَفِّفِينَ ۝ الَّذِينَ إِذَا اكْتَالُوا عَلَى النَّاسِ يَسْتَوْفُونَ ۝ وَإِذَا كَالُوهُمْ أَوْ وَزَنُوهُمْ يُخْسِرُونَ﴾

"Woe to those who skimp, who, when they take by measure from people, take in full, but when they give to them by measure or by weight, give less." (al-Mutaffifin 1–3)

### Mention of What He Forbade Regarding Sales

The Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) transmitted that the Prophet ﷺ forbade two conditions within a single sale. An example is a seller who says, "I sell you this commodity for such a price in cash, or for such a price on credit," leaving the choice to the buyer, so that whichever he takes — the lesser amount paid immediately or the greater amount deferred — is binding, and the contract closes on that basis. Such a sale is impermissible because the price remains indeterminate. The following are of the same kind:

- Selling a thing for dinars on the condition that the seller receive their equivalent value in dirhams at a fixed rate.
- Selling on the condition that the other party in turn sells him some other thing — whether guaranteed or not, for immediate or deferred delivery.
- Selling for a fixed term at a set price, then raising the price each time the term is extended.

All of this, and whatever resembles it, constitutes two conditions in one sale. The sale is corrupt when the two parties contract upon it and part upon it. If, however, what passed between them was negotiation only, and they afterward agreed on one of the two options — annulling the other and parting upon that single agreed term — the sale is permissible, and it stands as whatever they settled upon.

They also narrated that he forbade profiting from what one does not yet guarantee (*ribh ma lam yudman*): something measured or weighed that the seller is owed by a debtor, or a provision due to come to him, which he sells before he has taken possession of it. Of the same kind is the craftsman who accepts a piece of work for a wage and then hands it to another to complete for less than he undertook it, pocketing the difference — having neither labored on it nor stood surety for it. If, however, he has done something to it, or contributed some part of the work himself, the surplus is lawful to him.

Of the same kind is a man who rents a dwelling and then sublets it for more than he pays; this is not permitted. He is, however, allowed to sublet part of it for the same amount he himself pays and to live in the remainder. And if he has tended the property in some way — kept it up or attended to its affairs — the surplus becomes lawful to him.

The same principle applies to a *khan* that a man rents and then opens for business: he hangs a curtain over its door, sweeps it, attends to its affairs, and sublets its rooms at a profit. In return for the care he has expended, there is no harm in that surplus.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ is reported to have forbidden any sale joined to a loan (*bay wa salaf*) — as when a man says to another, "I will sell you such-and-such on condition that you lend me such-and-such," or "Lend me this sum on the understanding that I owe you so much." A sale contracted on that footing is void: the borrower owes only what was actually lent, and the sale is annulled. If, however, the loan was given without being made a condition of the sale, the sale stands unimpaired.

They also narrated that he forbade selling what one does not possess (*bay ma laysa indak*) — as when a man bargains over something he does not yet have. If such a sale is contracted, the thing belongs to the buyer, and the buyer retains the option once he sees it.

Of the same kind is selling goods for guaranteed future delivery at a time when no such goods exist — grapes or fruit, for instance, in a season when none are available. This is the forbidden *kali* for *kali*: debt exchanged for debt, which is not permissible. The case runs as follows: a man hands another a sum of dinars for a specified quantity of food to be delivered at a set time; when the time arrives and no food can be found, he purchases it from a man who owes him a debt payable at a later date, and sets that food against a deferred price. This is not permissible, for it amounts to a debt nested within a debt.

Likewise, when a debt has fallen due and the two parties agree to extend the term in exchange for an increase in the amount owed, that too is unlawful. If, however, the debtor is released from part of the debt and pays the remainder early, before the term expires, there is no harm in that — for had the creditor remitted the whole debt to him, that would have been a good and praiseworthy act.

Also counted among transactions of *kali* for *kali* is the case where a man owes another a debt and the creditor arranges for him to perform work against it by mutual agreement. Such an arrangement is void. The worker is entitled to the wage customary for someone of his station; if one or both parties have already acted on the agreement, any surplus is returned, or recovered where something remains outstanding. If, however, a fixed-term debt is settled early — before it falls due — in exchange for the remission of part of it, there is no harm in that.

Of the same character is the case where a man hires a riding beast and then transfers that hire to another party: this is not permissible. Similarly, where a debt owed to a group of men is divided on the condition that each member collects the share falling to him, that too is impermissible, and whatever any one of them collects is pooled among them all. Any transaction that falls within this meaning — entering the category of debt exchanged for debt — belongs to the class of *kali* for *kali*.

Where two men each owe the other a debt, whether in foodstuffs or other goods, and neither knows the exact amount the other owes him, yet they mutually agree that each releases his fellow from what he owes in exchange for what is his own — there is no harm in that. It is a matter they have settled by mutual agreement, unspecified in amount, and it does not fall within the category of *kali* for *kali*.

The scholars permitted the sale of animals one for another, even one for more than its like. It is narrated that Ali sold a camel of his named Usayfir for twenty camels to be delivered at a future date — and this is permissible when the camels are described. They forbade the sale of meat for a live animal, and they forbade a man bidding over the bid of his brother (*sawm al-rajul ala sawm akhihi*). This prohibition applies once the seller has inclined toward concluding the sale; but the mere raising of offers in a transaction still open to public call, or one held open for bidding, is no harm. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ himself sold by auction to the highest bidder some of what he was commanded to sell. The scholars also permitted the resale at cost (*tawliyah*) of food before taking possession of it — in the purchase of one who buys fruits still on the trees, and in the sale of food by the seller's own measure when the buyer is aware of this and trusts him in it.

The scholars forbade the hoarding of food (*ihtikar*), and it is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was severe and stern on the matter. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad said that the Messenger of Allah was harsh in his reproof of Hakim ibn Hizam — a man of Quraysh of great wealth who, whenever food entered Madinah, would buy up all of it and hoard it to sell at whatever price he chose. He said: as for a man who buys food while it is plentiful among the people in order to store it and trade in it, there is no harm in that, so long as the people can still find what they need to buy. But when none is to be found, he has no right to hoard it against them and leave them to perish; he must bring it out and sell it.

The scholars also forbade pricing above the prevailing rate of the place (*al-tasir*). Whoever departs from the local price is told: either sell at the people's price, as they sell, or take your goods out of their market, so that you bring no inflation upon them.

Ali was asked about an unjust ruler (*sultan jair*) who seizes a man and compels him, through that pressure, to sell his property — whether the man may afterward reclaim it. He said: No. The buyer did not compel him; on the contrary, the buyer did him a service by relieving him of harm through the purchase, provided the buyer himself applied no force and the compulsion came from the unjust ruler alone. A sale made under coercion is annulled only when the seller was directly coerced into it by the very person who bought — in such a case the seller may seek remedy against the one who forced him. But when it is only the unjust ruler who drove him to sell, and the seller, fearing punishment if he refused, sold to a buyer who neither compelled him nor was specifically designated by the ruler as the buyer, then the sale stands and cannot be revoked.

It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ instructed a man who had sold a house to place its price into something of like kind. This was a directive of discipline (*tadib*), for it has been related that when estates are sold and their proceeds are not reinvested in their like, that wealth comes to nothing. He also forbade buying and selling in the mosque, during the time of the Friday prayer, and before the rising of the sun. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad said that the second call to prayer on Friday — the one given before the Imam while he stands upon the pulpit — is what forbids buying and selling until the Friday prayer has been performed.

### On Currency Exchange (al-Sarf)

Currency exchange is governed by strict rules. The Prophet ﷺ is reported to have cursed every party to a transaction involving *riba*:

- the one who consumes it
- the one who pays it
- the one who sells through it
- the one who buys through it
- the one who records it
- its two witnesses

He further declared that the consumer of *riba* will be raised on the Day of Resurrection as a madman. The Commander of the Believers, Ali, said that *riba* is among the major sins.

Allah Almighty said:

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا لَا تَأْكُلُوا الرِّبَا أَضْعَافًا مُضَاعَفَةً وَاتَّقُوا اللَّهَ لَعَلَّكُمْ تُفْلِحُونَ﴾

"O you who believe, do not devour riba, doubled and multiplied, and fear Allah, that you may prosper." (Al Imran 130)

Abu Abdullah al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) was asked about the words of Allah Almighty, ﴿يَمْحَقُ اللَّهُ الرِّبَا وَيُرْبِي الصَّدَقَاتِ﴾, "Allah blots out *riba* and causes acts of charity to grow." The question put to him was this: there are those who deal in *riba* and yet grow great in wealth — how then is it blotted out?

He said: "And what blotting could be more thorough than that of a single dirham of *riba*? If its owner repents of it, he returns it to its rightful owners and nothing of it remains to him; and if he withholds it and does not repent, He casts him into the Fire."

The people of the covenant (*ahl al-dhimmah*), it was held, are to be barred from dealing in *riba* and from practicing it openly. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali related that the Messenger of Allah (ع and his family) did not accept the *jizyah* from the people of the covenant until he had laid down certain conditions upon them: that they would not consume *riba* nor deal in it, nor eat the flesh of swine, nor marry their sisters, the daughters of their brothers, or the daughters of their sisters. Whoever among them violates these conditions today has forfeited the covenant of protection. For He, exalted be the Speaker, has said:

﴿فَبِظُلْمٍ مِنَ الَّذِينَ هَادُوا حَرَّمْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ طَيِّبَاتٍ أُحِلَّتْ لَهُمْ وَبِصَدِّهِمْ عَنْ سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ كَثِيرًا ۝ وَأَخْذِهِمُ الرِّبَا وَقَدْ نُهُوا عَنْهُ وَأَكْلِهِمْ أَمْوَالَ النَّاسِ بِالْبَاطِلِ وَأَعْتَدْنَا لِلْكَافِرِينَ مِنْهُمْ عَذَابًا أَلِيمًا﴾

*Riba* is forbidden under the Jews' own Law, even though they deem it lawful for themselves. In the Arabic language, *riba* means increase. The wealth grew — *raba al-mal yarbu* — meaning it increased, and its owner makes it grow (*yurbi*) when he adds to it. From this same root, raised ground is called *rabwah*, for its rising above the surrounding land. Yet not every increase that comes from a lawful source, even one that follows this same pattern, falls within the *riba* that is forbidden. The forbidden *riba* is specifically what the Imams — may Allah bless them — have transmitted from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: the exchange of measured or weighed goods at a disparity, kind against its own kind. Such an exchange is not permissible except like for like, hand to hand, with neither increase nor decrease on either side.

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Gold for gold, and silver for silver, hand to hand and weight for weight; whoever increases or seeks increase has dealt in *riba*. And wheat for wheat, barley for barley, flour for flour, dates for dates, raisins for raisins, corn for corn, basket for basket, and rice for rice, measure for measure; whoever increases or seeks increase has dealt in *riba*."

Muhammad ibn Ali said that no copper coin (*fulus*), nor anything else, may be introduced into an exchange of gold for gold or silver for silver as an addition to the weight.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad said that no increase is permissible in such exchanges, even when one of the two kinds is of finer quality than the other. When gold is sold for gold, silver for silver, or any measured or weighed commodity for its like, the exchange is valid only weight for weight among things that are weighed, or measure for measure among things that are measured.

Should a man trade refined gold (*ibriz*) of the purest grade for gold of the lowest grade, the exchange remains valid only weight for weight, so long as the name of gold still applies to both. The rule holds until a piece contains so much copper that copper predominates — until it is reckoned as copper and the name of gold no longer falls upon it. At that point it may be purchased with gold as copper is purchased, meaning at a disparity. The same principle governs silver against silver, and extends equally to everything that is measured or weighed.

When two different metals are joined in a single object — a decorated sword, a ring set with both — al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) taught that it should be sold against the opposite kind: gold against silver, or silver against gold. It is sold at the higher value, until it is established that the price exceeds the worth of the precious metal contained in it, so that gold is matched against gold and silver against silver, weight for weight, while the remainder of the price falls upon the sword, the ring, or whatever the object may be.

He also said that it is permissible to take dirhams in place of dinars, and dinars in place of dirhams. When a man is owed dinars — whether as an advance, from a sale, or from any other rightful claim — he may receive dirhams instead, at their value or at whatever rate the two parties agree upon; and likewise, when he is owed dirhams, he may receive dinars in their place.

He said that exchange (*sarf*) is lawful only hand to hand. If a man buys dinars for dirhams, dirhams for dinars, gold for silver, silver for gold, or any portion of one for the other, he must not part from his counterpart until he has taken delivery. If the other party says, "Send a messenger and he will settle it for you," that offer should not be accepted. Instead the buyer should say, "Give and take," and remain with the man rather than leave him. If he does send a messenger along with the other party, he must instruct that messenger himself to take delivery on the spot before parting. Should either party depart before delivery is taken, the exchange between them is void.

Whoever repays a loan of dirhams or dinars with something better than what was owed has done nothing wrong, provided the improvement springs from the borrower's own willing generosity and was not stipulated as a condition at the time the loan was made.

### On the Sale of Food to One Another

The pure Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ transmitted his prohibition of any disparity in the exchange of goods of the same kind, where those goods are measured or weighed, as has already been noted. Whoever buys something for another quantity of its own kind may take no excess on either side. When the two kinds differ, however, disparity between them is permitted — just as it is permitted between silver and gold, or between iron and comparable metals whose kinds differ — so long as both belong to what is customarily weighed or measured.

On this basis, al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) ruled as follows:

- It is not permissible to sell a sa of almonds for two sa's of almonds, nor a sa of dates for two sa's of dates.
- It is permissible to sell a sa of wheat for two sa's of dates, and a sa of dates for two sa's of raisins.

Foodstuffs and the dried fruits of the land answer to one rule: when the two kinds differ, a disparity between them causes no harm, provided the exchange is hand to hand. On deferred terms, such an exchange is not lawful.

Barley and wheat are a single kind, so a disparity between them is not permitted. Likewise, wheat, flour, and sawiq may be exchanged only measure for measure.

It was said to him that there is a surplus in the grain itself. He answered that it carries a cost — the milling and the other labor of preparation. It was said that this was so. He said that the one is therefore set against the other.

The Master said that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) forbade the sale of fresh, moist dates for dried dates, because when the moist dates dry they diminish in measure. He permitted the sale of garments one for another — one garment for more than one. The Master also said that the Messenger of Allah forbade the sale of food for food by guesswork, without measure, but permitted the exchange of bread for flour, and vinegar for vinegar even when their kinds differ, and the molasses of sugar cane for the honey of bees, like for like, hand to hand.

### On the Option of the Two Parties to a Sale

The pure Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ narrated that the two parties to a transaction retain the right to withdraw until they part by mutual consent. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad explained that this parting is the parting of their bodies from the place in which they concluded the sale. He related that his father (رض) bought a piece of land, and when he wished to make the purchase binding upon himself, he rose, walked a few steps, and then returned — intending by this to render the sale binding. He said that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) said that Muslims are bound by their conditions, except a condition that contradicts the Book of Allah, mighty and majestic.

He then recalled the story of Barirah, a bondwoman belonging to people who had drawn up a contract of emancipation with her. She approached one of the wives of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ seeking help with her emancipation payment, and that wife said to her: "I will pay what you owe and set you free." Her masters, however, refused: "We will not sell her to one who frees her unless the right of patronage (al-wala) remains with us." When the matter was brought to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he said: "Buy her and free her, for patronage belongs to the one who frees." He then addressed the people and said: "What is the matter with people who stipulate conditions not found in the Book of Allah? Every condition that contradicts the Book of Allah is void." Whoever makes a sale and stipulates a permissible condition in the contract, that condition is binding; but whoever stipulates what is not permissible, the condition is void. This is precisely what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ applied in the case of Barirah: he refused to honour the condition of patronage set by those who sold her, having already declared that patronage belongs to the one who frees.

Scholars differed on the question of a sale made with an attached condition. One group held that whoever sells something and stipulates a condition in the contract renders that condition void, arguing from a report transmitted in general terms from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ that he forbade a sale coupled with a condition. A second group held that both the sale and the condition are binding, citing the report that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ purchased a camel from Jabir ibn Abdullah al-Ansari during one of his expeditions on the condition that Jabir could ride it back to Madinah. A third group held that the sale stands but the condition is void, citing the account of Barirah already mentioned.

The teaching transmitted from the People of the House, may Allah's blessings be upon them, resolves all of this, establishes the sound position, and makes the matter clear. The condition stipulated by Barirah's masters was voided only because they had stipulated something impermissible: the Messenger of Allah ﷺ had already ruled that patronage belongs to the one who grants freedom, yet they stipulated that patronage remain with themselves rather than with the one who freed her. As for the Messenger of Allah's ﷺ permitting Jabir ibn Abdullah the condition of riding the camel he had sold — that was a lawful arrangement, neither forbidding what is permitted nor making lawful what is forbidden. As for the report that he forbade a sale coupled with a condition, if that report is sound, it is a general statement whose intended meaning is a condition that is itself unlawful and impermissible. On this basis, the People of the House (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) held that any sale containing a condition must be examined: if the condition is lawful, it stands and is binding; if it is unlawful, it is neither binding nor enforced — while the sale itself remains valid in either case.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) made this plain: if a man sells a bondwoman and stipulates in the contract that the buyer shall not sell her, shall not give her away, and that she shall not pass by inheritance should he die, then the first two conditions — that she not be sold and not be given away — are binding, because those are his to grant. The third condition, however, that she not be inherited, is void, because Allah, mighty and majestic, has ordained inheritance for a man's heirs; whoever stipulates that they shall have no share contradicts what Allah has decreed. This position of the People of the House diverges from what the generality of scholars have held, yet its proof is evident.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad also said: whoever buys something on the understanding that he holds an option over it for a fixed term, and the thing perishes within that term before the buyer has made his choice, the loss falls upon the seller's property, and the buyer must swear that he had neither chosen the goods nor accepted them. If he refuses to swear, the sale becomes binding upon him.

The Master said that the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) granted the buyer of an animal a three-day option, whether or not it had been stipulated in the contract, and that the seller holds no such option once the two parties have parted. Should the buyer perform some new act upon the animal before the three days expire, the sale becomes binding upon him.

The boy asked what was meant by such an act. The Master said it was as when the animal is a bondwoman and the buyer touches her, or kisses her, or looks upon what had been forbidden to him before the purchase — and likewise if he has intercourse with her. If he offers her for sale, he is made to swear that he did not offer her intending to keep her, but only wishing to inspect the matter before returning her if he should choose to do so.

The Master said that if a buyer sells what he purchased while his option still stands, then:

- If he had called a witness beforehand, stating that he had chosen the goods and was satisfied with them, the surplus of the price belongs to him.
- If he called no witness, he must swear to that effect, and if he refuses the oath, the surplus belongs to the seller.

The Master said that whoever buys a commodity and goes off to bring the price, but does not return with it until three days have passed, leaves the seller with a choice:

- He may demand the price.
- He may sell the goods to another.
- He may hold the goods back and rescind the sale.

After the three days, the buyer holds no standing claim upon the goods.

If a buyer holds an option for a fixed term, spends on the goods, and draws profit or use from them, then later chooses to return the purchase, he must return whatever he gained from it — while what he spent upon it remains his to recover. And if a buyer purchases a commodity on the understanding that the option belongs to another party, the option rests with the one for whom it was made.

### On the Rulings Concerning Defects

The saying of the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family), "Whoever deceives us is not of us," together with its explanation and his prohibition of deceit, has already been mentioned. Whoever knows of a defect in what he sells and conceals it has committed deceit. Equally, no one who knows of a defect should hide it from the buyer, for the Messenger of Allah (may Allah bless him and his family) said that sincere counsel is part of religion. He also said that it is not lawful for a Muslim to sell to his brother goods in which he knows there is a defect without making it plain, nor is it lawful for one who knows of it to keep it hidden.

Whoever wishes to sell free of liability for a defect must disclose that defect to the buyer and state it clearly. It does not suffice to say, "I sell to you with disavowal (*baraa*)," without naming the specific defect from which he disclaims liability, informing the buyer of it, and showing it to him. If he does no more than say, "I sell to you with disavowal," and the buyer later encounters a defect, the buyer may hold him to account for it — provided the buyer had not already seen and accepted it.

If a group buys a commodity and divides it among themselves, and one of them finds a defect in the portion that fell to him, he may claim its diminished value from the seller. If the commodity remains undivided, or if a single buyer purchased the whole and finds a defect in part of it, he likewise claims the value of the defect — unless the defective part is the very face of the commodity, in which case he may return the whole if he chooses. If the commodity is of the kind sold by weight or measure, or is otherwise uniform — cotton, linen, silk, foodstuffs, and the like — and a defect is found in part of it, the seller replaces that part with an equal quantity of the same kind.

When the buyer discovers a defect and the seller says to him, "Keep it as it is, or return it — the choice is yours," the buyer has no recourse beyond that choice: he may keep the goods or return them. If he asks instead for the value of the defect, he has no right to it unless the seller agrees.

If a buyer acquires goods, then causes some new damage to them or introduces a defect of his own, and subsequently discovers an old defect for which the seller had not absolved him, he may hold the seller to account — but he must first pay the seller the value of the damage he himself caused. He may then return the goods if he wishes, or keep them along with their defect. If, however, the seller deliberately concealed the defect from him, the buyer may return the goods and owes nothing for whatever diminishment occurred in his hands. This right of return rests on clear evidence of the concealment; in the absence of such evidence, the seller swears that he neither knew of the defect nor practiced any deception regarding it.

When a buyer presses a claim against the seller on account of a defect, the seller may require him to take an oath. The buyer swears:

- that he had no knowledge of the defect before the purchase, nor at the moment of it;
- that since learning of it he has neither put the goods to use, nor derived profit from them, nor permitted anyone else their use.

If he takes that oath, he is entitled to return the goods, or to receive the assessed value of the defect where both parties agree to that settlement, or where the case is one in which such a value is owed. If, on the other hand, he refuses the oath — or it emerges that he was aware of the defect beforehand, or that he profited from the goods after discovering it, or that he offered them for sale — then the purchase stands binding upon him and he has no further claim against the seller.

It is related from the Commander of the Believers, Ali (may Allah's blessings be upon him), and from Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn and Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon them), concerning a man who buys a bondwoman, has intercourse with her, and then discovers a defect in her: he may not return her, but he may claim the assessed value of the defect from the seller — unless he finds her to be pregnant, in which case he returns her and recovers half of a tenth of her value along with her.

They also said that a purchased slave is returnable under the warranty — al-uhda — for any of the following conditions arising within one year while in the buyer's possession:

- madness
- leprosy
- vitiligo
- al-qarn

Should any of these appear within that year, the liability falls upon the seller. So too does the calamity of death. This warranty applies specifically to slaves, not to other animals.

It is further reported from Ali (may Allah's blessings be upon him) that he said: the warranty on a slave covers the gravest disease for one year, and the calamity of death for three days.

Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) said: if the seller, at the moment of concluding the sale, explicitly disclaims to the buyer both the year's warranty and the three-day option for all animals, and the buyer releases him from these, that release is binding and the buyer has no recourse to either.

On this basis, the practice among people today is to write into the deeds for the purchase of slaves a disclaimer of the year's warranty and of the three-day option, and into the deeds for other animals a disclaimer of the three-day option. Al-Mahdi (may Allah's blessings be upon him), according to what has been transmitted, ordered that this be written into the deeds so that people would not later turn against one another and draw out their disputes. Whoever consents to the disclaimer is bound by it; whoever dislikes it is not compelled to accept it. And if the seller is content to omit the disclaimer entirely, he is not compelled to include it, and the rules described previously apply to him.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) said: there is no warranty in a sale concluded with disavowal, nor in the sale of an inheritance — neither the year's warranty nor the three-day option.
