**The Marketplace: Honest Earning, Trade, and Property**

**On the Sale of Murabaha**

Selling by murabaha — in which a price is set as the cost of purchase together with a stated profit — is permissible when both elements are declared plainly. Yet the pure Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt of the Messenger of Allah disliked the practice of conducting such a sale on the condition that the profit be fixed as a proportion of the price, because that resemblance to riba. When a man says, "I will sell you this commodity at a profit of one-tenth of its price," or any similar formula, the increase is no longer simply a profit; it has become an addition folded into the price itself, and in that form it comes to resemble riba. This is precisely the form of sale practiced among the merchants of Iraq, who say, "I will sell you this commodity for dowzadeh," or "for yazda" — Persian words meaning "for every ten, twelve," or "for every ten, one."

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad related that his father once received goods from Egypt. He prepared food and invited the merchants to his home so that they might purchase the goods. He ordered that they be fed, and they ate; then he ordered the goods to be brought out before them. The merchants said, "We will take them from you at dowzadeh." He replied, "No. I bought these goods for ten thousand dinars, and I will sell them to you for twelve thousand." They said, "We accept," and he handed the goods over to them.

Whoever buys goods and then incurs additional expenses — freight, the cost of containers, and the like — may sell them by Murabaha and reckon those expenses into the price. He should state that the goods stand him at such and such in total. He must not say that he bought them for a sum that already includes his added expenditure, for that would be a lie and would draw him toward the boundary of riba, unless he sets out the purchase price, the profit, and the expenditure separately, or combines them openly by saying, "This stands me at such and such in total." He must not claim he bought a thing for more than he actually paid.

He was asked about a man who bought a quantity of merchandise, divided it into parts, and wished to sell each part by Murabaha for what it had cost him within the whole. He replied that this was not permissible, unless the seller made clear to the buyer that he himself had apportioned the cost in that way.

He was asked about a man who bought a commodity on a deferred term of payment — that is, upon nazira — and then sold it on by Murabaha without informing the buyer of that deferment, and the buyer afterward came to learn of it. He replied that the buyer was entitled, if he wished, to the same term of deferment the seller had enjoyed, unless the seller had said to him at the time of the contract, "On this day it stands me at such a price, and I sell it to you for such a price," and had not phrased it as a fixed rate of profit.

If a man buys a garment for one dinar yet pays for it in dirhams, or agrees a price in dirhams and pays with a dinar, he may sell it by Murabaha at the price he paid, without specifying which currency he actually tendered. This rests on the ruling that it is permissible to discharge a debt of gold with silver, and a debt of silver with gold. Once he has purchased the article at the agreed price of gold or silver, and that price has become a binding obligation between him and the seller, whatever he afterward pays in settlement of it is a lawful discharge — and the sale holds firm against the one who made it.

He said that a man who buys his own slave and then sells him by Murabaha may do so, because such use does not diminish the slave's value and is not something for which compensation is owed. The same applies to:

- a man who buys a beast and rides it,
- a man who buys a slave and puts him to work, or
- a man who buys a garment and wears it —

provided, in each case, that the use causes no wear that lessens the article's worth. To disclose such use to the buyer is the safer course for the seller where his religion is concerned; yet if he does not disclose it, no liability falls upon him, as the narrations have come down.

On al-salam

> رِّجَالِكُمْ ۖ فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌۭ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا تَدَايَنْتُمْ بِدَيْنٍ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى فَاكْتُبُوهُ﴾, "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down" (al-Baqarah: 282). The pure Imams of the family of the Messenger of Allah narrated that he said: Whoever enters into a sale for an unknown term, or for an unspecified thing, has not made a true sale.

They taught that al-salam rests on four conditions, and that the contract is void if any one of them is absent or breached:

1. The goods must be described by a known and precise description.
2. Their measure must be named — by volume or by weight, according to the nature of the goods.
3. The place of delivery must be specified.
4. The term at which delivery falls due must be stated.

They further held that a salam contract is not concluded unless the price is paid before the two parties part from the place where they contracted. If the price is not handed over at that session, the transaction becomes a debt exchanged for a debt — and the Messenger of Allah forbade that.

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad held that whoever enters a salam contract for the produce of a particular village or named locality may not do so until that locality's soundness becomes apparent. Where no locality is specified, however, the salam is permissible and stands as a binding obligation on the one who received the advance. He also permitted a salam contract with a seller who does not yet possess what he has undertaken to deliver, provided that, at the time of guarantee, the goods lie within his means when delivery falls due — so that he may then acquire them, pay for them, and hand them over. The Imams further permitted salam contracts in animals, where the animal is sufficiently known and precisely described.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man who enters a salam contract for a known thing and then receives either less than it or more than it. He said that if this is by mutual consent, there is no harm in it. The Imams permitted salam in well-known, described garments, and held that if a man takes back his capital — in whole or in part — without anything added to it, that is permissible; but if he takes back something more, it is not.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about the holder of a salam obligation who pays the price to the entitled party, and that party then says to him, "Buy it for yourself and take what is due to you." He disliked this, and said that the man should have another person carry out the purchase, and should not himself undertake both the buying for his own benefit and the taking of delivery from himself.

He was then asked about a holder of a salam obligation that falls due who cannot find the specific thing owed but finds others of its kind — beasts or goods — and hands those over at their value. He said there was no harm in that. Likewise, if a man had sold food for dirhams and when the term arrived said he had no dirhams but offered food instead, there was no harm in the creditor accepting food from him, since his right was in dirhams and he might take with them whatever he wished. The Imams held it reprehensible to enter salam contracts for things that do not keep, such as fresh fruit, meat, and the like.

**On the Conditions and Rulings Governing Sale Contracts**

Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad said: whoever buys a slave and finds money with him, that money belongs to the seller, unless the buyer stipulated otherwise in the contract. If he did stipulate it, the seller has no claim to it, even if it exceeds the price of the slave. Whatever a slave possesses and holds in his hand at the time of sale is reckoned as part of his price. This does not fall under the forbidden riba, particularly in any of the following circumstances:

- the exchange involves goods on both sides;
- the thing being sold is a tangible object and the slave was bought with goods;
- the slave was himself a tangible object bought with currency;
- the slave was himself currency bought with a tangible object.

In all such cases the contract of sale is valid, and there is no disagreement on the point.

The form of a sale that is soundly contracted, and on which there is no dispute, is as follows. One man says to another, "Sell me this slave of yours" — or "this commodity of yours" — "for such and such," naming something lawful as the price, and the other replies, "I have sold it to you." Alternatively, the seller may begin by saying, "I have sold you this for such and such," and the buyer answers, "I have bought it," or "I accept this purchase." By these words the sale is concluded between them.

After the contract is made, both parties retain the right of option for as long as they remain together in the place where they contracted, and have not yet parted bodily from one another. Either party may retract before they separate, and the sale is annulled by that retraction. The sale is completed only by their parting, as described above.

Jafar ibn Muhammad addressed the case of two contracting parties in which the buyer claims, "I have handed you the price," while the commodity is still in his possession, and the seller says, "You handed me nothing." The ruling turns on the nature of the transaction:

- If it is a transaction of the kind in which witnesses are customarily called and testimony is ordinarily taken, the buyer's claim of payment is not accepted without proof. In that case the seller must swear that he did not receive the price and obtained nothing of it from the buyer in any way.
- If it is a transaction of the kind in which witnesses are not customarily called, the word of the party in whose hand the thing lies prevails, together with his oath.

The Master said: if a seller later claims he erred in a sale — that he did not know the true price at the time, or intended otherwise and was mistaken — the matter is examined by reference to value. If the gap between his selling price and the true value falls within the range by which people commonly differ in transactions of that kind, the sale stands and his claim is set aside. If the disparity is great, exceeding what people ordinarily tolerate, the sale is returned to him; and the buyer may require him to swear that he did indeed err, as he claims.

From Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī: he was asked about a man who appointed an agent to sell his goods, where the agent claimed to have sold them at an undervalue, and the owner sought to undo the sale and recover the goods. He said: the matter is again examined by reference to value. If the value on the day of sale matched the price at which it was sold, or the difference fell within the range by which people commonly differ, the sale is valid and cannot be undone. If the value was greater by a margin beyond what people ordinarily tolerate, the sale is returned. Should the buyer wish to put the owner — who seeks the return — to his oath, swearing that he neither consented to his agent's sale nor ratified it after learning of the loss, that is the buyer's right; and if the owner refuses to swear, the buyer has no further claim.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali was asked about two agents jointly appointed to sell something, where one of them sold it without the other. He said that the sale was not valid, unless authority had been granted to whichever of them might act alone — when acting alone — or to both together, when acting together.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man bargaining over a slave girl whose owner sold her to him at his discretion, saying, "I have sold her to you for whatever price you wish." The buyer accepted the sale, then named a price the seller found unsatisfactory and considered too low. He said that her value on the day of the sale must be examined. If the price offered falls short of that value, the buyer must make up the difference, for although the seller left the price to the buyer's judgment, that judgment may not be exercised against the seller unjustly.

He said that whatever a judge or a ruler sells in settlement of an obligatory debt, or on behalf of a child, or in matters resembling these, carries no warranty or liability of recourse upon the one who ordered the sale. The sale is made from the property of the one against whom it is ordered, as his own obligation, even if he possesses no other wealth.

He said that whoever trades with the property of an orphan — whether as executor, guardian, or in any other capacity — if he gains a profit, the profit belongs to the orphan; and if he suffers a loss, the loss falls upon the one who traded with it, and he must make it good from the orphan's funds, because he overstepped his bounds in doing so.

He also addressed the case of a slave whose master gave him money, which the slave used to purchase his own freedom, and whose master subsequently learned of it. In that situation, the master reclaims the money the slave received, and the slave remains in his ownership, the case reverting to the condition it was in before. This applies when the money had been earned by the slave and came to him without his master's permission. If, however, the master had released that money to him, made him a gift of something, or it had reached him through a lawful channel, and he used it to buy his freedom, then the purchase stands. A slave may also enter into a contract of manumission — *mukataba* — paying its installments out of his earnings; once he has paid the full amount stipulated upon him, he is freed.

It has been narrated from the Imams that when a man dies leaving no heir but a slave he owns, the slave is purchased out of the estate — provided his master consents to the sale — and the remainder of the estate is then given to him as his inheritance. If the master refuses to sell, the slave does not inherit, and the inheritance passes to the public treasury, there being no other heir.

He also addressed the sale of a house for a house, a share for a share, a quarter for a quarter, and the sale of a part of any such thing for a part of another: all of this is permissible, so long as both parties know precisely what they are exchanging.

From the Commander of the Faithful, Ali: he gave judgment in the case of two men who had together bought a commodity from a single seller. After the sale was concluded, both left to fetch the price. The first to return paid his share, and Ali ruled that he was entitled to take the goods from the seller. When the second man returned and paid the first half of the price, he became a partner in the goods.

A further case was narrated concerning a woman of Quraysh who held a large sum of money in trust. Two men came to her, deposited the whole amount, and said, "Do not release it to either one of us without the other." Some time later, one of them returned bearing a sign that had been agreed between him and his companion. He presented it to her and said, "He has sent me to collect the money, and this is the token between him and you." She released the money to him, and he departed with it.

The second man then came and demanded his share. She said, "Your companion has already taken it. He brought your message and the token — such and such — that was agreed between me and you." He said, "I sent nothing to you, and I gave him no token."

The matter was brought before Umar, and he gave judgment against her for the money. She then went to Ali seeking his help, and he said to Umar, "Did these two not instruct her that the money was not to be released to either one of them without the other?" Umar said, "Yes." Ali said, "Then he has no right to hold her liable until he brings his companion with him."

The woman was released, and the device that had been contrived against her was undone.

It is related from Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) that an emissary of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ came from Yemen with captives. When they reached al-Jahfa their provisions ran out, and they sold a slave girl from among the captives — a girl whose mother was with her — and brought the mother forward without her. When news of this reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, he disapproved and ordered that the girl be returned, saying: "Do not separate kindred by sale" (لَا تُفَرِّقُوا بَيْنَ ذَوِي الْأَرْحَامِ بِالْبَيْعِ).

Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) also addressed the case of a man who buys a commodity and then seeks to return it, but the seller refuses. The buyer, wishing to be rid of the transaction, surrenders part of the price in exchange for the seller accepting the return. The Imam held that the buyer may reclaim from the seller whatever he gave up in that surrender, provided the seller has genuinely accepted the return — for a valid rescission is not accomplished merely by remitting part of the price. If, however, the seller purchases from the buyer some other, entirely separate commodity for less than the price at which he originally sold to him, that is permissible.

**On Debts**

The pure Imams from the household of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ related that he said: Allah the Almighty is with the debtor until he discharges his debt, so long as he intends to discharge it and the debt was not incurred for something Allah hates. And he said: whoever frees a captive, or relieves one burdened by debt, and grants respite to one in hardship or remits what is owed him, will stand beneath the shade of the Throne on a Day when there is no shade but His shade.

The Master said: "Whoever extends a loan has the reward of charity for it." Then, afterward, he said: "Whoever extends a loan has the reward of charity for it every day." Ali (may Allah's blessings be upon him) said: "O Messenger of Allah, before this you said that whoever extends a loan has the reward of charity, and now you say every day?" He replied: "If a man lends to a fixed term, he is as one who has given it in charity; and when the term has passed and he grants further respite, it is for him the reward of charity every day until he collects it."

A man bound by a contract of manumission once stood before Ali seeking his help, but Ali found at that moment nothing to give him. So he said to him: "Shall I direct you to something better than that?" The man said: "Yes, what is it?" Ali said: "Something I heard from the Messenger of Allah (and his family). He said: were there upon you a debt as great as Sabr, Allah the Almighty would discharge it for you." And Sabr is a mountain in Yemen. The man said: "And what is it?" Ali said: "Say: O Allah, suffice me by what You have made lawful so that I need not what You have made unlawful, and enrich me by Your bounty so that I need none besides You" (اَللَّهُمَّ اكْفِنِي بِحَلَالِكَ عَنْ حَرَامِكَ وَاغْنِنِي بِفَضْلِكَ عَمَّنْ سِوَاكَ).

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade any loan that draws a benefit. Ali (may Allah's blessings be upon him) said that none should accept the riding of a beast or the loan of goods from a man to whom he has given a loan. Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) likewise disapproved of a creditor lodging with his debtor and eating his food, drinking his drink, or feeding from his fodder. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali (may Allah's blessings be upon him) stated the principle plainly: every loan that draws a benefit is riba.

This applies when the benefit arises from a stipulation or an intention — as when a creditor lodges with his debtor, eats his food, and feeds from his fodder, since the debtor may be doing so solely on account of the loan. If, however, the benefit is freely offered and was already customary between the two parties independent of the loan, there is no harm in it. It has also been transmitted from them that one who advances dirhams or dinars and is repaid in better coin commits no wrong, provided he did not stipulate it.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) was asked about a man whose regular customer or business partner borrows from him — the lender lending precisely because he profits from that borrower through their buying and selling together — and about brokers who advance money to people against their crops, intending to sell on their behalf and recover the loan from the proceeds, and who would not lend at all were that arrangement not in place. He permitted this where it is well-known and customary between the parties, but disapproved of any element from which the lender derives a direct benefit, on account of the Prophet's prohibition of a loan that draws a benefit.

It is also related of Ali, of al-Husayn ibn Ali, of Muhammad ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn, and of Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon them all) that they permitted the bills of exchange known as al-safatij: money that a man borrows in one land on the understanding that he, or another acting on his behalf, will repay it in another land. They saw no harm in this, for it is simply a loan and a debt.

It is related of them (may Allah's blessings be upon them) that dealing on credit is permitted, provided the contract is properly formed. If a man owes a debt that has fallen due and says to his creditor, "I cannot find what I might pay you with, but sell me something on a deferred term, and I will sell it and pay you from the proceeds," and the creditor does so, there is no harm in it.

If, however, the creditor transacts with him in words alone, in a manner that is not lawful, there is harm. An example would be his saying, "Lend me one hundred dinars for two hundred," or any similar increase tied to a named term, and then dressing this as a sale — selling the man something at a nominally valid price that he has inflated by that same increase, payable at that same term. Bargaining over such an increase is disliked. To leave it aside entirely and intend a plain sale, with no mention of any increase, is the safer course.

A sale contract validly concluded after such bargaining is, nevertheless, permissible. The situation resembles that of a man and a woman who exchange words bargaining over an unlawful union and then abandon it and contract a sound marriage between them: the bargaining and the back-and-forth over what is immoral is disliked and forbidden, yet it does not invalidate the marriage they afterward contract, nor anything that proceeds from it. Their returning to what is lawful, with repentance from what they had bargained over, is well, if Allah wills.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon him) was asked about a man who says to another, "Buy me such-and-such goods for so much, and I will buy them from you at a deferred price for so much, with such-and-such an increase." He replied that there is no harm in this, since the buyer acquires the goods only after the other man has come to own them. He also permitted the following: a creditor who is owed a debt payable at a future term, and who finds himself in need of it before that term arrives, may remit part of the debt so that the debtor pays the remainder early, or may accept partial payment on condition that the rest is extended to a later term — and there is no harm in either arrangement, so long as nothing is added above the original capital.

**On Transfer of Debt and Suretyship**

A transfer of debt (حَوَل) is the assignment, by a creditor, of the debt owed to him onto a third party. Suretyship (al-kafala) is the bearing of another's burden on his behalf; the one who bears it is called surety, guarantor, pledge, warrant, and underwriter, and whoever takes on such a burden is obliged to discharge what he has undertaken. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "The underwriter is liable" (اَلزَّعِيمُ غَارِمٌ). The underwriter, as stated, is the bearer of the burden. Allah says: "They said, while turning toward them: What is it you are missing? They said: We are missing the king's measuring-cup, and for whoever brings it there is a camel's load" (Yusuf 71–72), and then, "and I am underwriter for it" (وَأَنَا۠ بِهِۦ زَعِيمٌۭ) — that is, the bearer of the burden.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali and Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad (may Allah's blessings be upon them) said: when a man transfers onto another a debt he is owed, the creditor may pursue whichever of the two he wishes — either the original debtor or the one onto whom the debt was transferred — unless he has already discharged the original debtor. If that discharge was made at the time of the transfer, the creditor may pursue only the one onto whom the debt was transferred, and he has no claim against the original debtor he discharged.

When two men together stand surety for one man's debt, the creditor may take from whichever of the two sureties he wishes, unless they stipulated that the suretyship is divided equally between them. If no such stipulation was made and each gave an unrestricted suretyship, he may take the whole from whichever of them he can reach. If they stipulated in the contract of suretyship that each is surety for the other, he may take from whichever he wishes, and the one from whom he takes then recovers from his fellow surety half of what he paid. If one surety is added after another, all of them are sureties together, and he may take from whichever he wishes, unless he has discharged one of them.

Where the surety has guaranteed a sum of money, or the very thing for which he stood surety, he must discharge that obligation unless the creditor releases him from it. Producing the person on whose behalf he stood surety does not suffice in such a case. If, however, the suretyship was one of person — guaranteeing the individual's appearance — and he produces that person to the creditor on the agreed terms and is thereby quit of him, he is fully discharged and nothing further remains upon him.

If he undertook to produce the person without restriction, he must do so whenever called upon. If the suretyship runs to a fixed term, the creditor has no recourse against the surety until that term has passed; should the surety then fail to produce the person, he becomes liable for what is owed — unless the person has died. If the person has died and the surety bore responsibility only for his appearance, nothing remains upon the surety.

If the person is absent and the surety says, "I will pay what is owed upon him," and the amount owed is unknown, the surety is liable for no more than what is proven. If the amount is known, only that amount is upon him.

If the matter is one in which the person must of necessity be produced — on account of an oath that has become due upon him, a vow of abstention, his being held, or the like — then he must be produced without exception, unless he dies or the creditor releases the surety from his obligation.

There is no suretyship in a prescribed penalty. Whoever has become liable for a hadd, or retribution, or execution, or amputation cannot be released against a surety in that matter; rather, the penalty is exacted from him directly. If witnesses testify to it and he must be held until the testimony is established, he is detained, and no surety is accepted for him — for if he were to slip away, the retribution could not be exacted from the surety in his place. Nor does suretyship bind a slave to stand as surety, even if he has been permitted to trade, unless his master grants him leave to do so.

**On Interdiction and the Spendthrift**

Interdiction (al-hajr) is restraint. Allah the Almighty has said: "And test the orphans" (al-Nisa 6) — meaning, try them — "until, when they reach marriageable age," meaning puberty, "then, if you perceive in them sound judgment, hand over to them their wealth." And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ forbade the wasting of wealth, and Allah the Almighty has said: "And do not squander wastefully; indeed the squanderers are the brothers of the devils" (al-Isra 26–27).

The child is therefore barred from his wealth by the ruling of the Book until he comes of age and sound judgment and care for his property are recognized in him, whereupon his wealth is handed over to him. The bar was imposed on account of the danger of foolishness and squandering. If he comes of age and remains foolish and wasteful, he remains under interdiction; and likewise, if these qualities arise in him after maturity, he is placed under interdiction.

ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah's blessings be upon him) placed ʿAbdullāh ibn Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib (may Allah's blessings be upon him) under interdiction when his squandering of wealth was established, and brought the matter before ʿUthmān during his caliphate, calling upon him to act. ʿUthmān hesitated. Later, ʿAbdullāh purchased a salt marsh for sixty thousand, and ʿUthmān said: "By Allah, it would not please me to own it even for these two sandals of mine." ʿAlī (may Allah's blessings be upon him) then came to him and said: "Will you not interdict your nephew?"

The insane person is likewise placed under interdiction. Whoever falls under interdiction has his maintenance met from his own wealth in a fitting measure, and a guardian is appointed to protect that wealth and spend from it on his behalf. When the foolish one becomes upright, the squanderer becomes careful, and the insane one regains his reason — and those whose testimony is acceptable bear witness to the change — the interdiction is lifted. Should they relapse, it is reimposed. Whatever they disposed of from their wealth while under interdiction is likewise void.

**On Bankruptcy**

A man who falls into bankruptcy — owing debts he cannot pay, with nothing left to sell and no wealth to draw on — may not be imprisoned once his insolvency is established. If he owes debts to a group of creditors and what remains in his hand falls short of the total owed, that remainder is divided among them proportionally: each creditor receives a share corresponding to his debt, and each bears the shortfall in the same proportion.

By way of example: a man goes bankrupt owing one creditor a hundred dinars and another two hundred, and only thirty dinars are found in his possession. The owner of the hundred receives ten, and the owner of the two hundred receives twenty. The same reckoning applies whatever the amounts, however few or many the creditors.

If a creditor finds in the bankrupt's possession something he had sold him — or part of it — that creditor has a stronger claim to that specific property than any of the other creditors, until he has recovered his debt in full. Should the sale of that property yield a surplus beyond what he is owed, the remainder passes to the other creditors.

The bankrupt may not dispose of his assets independently, setting the creditors aside, until he has discharged what he owes them. The assets are to be examined carefully, with the creditors bidding against one another, until the price holds firm and no higher offer can be found. When all parties — creditors and bankrupt alike — are satisfied and consent to the sale, the assets are sold and the proceeds divided among the creditors in proportion to their claims.

Should the bankrupt refuse to sell, or should one of the creditors withhold consent, and the matter is brought before the competent authority, and it is attested before him that the sale was conducted with the utmost diligence and at the best attainable price, he orders the assets sold and the proceeds apportioned among the creditors. If the proceeds fall short of the debts, they are distributed accordingly. If they cover the debts and leave a surplus, that surplus is returned to the bankrupt. If only part of the assets is needed to settle what is owed, and the bankrupt does not wish all of them sold, only so much is sold as is required to discharge the debts upon him.

Once the creditors have come forward, a bankrupt's acknowledgment of a new debt is not accepted unless the person named in it produces clear evidence, or the creditors themselves affirm its truth. Any debt he acknowledged while he was still solvent, however, stands without question. And if something comes into his hands from which wages are owed to him, he may step forward to claim it alongside the other creditors, holding the better right to it until his wages have been paid from it.

A question was put to Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad concerning a man who buys a slave and frees him, or takes a concubine who bears him a child, or gives something away in charity — and who afterward falls into bankruptcy. How do those earlier acts stand?

He replied that if the man made the purchase at a fair price while he was still solvent, before any bankruptcy had been established against him, and only later became insolvent, then the manumission and the charity both hold. The seller in that case takes his place among the creditors and is treated as they are with respect to whatever remains in the man's possession. If, on the other hand, the man was already destitute and had nothing of substance to give, neither the manumission nor the charity is valid, for he was disposing of what was not truly his to dispose of.

It has been narrated from the People of the House that the Commander of the Faithful (ع) held that a mother by virtue of her child — the umm walad — may be sold for the price of her own freedom. That is, if a man purchases her and she bears him a child, and he dies possessing nothing else, she stands as the equivalent of what he owed. If, however, he had means, the seller takes his portion alongside the other creditors, and whatever portion of the debt remains continues as an obligation upon the freed person, to be sought whenever that person becomes able, at which point it must be paid.

Whichever of the two — the freed man or the freed woman — finds it easier to discharge the remainder may be called upon to do so, and the path of least difficulty is followed. The one who has been freed may not, however, be compelled back into service — neither as a concubine nor in any other capacity of ownership — nor may what remains of the debt be demanded of such a person in the manner it would be demanded of one still enslaved.

If the one who freed them dies with nothing to his name, yet the freed person's assessed worth exceeds what was owed, preference is given to completing the manumission at that assessed value. Where a charitable gift is involved, preference is given to ensuring the charity reaches its recipient in full, and whatever remains beyond the debt is returned.

A man who carries debts and owns slaves whose sale would cover those debts may not free them; the slaves are sold and the debt discharged, provided he has no other funds. If he does have other funds, then what already passed through his hands stands: what he spent, what he sold, and what some creditors received while others did not — all of it holds, and it is lawful for whoever received it. A man may not discharge a debt, nor sell, nor buy, except by lawful means. So long as a solvent man is still trading openly and his creditors have not moved against him, what he pays out and what he sells is valid for those who receive it; he is restrained from such dealings only once his creditors have come forward and his bankruptcy has been declared. The wife, for her part, stands among the creditors and contends for her dowry, and she is not deprived of her right.

When a creditor or claimant comes forward and the man against whom the claim is made acknowledges it — or proof is established against him and judgment is given — and he then pleads that he has nothing while the claimant calls him a liar, the question of where the burden of proof falls turns on the nature of the obligation:

- If it arose from a debt, or from something that actually reached his hands, the burden falls on him to prove that he lost it and that it left his possession.
- If what was owed never reached his hands — a liability arising from an offense, from standing as surety, from a transfer of debt by hawala, from the maintenance of a dependent, or from a woman's dowry — his plea of insolvency is accepted upon his oath, and the burden shifts to the one pressing the claim.

As for property he claims to own: if he can prove any of it, he is held to it. If he cannot, it stands as a debt against him, to be collected whenever he becomes able. Whenever it appears that he has something in hand, it is sold and his debts are paid from the proceeds.

If witnesses testify that he is in fact wealthy and that the means to satisfy his debt are merely concealed, he is imprisoned and pressed until he pays. If, when confronted, he says to his opponent, "I will settle your right and give you what I owe," and enters no plea of insolvency, that word is taken at face value, and he is held to it — imprisoned until he discharges the obligation. When a debtor who has visible property turns obstinate, the judge imprisons him and presses him to sell, disciplining him should he delay; if he persists, the sale is carried out on his behalf. And if he acknowledges the debt, or it is proven that he has funds, yet still withholds payment, he is imprisoned at his opponent's request and compelled until he renders what he owes.

On tenant farming and musaqah: tenant farming, or muzaraah, is a partnership in cultivation in which each party holds a defined share of the produce — or in which a man sows another man's land using his own oxen or his own seed in return for a known portion of the yield. Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about this and permitted it. He said that the Messenger of Allah and his family gave the land of Khaybar to the Jews on the condition that they cultivate it and receive half of what it produced, and he apportioned it with them on that basis. The land held palms and trees, and whoever worked it took a third or a quarter. Whatever the two parties agree upon, whether little or much, is permissible.

It is likewise permissible to rent land for a fixed term in order to cultivate it for a known and understood consideration. He disapproved, however, of renting land for wheat on the condition that wheat be grown in it. The tenant farmer may undertake whatever the parties stipulate as to labor, plowing, oxen, and the rest, and according to whatever they agree, whether the land belongs to both of them or to one alone. What he disliked was that they fix a separate known share for the seed, a separate share for the land, and a separate share for the oxen; rather, each party should stipulate for himself a known portion of the whole yield.

Musaqah is work upon land bearing trees, undertaken by a worker in return for a defined share of the produce. Jafar ibn Muhammad said that if a man is given land to plow, water, and tend — land holding pomegranates, palms, fruits, legumes, or the like — on the condition that he receive half of what it yields, or whatever portion the two parties agree upon, that arrangement is permissible. The same holds when land is handed over to be built up and cultivated.

If the worker plants the land and then claims that the owner had given him leave to do so, while the owner denies it, the word stands with the owner, confirmed by his oath — unless it was known at the time of planting that the worker had permission. In that case the worker swears, and he is entitled to the equivalent of a tenant's wage for that land. If, however, he advances a claim that does not fit the circumstances, he owes the customary rent of the land instead.

The same principle applies when the owner had no knowledge of the planting and holds no proof against the worker: if the worker swears that he did not rent the land on the terms alleged against him, the cultivator is liable for the equivalent of the land's rent. The owner, for his part, has no right to tear up the standing crop.

Where the cultivators plowed as trespassers and this is proven against them, and neither party will take the oath once it has been offered, and no fault is established on the owner's side, the owner is given a choice: he may claim the equivalent of the land's rent from them, or he may pay their expenses and the cost of their planting and take the crop for himself. He may not uproot it, for tearing up a standing crop is an act of corruption.

He also said that if a man plows a piece of land and another asks to share in what he has plowed — on the condition that he contribute half the seed and half the costs — and the two agree, the arrangement is permissible.

He said further that there is no harm in a man giving his ruined land to another who will restore it for a fixed period, on the condition that everything it produces during that time belongs to the one who works it; when the agreed term has passed, the land returns to its owner in improved condition.

Likewise, if the land carries a tribute charge and another man takes it on together with that charge, there is no harm in the arrangement. He may sow it. If he leaves it unsown, and the owner neither prevents him nor stands between him and the land, he owes the rent for the full term he contracted — whether he chooses to plow or to leave it fallow — unless it was stipulated at the outset that no rent falls due except when he actually plows.

The choice between plowing and leaving the land rests with him, and he is bound by the condition placed upon him; where such a condition was made, both parties are held to what they contracted.

He was asked about the people of a village burdened with a tribute that the ruler pressed upon them harshly, who then assigned the matter to a man on the condition that whatever he paid on their behalf — little or much — would discharge their obligation, and that any surplus beyond what was demanded would be his. He replied that if they agreed to this willingly, the arrangement is permissible, and the man who took the burden from them is entitled to the surplus they agreed upon.

On rents and hire: the Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah narrated that there was found in the sheath of a sword a writing that bore the curse of Allah, of the angels, of the prophets and the messengers, and the curse of the Prophet Muhammad upon whoever claims as his father one who is not his father, or claims as his patron one who is not his patron, or wrongs a hired laborer of his wage, or moves the landmark boundaries of a road. Ali, the Commander of the Faithful, said, "I found this writing in the sheath of the sword of the Messenger of Allah and his family, and I know it." That subject is a long one, and its full treatment belongs elsewhere.

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿قُل لَّا أَسْأَلُكُ عَلَيْهِ أَجْرًا إِلَّا الْمَوَدَّةَ فِى الْقُرْبَى﴾, "Say: I do not ask you for any reward for it except affection in kinship" (Al-Shura 23). This verse too opens onto a longer discourse that belongs in its own place.

The consensus transmitted from the Imams holds that a man may lease out himself, those under his charge, and whatever he owns — whether a beast, a tool, a ship, land, a dwelling, or anything else — in all its lawful forms. The wage for such a lease is lawful, and earning it is permitted, provided the hire is contracted for a fixed term, a known purpose, and on terms that are right and allowed. None of this holds where the subject of the hire is something unlawful to profit from or unlawful to do. That is a foundational principle from which many particular rulings branch.

A man who has no authority over himself cannot validly hire himself out, nor can he hire out what he does not own and has no right over. A man who holds something it is not lawful for him to own — one who has seized a free person, for instance, or who keeps instruments of forbidden amusement — may not rent these out, and no one may lawfully hire them from him. Nor may a man lease even what he rightfully owns to one who will use it for an unlawful end: as when a man hires out himself, his beast, his tools, or his ship for the making of wine, for carrying it, or for anything of that kind.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about taking a wage for teaching the Quran, and he found it objectionable. He related that a man had once said to the Commander of the Faithful, Ali, "I love you, O Commander of the Faithful." Ali replied, "But I hold something against you." The man asked why, and Ali said, "Because you take a wage for teaching the Quran, and I have heard the Messenger of Allah and his family say that whoever takes the teaching of the Quran as a livelihood will have that as his only portion on the Day of Resurrection."

Yet they permitted the taking of wages for teaching writing, literature, and the other subjects that teachers impart to children, and they themselves paid such wages; had it been forbidden or even disliked, they would not have paid it. What was disliked was solely the wage for teaching the Quran on its own. When a teacher instructs children in the Quran together with other subjects for which a wage may lawfully be taken, there is no harm in it, and the wage falls upon what is lawful rather than upon what is not.

It is narrated that the Messenger of God and his family married a woman to one of his companions on the condition that he teach her a surah of the Quran. The report survives only in summary and does not state that he made the teaching itself her dowry; and a marriage may be valid even without a named dowry, as the matters of marriage will address. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali was asked about a man over whom the Quran is recited, who, once the recitation is complete, prepares food as people customarily do and invites those who recited with him, including the one who led the recitation. He replied that there is no harm in it, so long as it is not done for the sake of the Quran recitation itself.

The scholars also permitted the taking of a wage for ruqyah performed by means of the Book of God and His names. It is narrated that the Messenger of God and his family dispatched a company who passed by one of the Arab encampments and lodged there. The chief of that encampment was stung, and its people came to ask whether any among the company could perform ruqyah. One of the companions recited the opening chapter of the Book, al-Fatihah, over him, and he recovered. The company was given thirty sheep, which they accepted. When they returned to the Messenger of God and his family and recounted what had happened, he allowed them to keep what they had taken.

Abu Abdullah al-Sadiq, Jafar ibn Muhammad, was asked about a man who pays another a wage on the condition that the other teach him a craft and allow him to work alongside him. He permitted it. This falls within what was established earlier: if the craft is lawful, the arrangement is permitted. Whoever hires, or is hired, to teach something unlawful — singing, idle entertainment, and the like — the arrangement is not permitted.

On the question of the muezzin, it was related that the Commander of the Faithful said the muezzin's wage falls among unlawful gain, *suht*, yet he also said there is no harm in the muezzin receiving a stipend from the public treasury. The apparent intent is that he disliked only the muezzin taking a wage directly from those for whom he calls the adhan. By the same principle, it was held undesirable for an imam to take a wage from those he leads in prayer, or for a judge to take one from the parties between whom he adjudicates — while it was permitted for all of them to be sustained from the Bayt al-Mal, the House of Wealth.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about the wage of the broker — the samsar — engaged by either the seller or the buyer, and he permitted it, provided the transaction on which the broker is hired is itself lawful. He was also asked about a broker who is given a commodity to sell and is set a price for it, on the condition that whatever he obtains above that price is his as his fee, and he permitted that arrangement as well. It was further held that a hired worker or craftsman who spoils or destroys what he was engaged to handle is liable for the damage — as with the fuller who tears a garment, or the tailor or the dyer who ruins it.

A hired worker who spoils a task entrusted to him — who cuts a garment wrongly or departs from his instructions — and likewise a porter or carrier who breaks what he was paid to transport, bears responsibility for the loss whenever the goods were surrendered into his keeping and he himself took charge of them. Where a man merely lets out his animal while the renter accompanies his own goods, however, and those goods are broken or damaged while in the renter's charge, no liability falls on the animal's owner.

If the hired worker or porter claims that what was handed to him was lost from his hands, and the one who delivered it denies this, the burden of proof lies with the claimant, and the oath falls on the one who handed over the goods — swearing that he does not know it to have been lost. The worker or porter remains liable unless he can produce proof of the loss; yet if proof establishes that the goods were stolen or wrested from his hands by force, nothing is owed by him.

Leasing and hiring are permitted for a price paid in specie or in goods. Jafar ibn Muhammad — prayers of Allah be upon him — was asked about taking the use of one house in exchange for the use of another, and he said, "There is nothing wrong with that." He was also asked about a man who rents dwellings by the month on the understanding that if he occupies them for a single day he is bound for the whole month, or for the whole year. The Master said that the man is held to whatever he has bound himself to.

When two parties dispute the payment of rent, with the house owner wishing to take payment in advance and the renter saying, "I will not pay you until the end of the month or the year," the Master ruled as follows: if they stipulated this arrangement as a condition at the outset, it stands as they contracted it; if they laid down no condition, the owner may take the rent day by day, each day as it falls due.

He was also asked about a man who rents a house that has trees on the property and stipulates their fruit as part of the rental agreement. The Master said that this is permissible if the fruit was already in blossom at the time the contract was made — or if some of it was in blossom, or if there was some present yield alongside it. If none of these conditions held, the stipulation is not permissible, and the rental contract itself is void if it was concluded on that footing.

When asked about a man who rents a house that has been partly demolished, or that came to him through inheritance, or whose rooms leak when rain falls — and the renter presses the owner to carry out repairs — the Master said that the owner cannot be compelled to do so. If the damage harms the renter, however, he may reduce the rent and vacate, owing only for what he has already occupied. If the damage works no harm, the rental is not dissolved. The Master added that even where the renter has not stipulated that the owner repair what has decayed and clear out its drains, that obligation still falls upon the owner without any stipulation, because it is among the things known by custom to be incumbent upon the owner of a house. He also said that it is not permissible for the renter to bring into the house anything that would harm it, unless he has stipulated that right in the rental contract.

When asked about a dispute between renter and owner over the amount of the rent — the owner claiming the greater sum and the renter the lesser, whether or not the renter has already occupied the house — the Master said that both parties take an oath. Whichever of them shrinks from the oath, the word of the other prevails, provided that other has sworn. If both swear, or both refuse the oath together, the rental is dissolved.

When asked about the hire of undivided property (kira al-musha), the Master said that the hire of undivided property is permissible, just as its sale is permissible.

The Master was then asked about a man living in another man's house who claims he was given lodging there free of charge, while the house's owner says, "No — I let it to you for such and such a sum," and neither party has proof. The Master said that the owner swears he did not lodge the man without charge, and the resident then owes him the fair rental value — unless that fair value exceeds what the owner himself claimed to have charged, in which case the owner receives only the amount he acknowledged and no more. Likewise, if the renter claims the owner instructed him to spend on the house and to repair it, and he did so, but the owner denies having given any such instruction, then where the renter has no proof, the owner swears that he issued no such order, and the renter is entitled to recover the materials of the repair.

The Master was also asked about a man who rents a house in which the owner's goods are stored, on the condition that the owner clears them out, and who after the contract is concluded finds the owner slow to remove them. The Master said that in such a case the owner is owed rent only to the extent the renter was actually able to occupy the house.

The Master was then asked about a house damaged, in whole or in part, through some act of the renter that had not been stipulated in the rental contract. He said that the renter guarantees whatever damage he caused in that way — unless the act in question is one that tenants customarily perform, in which case no liability falls on him even without an explicit stipulation, so long as it remains within what is commonly understood. Not every action a renter takes needs to be spelled out as a condition.

He was asked about an animal or a ship damaged before reaching the destination for which it was hired. He said that whoever hired a particular animal or ship — having seen it, inspected it, and taken it into his charge — finds the hire dissolved when it is damaged, and owes only the proportional rent for the distance already traveled. If, however, he hired carriage without naming any particular animal or ship, the carrier (*makari*) must furnish a substitute of equal quality to carry the load to the agreed destination, and the full rent remains due.

He was asked about one who hires an animal for a known number of days — to ride it, load it, grind with it, or thresh with it — fixing no precise schedule but naming only the intended use. He said that this arrangement is permissible, and the renter may put the animal to that use within just bounds. He must not press it beyond proper use, and the owner may not cut the agreed period short. If the renter named no intended use and then wishes to put the animal to some labor that would harm or diminish it, he has no right to do so.

When someone asked about a person who hires an animal or a ship to carry a known load, on the condition that it be delivered within a fixed period, and then fails to deliver within that period and exceeds it, the Master said that a hire on such terms is void, and the hirer owes only the equivalent wage.

It was related of Ali (prayers of Allah be upon him) that he gave judgment concerning a man who hired an animal to a named destination and then took it beyond that point, so that it perished. Ali held him liable for the animal itself but did not also charge him rent for the distance beyond the agreed limit. Al-Sadiq Jafar ibn Muhammad (prayers of Allah be upon him) added: if the animal did not perish, and the renter took it beyond the stipulated limit, then when its owner calls him to account for the excess, the owner may — as he chooses — either take a wage commensurate with that excess or take compensation for the diminishment the excess caused, but he may not take both together.

Likewise, if a man hires an animal for a day or several days and then keeps it beyond that term, the owner has the choice between taking the proportional rent for the time held after the term expired and taking the equivalent hire rate. If the animal perishes while he has held it past the stipulated term, he is a guarantor of its value.

When asked about a dispute between two parties over the distance of a journey — the renter claiming a far destination while the animal's owner claims a near one, both agreeing that a hire took place — the Master said: the burden of proof falls on the one making the greater claim, which is the renter. If the renter produces no proof, the oath passes to the carrier (*makari*). If the two parties agree on the destination but differ over the route, the burden of proof falls on whoever claims the more arduous of the two roads, and the oath falls on the other. If the routes are equal in difficulty and the dispute is simply over which was contracted, the matter turns on whether the journey has begun:

- If the renter has neither ridden nor set out, both parties take an oath and the contract is dissolved when neither produces proof; whoever refuses the oath is bound by his fellow's claim.
- If the renter has already ridden or set out, the owner's word prevails and the renter stands as the claimant.

When asked about a man who hires carriage to a country, and the carrier, upon reaching the first settlement of that country, wishes the renter to alight there, while the renter insists on being taken to its farthest point — no particular place within that country having been named in the contract, as when a man hires carriage to Iraq, to Khurasan, to the Levant (al-Shām), to Africa (Ifrīqiya), or to any country of that kind — the Master said: in such a case, the obligation is discharged upon reaching the chief city of that region: the one that is its mother-city, the one renowned as its heart, the one by whose name the region is known, and the one that travelers customarily have in mind when they set out for it.

He was then asked about land taken on hire that is struck by calamity — flooding, the recession of water, the drying of a spring, or the cutting off of a river by which it was irrigated. The Master said: if the renter wishes to spend from that year's rent on restoring it, he may do so, and the cost falls upon the landowner; otherwise, he owes only in proportion to what he has cultivated and benefited from, and the hire is dissolved from that point forward.

He was asked about a hire in which an option (khiyār) is stipulated. The Master said: whatever is stipulated from among what is lawful and permissible stands as valid; whatever is not lawful and not permissible does not stand, and the hire itself remains in force as it is.

He was asked about a man who delivers wheat to the miller, or sesame to the oil-presser, stipulating a known measure to be returned to him in exchange for a fixed wage for the work. The Master said: to fix the arrangement in that manner is not permissible. The miller and the oil-presser are entitled to a fair wage for their labor, and the owner of the wheat or the sesame takes back whatever each of them actually produces.

He was asked about the earnings of the cupper (al-ḥajjām), and he saw no harm in them. The Master said: the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace — paid the cupper, and the Imams continue to pay them to this day; had it been unlawful, they would never have given it to them.

He was asked about the craftsman approached by someone wanting work done, who promises what he later cannot deliver — a tailor, for instance, shown a garment who says he will cut matching cloth and then finds the cloth falls short; or a goldsmith who says a piece will require a certain weight of gold or silver, begins the work, melts the metal, and finds he cannot finish it; or one who presents gold or silver as sound when it proves to be base. The Master said: if each of them spoke to the best of his knowledge and the full extent of his effort, and then erred, nothing is held against him. But if it is established, or commonly known of him, that he intended to deceive his client, he is liable for whatever he has spoiled.

On Pledges

> رِّجَالِكُمْ ۖ فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌۭ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ

﴿يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا إِذَا تَدَايَنْتُمْ بِدَيْنٍ إِلَى أَجَلٍ مُسَمًّى فَاكْتُبُوهُ﴾, "O you who believe, when you contract a debt for a specified term, write it down" (al-Baqarah: 282), and ﴿وَلَمْ تَجِدُوا كَاتِبًا فَرِهَانٌ مَقْبُوضَةٌ﴾, "and you do not find a scribe, then a pledge taken in hand" (al-Baqarah: 283). These verses establish that a pledge (رَهِن) is valid only once it has been taken into possession; whatever has not been received is no pledge at all. Whatever may be sold may likewise be pledged. Whoever takes an undivided share in pledge receives possession of it in the same way an undivided share is received in a sale. The one holding a pledge may not derive any benefit from it. If the pledge perishes, the loss falls upon the wealth of the pledgor (رَهِن), unless the pledgee brought about its destruction. When a pledge is destroyed, the pledgee has no right to demand a replacement; his only recourse is to claim his debt when it falls due.

If the pledgor and the pledgee disagree over what the pledge was intended to secure, the burden of proof rests on the one claiming the greater amount, who is the pledgee, and the oath falls upon the pledgor regarding the excess claimed against him. If the pledge has already perished and the parties then differ over its value, the burden of proof again rests on the one claiming the surplus — here the pledgor, since the pledge was in his possession — and the pledgee swears regarding the excess he claims.

The pledgee may not sell the pledge when its term falls due except by order of a judge, and only after the debt has been established before him. If the pledgor is absent, the judge orders the pledge sold on his behalf and the pledgor's due paid from the proceeds — just as an absent debtor's property is sold for his debt, the judge acting in the pledgor's stead. Should the pledgee sell the pledge — whether at maturity, after it, or before it — without the pledgor having authorized him to do so, he is liable for it; and whatever he has enjoyed or profited from the pledge belongs to the pledgor.

The pledgor, for his part, may not sell the pledge, give it away, donate it as charity, free it if it is a slave, or remove it from his ownership by any means whatever, until he has redeemed it. The pledgee does not sell it either; rather, the matter is referred to the judge, who sells it on behalf of the absent party once the debt is established before him, appointing someone to carry out the sale and settle the debt from its proceeds, just as is done with property not held in pledge.

If, however, the pledgor has authorized the pledgee to sell the pledge at maturity, and the pledgee then sells it — calling witnesses, striving to obtain the highest price, and conducting the sale to the fullest — nothing is held against him in that, even should the pledgor suspect him in the sale and wish to have him swear to it.

If the pledgee wishes to purchase the pledge himself, there is no objection, provided both parties agree: the price is set against the debt, and any surplus is settled between them.

**On Partnership**

Partnership in wealth — al-shirka — is permissible under the teaching of the Imams of the Ahl al-Bayt (prayers of Allah be upon them) when two men, or a group, enter into it together. Each party contributes wealth of his own and mingles it with his partner's until the funds form a single pool, no longer separately distinguishable, from which they buy and sell together. Profit arising from that pool is shared between them; any loss falls upon them in proportion to what each contributed.

Neither partner may sell, buy, or initiate any new transaction involving their common fund without the knowledge and consent of the other. If, however, each grants the other full discretion to act as he sees fit, that latitude is permitted and the other partner has no claim against him for it — unless he wrongs him. In that case, the aggrieved partner may say to him:

"You have betrayed me," or "You favored another over me in buying and selling," or "in what I entrusted to your charge," or "you set out to squander my wealth" —

or words to that effect. The aggrieved party then has the right to require his partner's oath that he committed no such wrong and intended none of it.

Where the two partners hold equal shares and stipulate that profit and loss are likewise to be divided equally, that stipulation is binding. Where they stipulate an unequal division, the profit is distributed as stipulated, while loss is borne in proportion to each partner's capital, regardless of what was agreed regarding profit.

When two partners contribute capital and labor in equal measure, both profit and loss are divided according to their agreed terms. If they stipulate a different arrangement, profit follows what they have stipulated, while loss remains proportional to the capital each has put in. The same principle holds when their contributions are unequal, so that one partner brings more than the other: profit is shared according to their agreement, but loss is borne in proportion to the capital.

When the money belongs to only one of the two partners, the arrangement becomes mudaraba — that is, speculation — and the partner who contributes no capital is the mudarib, the working partner. The terms may stipulate that the mudarib alone shall work the money and trade with it, or that both partners shall work together; either way, both are bound by what they have stipulated. Profit is divided between them according to their contract, but loss falls upon the owner of the money alone and not upon the mudarib. If the owner of the money guarantees the mudarib against any shortfall or loss he might incur, that guarantee voids the arrangement: it is no longer a valid mudaraba or partnership but becomes a loan. The borrower then keeps whatever gain he earns, and he must guarantee the principal as he would for any loan taken upon himself.

When the mudarib violates any condition the owner of the money stipulated — whether in what he buys, what he trades in, where he travels, or any other term of the mudaraba contract — profit is still divided between them according to their agreement. Yet if a loss occurs, or the money passes out of his hands, he is its guarantor and answerable for whatever is lost, because he transgressed the terms.

If a man gives money to another to work with and trade in, on the condition that the recipient returns a specified, fixed profit, that arrangement is not permissible and is not binding upon the recipient. It is riba, which is unlawful, and he must return whatever he took and repent to Allah Almighty for it. The single exception arises when the one handing over the money is the master and the recipient his slave: what is paid to the slave is then lawful and permitted to him. There is no riba between a master and his slave, because the slave's wealth belongs to his master in any case.

When one of the partners dies, the partnership is dissolved. Any partner may also annul and dissolve it whenever he wishes. If a partner or a mudarib is accused of wrongdoing, he clears himself by oath.

Partnership is disliked when it is formed over goods that remain distinct and are not mingled — each contribution kept separate from the other. When two parties share in what each holds apart, whatever each one holds remains his own, whether it increases or decreases. If they wish to enter a genuine partnership, however, each may sell to the other half of the separate goods in his possession at a known price, commit to that sale, and on that basis form a valid partnership.

It is disliked for a Muslim to enter into partnership with a dhimmi, or for a believer to partner with one who differs from him in religion. Such a partner may buy and sell in ways the believer does not permit and cannot prevent, and that opens the door to unlawful gain and riba-tainted wealth entering his holdings. If, however, the believer or Muslim himself oversees all buying and selling and the dhimmi or the differing party has no hand in any transaction, the partnership is unobjectionable.

When a mudarib dies leaving a debt he owes, speculation funds entrusted to him, and deposits held in his keeping, and none of these is found intact within his estate, the ruling distinguishes the debt from the trust. The debt is binding, because it rested upon his personal liability. The speculation funds and the deposit are a different matter — he held them as a trustee. If they are not found in his estate by their own substance, and no proof is established against him that he consumed them, was compensated for them, destroyed them, mingled them with his own wealth, or did anything else that would render him liable, then nothing is required of his heirs beyond an oath: that they do not know him to have done any such thing, that they have not done it themselves, and that none of it is in their possession.

If the holder of such a claim names, before his death, the party to whom a particular asset belongs, that asset goes to the one he named. If he did not hand it over before dying, however, the debt takes precedence and is satisfied first.

When the funds are already fully committed, they may not be shared with an absent partner, and partnership with one who is absent is not valid.

If a man is owed a debt and, before recovering it, attempts to bring that debt into a partnership or a mudaraba with the debtor, the arrangement is not valid and no partnership or mudaraba is formed — not until the creditor takes actual possession of the debt and hands it over. Only then may he use it to form a partnership or mudaraba.

When two partners separate and settle accounts while a debt from their partnership remains outstanding, they may not divide that debt on the condition that each recovers only his assigned share, to be held separately if a dispute arises later. What is required is that whatever either partner recovers belongs to both of them in common, and whatever portion of the debt is lost falls upon both alike. If, however, one says to the other, "Give me my capital" — or whatever sum they had agreed upon — "and yours is whatever exceeds it, and upon you falls whatever falls short," and both agree to this, then it is permissible for them to act on that agreement.

**On Pre-emption**

Pre-emption — *shufah* — applies to dwellings and real property when an undivided share or shares are sold: portions held in common that have not yet been partitioned between the seller and his partner or partners. In such a case, the partner holds a stronger claim to the sale than any stranger who has no share in it, and is the worthier pre-emptor. If one partner exercises his right while the others do not, he stands ahead of those who held back. If all come forward together, the property is shared equally among them, each taking according to his portion in the partnership. Where their shares differ, pre-emption follows those shares proportionally; where their shares are equal, it is divided equally among them.

Pre-emption does not apply to a neighbor or anyone else in property that has already been divided, nor does it apply to a river, a ship, an animal, or anything other than real estate and undivided shares — that is, land and whatever stands upon it of buildings or planted trees. Where a property is jointly owned and one partner sells his share, the other holds the stronger claim by pre-emption.

Pre-emption is preserved on behalf of a minor until he comes of age. If his guardian or whoever is responsible for his affairs is able to exercise it for him, and doing so would benefit the child, it should be taken on his behalf. It is likewise preserved for an absent partner until he returns or news of the sale reaches him, at which point he has up to a year to take it up or let it pass. A partner who is present has the same span: one year from the moment the sale comes to his knowledge, unless he surrenders his right before that time.

The right belongs to the pre-emptor by virtue of his partnership in what is sold — whether his share is small or large, and whether he holds a stake in the whole property or only in part. This includes a wall standing between two houses that belongs to both owners, or in which one of them holds a common share, or any other right they own together that the sale touches, whether slight or considerable. Pre-emption in such a thing belongs to whoever holds a share in it, however small or large that share may be.

Pre-emption belongs to the people of a private lane — al-Raighah — who share the lane without directly partnering with one another in ownership, provided no barrier separates them from the property in question. No such right exists in a public thoroughfare, because the people whose dwellings open onto a public street do not own it as the people of a private lane own theirs. They benefit from it only through their courtyards, and in this they stand on exactly the same footing as any passer-by. The right of pre-emption over what is sold along a public street therefore does not belong to those who front it; it belongs to the people of the private lane among themselves.

Where a house sits within a private lane and contains a dwelling, and that dwelling is sold, the people of the surrounding houses hold a stronger claim to pre-emption than the buyer, and they may exercise it over whatever is sold within the lane — because they hold ownership of their own courtyards, while the people of the lane itself own nothing of those interior houses. The same principle applies when a lane runs within a lane: the people of the inner lane may pre-empt what lies along their own path and passage. The people of the outer lane, including those at its upper reaches, may not pre-empt what lies below them, in which they hold no right and to which they have no path beyond the boundaries of their own portion of the lane. The question in every case is examined in light of shared rights, for it is the sharing of rights that governs.

Whoever holds a right in what is sold — or in any of the rights upon which the sale falls — is a partner, and therefore a pre-emptor. This reflects the principle of shared rights among the people of the lane.

If a man owned outright all the houses within his lane, it would be his right to open the lane from the outside, to possess the whole of it, and to bar anyone from entering or passing through it without his leave. So too, when there is a lane within a lane and the owner of the inner lane owns all the houses opening onto it, he may take possession of the whole and withhold it from others. The same applies to everything within the lane, except what is bordered by a wall belonging to others among the people of the lane — there his ownership reaches only to its boundary.

A Jew or a Christian has no right of pre-emption against a Muslim. Muslims, however, may exercise pre-emption in property they share with other Muslims and with dhimmis alike. Dhimmis, for their part, may pre-empt against one another in transactions where pre-emption would ordinarily apply, but they hold no such right against Muslims.

Pre-emption does not arise in the following cases:

- A gift
- Charity
- A grant of residence
- A life grant
- A grant made for the lifetime of the recipient

Nor does pre-emption apply when a sale is concluded against goods rather than a monetary price — as when a house is exchanged for another house, for a riding animal, or for any other livestock or merchandise. In such a case, the pre-emptor cannot claim the house by offering the value of the goods on which the transaction was concluded.

The same principle holds when a man gives a house as a dowry upon marrying a woman. Even if pre-emption would ordinarily be due in such a house, the pre-emptor cannot say, "I will pay a dowry equal to this woman's and take the house."

If, however, a house was sold for a price and a quantity of goods was received in settlement of that price, the pre-emptor is offered the house at the price on which the sale was concluded. Likewise, if the owner of a house marries a woman for a known dowry and then hands her a house in settlement of it, this constitutes a sale, and the pre-emptor may take the house for the dowry by which the woman received it. When what is subject to pre-emption is sold for something that has a known equivalent — measured wheat, dates, or anything else sold by measure or weight for which an equivalent is established — pre-emption is due, and the pre-emptor receives that equivalent in place of the price.

The pre-emptor may press his claim against either the seller or the buyer, depending on which party bears the obligation at the time. When a sale has been concluded and completed between the two parties, and the pre-emptor comes forward against the seller before the price has been collected from the buyer and pays it to him, what he receives in return is rightfully his. The buyer cannot block him or say, "I will pay what I bought it for and take it from you, since the pre-emption stands against me." The pre-emptor's claim rests upon the seller, and the buyer is bound to deliver. If, on the other hand, the buyer pays the price first and the pre-emptor then presses his claim against the buyer within the period in which the claim remains valid, that too is his right.

When property subject to pre-emption passes from buyer to buyer in a chain of successive sales — whether the pre-emptor is aware of them or not — he may press his claim against whichever party in that chain he chooses, paying that party the price that party itself paid to acquire the property, whether more or less than the original purchase price. This right holds as long as the pre-emption period has not expired and he has not relinquished his claim. He stands as pre-emptor at the moment of every sale in the chain, and his failure to act against any one of those sales does not forfeit his right while the period still runs.

The principle may be illustrated as follows. A buyer acquires property that is subject to another's right of pre-emption, then sells it to a second party for more or less than he paid; that second party sells to a third, and so on through a succession of owners. The pre-emptor may press his claim against any one of them he selects, provided the period reckoned from the original purchase has not elapsed and he has not surrendered his right.

If he presses his claim against the first buyer — who had, within the pre-emption period, already sold the property for more than he paid — the effect is to unwind that sale and every subsequent transfer. The pre-emptor then takes the property at the price the first buyer paid, delivering that amount to him. The same course applies to each party who came after: the claim against any one of them unwinds the chain from that point forward on the same terms.

Where a single house contains an upper and a lower dwelling, divided and sold separately, the owner of the upper has no pre-emption over the owner of the lower, nor the lower over the upper, provided the division took place before the sale. However one part stands above the other, the relationship between them is simply that of neighbors.
