Jafar ibn Muhammad, may Allah's blessings be upon him, was asked about the right of a woman over her husband — the fulfilling of which makes the husband a doer of good. He said that the husband feeds her, clothes her, and when she wrongs him, he pardons her. He added that his father, may Allah's blessings be upon him, had a wife who used to vex him, and he would forgive her, citing the words of the Messenger of Allah and his family:

«اَلْمَرْأَةُ كَالضِّلَعِ، إِنْ تَرَكْتَهَا اِنْتَفَعْتَ بِهَا، وَإِنْ أَقَمْتَهَا كَسَرْتَهَا»

"The woman is like a rib: if you leave it be, you take benefit from it, and if you try to straighten it, you break it."

It was then said to him, "But the woman is jealous over her husband." He said, "That is love."

He was also asked about a man who turns away from his wife because worship, fasting, and prayer occupy him entirely. He said that the wife of Uthman ibn Mazun came to the Messenger of Allah and said, "O Messenger of Allah, Uthman fasts the day and stands the night in prayer." The Messenger of Allah and his family understood what she intended. He went out to the mosque, where he found Uthman ibn Mazun standing in prayer, and said to him, "O Uthman, Allah, mighty and majestic, did not send me with monasticism; He sent me with the upright way. Whoever loves my nature, let him follow my Sunnah, and among my Sunnah is marriage." The Messenger of Allah and his family also forbade the striking of women where it is not warranted.

A man of the Ansar came to the Messenger of Allah and his family, bringing his daughter, and said, "O Messenger of Allah, her husband has struck her; grant her retaliation against him." The Messenger of Allah and his family granted her that.

Then Allah, mighty and majestic, sent down: «الرِّجَالُ قَوَّامُونَ عَلَى النِّسَاءِ بِمَا فَضَّلَ اللَّهُ بَعْضَهُمْ عَلَىٰ بَعْضٍ وَبِمَا أَنفَقُوا مِنْ أَمْوَالِهِمْ ۚ فَالصَّالِحَاتُ قَانِتَاتٌ حَافِظَاتٌ لِّلْغَيْبِ بِمَا حَفِظَ اللَّهُ ۚ وَاللَّاتِي تَخَافُونَ نُشُوزَهُنَّ فَعِظُوهُنَّ وَاهْجُرُوهُنَّ فِي الْمَضَاجِعِ وَاضْرِبُوهُنَّ ۖ فَإِنْ أَطَعْنَكُمْ فَلَا تَبْغُوا عَلَيْهِنَّ سَبِيلًا ۗ إِنَّ اللَّهَ كَانَ عَلِيًّا كَبِيرًا» "Men are the protectors and maintainers of women, because Allah has favored some of them over others, and because they spend of their wealth.

The Messenger of Allah then said: «أَرَدْتُ أَمْرًا وَأَرَادَ اللَّهُ غَيْرَهُ» "I intended one thing, and Allah intended another."

It is also reported from him that jealousy is a part of faith, and careless yielding is a part of hypocrisy — jealousy meaning that which is felt over what Allah has forbidden, and yielding meaning what brings men and women together for what is forbidden. In another report from Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him and upon the Messenger of Allah and his family, the Prophet forbade al-madhal, which is the abandonment of due jealousy. The root of the word derives from a man's making his secret known — that is, exposing it — and from this root comes the sense of a man's exposing his womenfolk to other men. Jealousy over what is lawful, however, is disliked and forbidden.

Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him, said: there is no jealousy in what is lawful. This is borne out by what the Messenger of Allah and his family did on the night he brought Fatimah, may Allah's blessings be upon her, to her husband, after she had become his wife. He said to them: «لَا تُحْدِثَا شَيْئًا حَتَّىٰ آتِيَكُمَا» "Do not do anything until I come to you." He said this after they had already lain down. Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him, held back accordingly, and the Messenger of Allah and his family entered, prayed for them, blessed them, and then departed.

The Messenger of Allah and his family said: «كُتِبَ الْجِهَادُ عَلَىٰ رِجَالِ أُمَّتِي وَالْغَيْرَةُ عَلَىٰ نِسَائِهَا، فَمَنْ صَبَرَتْ مِنْهُنَّ وَاحْتَسَبَتْ أَعْطَاهَا اللَّهُ أَجْرَ شَهِيدٍ» "Striving has been prescribed upon the men of my community, and jealousy upon its women; so whichever of them is patient and seeks her reward, Allah, mighty and majestic, grants her the reward of a martyr."

From him also came mention of women and what they ask of men. They burden men, he said, when they deck themselves in gold and wear silk — burdening the rich and wearing out the poor.

From Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him: whoever obeys his wife in four things, Allah casts him upon his face into the Fire:

- obeying her in attending wedding feasts
- obeying her in attending gatherings of wailing
- obeying her in paying visits
- obeying her in going to the bathhouses

**On Marriage Through Guardians**

The tradition passed down from the Imams of the Prophet's family runs: «لَا نِكَاحَ إِلَّا بِوَلِيٍّ وَشَاهِدَيْ عَدْلٍ» — "There is no marriage save with a guardian and two upright witnesses." Alongside this, the Prophet forbade that any woman be given in marriage until she has been consulted.

From Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him: "None of you should give his daughter in marriage until he consults her, for she knows herself best. If she keeps silent, or weeps, or laughs, that is her consent; and if she refuses, he does not marry her off."

A father's arrangement of marriage on behalf of his minor sons and daughters is permissible. Once they come of age, they have no right to dissolve that marriage. Likewise, when an agent is duly authorized to contract a marriage, the contract is valid.

From Ali, may Allah's blessings be upon him: "If a Muslim woman who has reached majority authorizes her Christian father to give her in marriage, and he does so, the marriage is valid. But if he gives her in marriage while she is still a child, it is not valid — for a disbeliever holds no guardianship over a Muslim."

When a woman delegates her marriage to two guardians simultaneously and each contracts her to a different man, the marriage belongs to the first contract made — provided that the first guardian was unaware of the other's contract. If both contracts are concluded at exactly the same moment, one is annulled and the matter begins again.

It is related from Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali and from Jafar ibn Muhammad that a paternal grandfather may contract the marriage of his son's minor daughter just as the father may, and he holds prior right in this even if both were to act at the same moment. All parties are bound by whichever contract was concluded first, even if the guardian whose contract is dissolved was unaware of the other at the time and learns of it only afterward — in which case the matter is resumed.

From Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali it is related that whatever testimony is admissible in financial matters is admissible in marriage, and the testimony of women and of slaves is accepted in it.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad: he was asked about two witnesses who testified that a woman's father had given her in marriage while she was unwilling, while a third witness testified that he had given her in marriage with her consent. He said that the marriage is valid with her consent. He was also asked about two witnesses, one of whom testified that the dowry was one thousand and the other that it was two thousand. He said that if she claims the greater amount, she takes an oath together with her witness, and it is decreed for her. If one witness testifies that her father gave her in marriage while she was a child, and the other testifies that he gave her in marriage when she was of age and without her consent, the testimony is void.

**Mentioning the Witnesses in Marriage**

What was noted earlier establishes the foundation: the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said that there is no marriage save with a guardian and two witnesses. This is the command, and upon it action is taken, and by it the marriage is established. It is related from Ali that he said a marriage is not valid except with a guardian and witnesses.

Abu Jafar and Abu Abdullah (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ) said that witnesses were appointed in marriage only for the sake of the child, so that his father may be known — and as a safeguard against either spouse denying the marriage, and out of caution before the authorities, lest the two be charged with living together unlawfully. For this reason, and for whatever resembles it, seeking witnesses in marriage is obligatory.

As for what lies between a person and Allah, Mighty and Majestic, nothing falls upon him if he does not call witnesses, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, mentioned witnessing in the matter of divorce but not in the matter of marriage. Yet witnesses in marriage cannot be dispensed with, because through them the marriage is established, lineage is confirmed, and doubt is removed — and upright persons bear witness to it. Among the witnesses, women and slaves are admissible, provided they are upright.

**Mentioning the Dowries**

Concerning the Commander of the Believers (ع), it is narrated that Allah, exalted be the One who speaks, said: ﴿ وَآتُوا النِّسَاءَ صَدُقَاتِهِنَّ نِحْلَةً ﴾. Ali said concerning the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, ﴿ وَآتُوا النِّسَاءَ صَدُقَاتِهِنَّ نِحْلَةً ﴾: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is saying: give them the gift by which you have made their private parts lawful to you. Whoever wrongs a woman in her dowry has made her private part lawful to himself through fornication."

The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Allah, Mighty and Majestic, forgives every sin save the sin of a man who has defrauded a hired laborer of his wage, or a woman of her dowry, or who has sold a free person."

It is also related from him that he said: "The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, did not marry any of his wives, nor did he give any of his daughters in marriage, for more than twelve uqiyyahs and a nashsh of silver." An uqiyyah is forty dirhams, and a nashsh is half an uqiyyah — five hundred dirhams in all — together with a woven cloak and a bed of ram's hide. This is the dowry of the Sunnah. No fixed limit is set upon dowries; whatever is named, whether little or much, the marriage is contracted upon it. It is, however, recommended that the matter be made easy.

Ali said: "Among the blessings of a woman is the ease of her marriage and the ease of her womb, so do not be excessive in the dowries of women, for that breeds enmity."

A man came to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and his family, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, I wish to marry a certain woman." The Prophet asked whether he had anything to give her. The man replied: "No, by Allah, I have nothing." The Prophet then looked at the ring on the man's hand and said: "This ring that is on your hand." The man said: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah." The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, said: "Then you have married her with this ring of yours."

Ease in marriage is thus a virtue, as the tradition attests, and there is equally no harm in going beyond it. Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿ وَآتَيْتُمْ إِحْدَاهُنَّ قِنطَارًا فَلَا تَأْخُذُوا مِنْهُ شَيْئًا ﴾. It is also reported of al-Husayn ibn Ali, peace be upon them both, that he married a woman and sent to her one hundred slave girls, each accompanied by a thousand dirhams.

It is reported from Abu Abdullah that he was asked about the dowry, and he said: "It is whatever the two spouses agree upon, be it little or much. But a dowry there must be, and no marriage is permissible without a dowry, though there is no harm in contracting it without one being named — he may not consummate it until he gives her something, whatever it may be." This accords with the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿ لَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ إِن طَلَّقْتُمُ النِّسَاءَ مَا لَمْ تَمَسُّوهُنَّ أَوْ تَفْرِضُوا لَهُنَّ فَرِيضَةً ﴾. A contract without a named dowry is therefore permissible, but consummation must wait until he gives her something. Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about this and said: "My father married a woman and did not name a dowry for her, and when he wished to consummate the marriage he took a garment from me and handed it to her."

He was asked about the words of Allah, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿ وَامْرَأَةً مُؤْمِنَةً إِن وَهَبَتْ نَفْسَهَا لِلنَّبِيِّ ﴾. He said that this dispensation was singled out for the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace. No marriage is sound without a dowry. If a man names no dowry for his wife and then dies before her, or divorces her before consummating the marriage, she has no dowry — yet he inherits from her and she from him, and she must observe the waiting period. If he has consummated the marriage, she is entitled to a dowry equivalent to that of women of her family, assessed according to her circumstances, her wealth, and her beauty, and measured against a man of comparable standing and means — provided the amount does not exceed the dowry of the Sunnah. Should it exceed that, the excess is returned to him. The dowry of the Sunnah, as previously noted, is five hundred dirhams.

It is also related from him concerning a man who married a woman leaving the dowry to her own determination: the marriage is valid. If the two parties then disagree over the amount, she is entitled to the equivalent of the dowry customary among women of her family — neither falling short nor going to excess — and it is not permissible for it to exceed the dowry of the Sunnah.

It is related from him that the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, forbade the marriage of exchange. Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: The marriage of exchange — shighar — is when a man gives his daughter in marriage to another man on the condition that the other gives him his daughter in marriage, with no dowry between them. He said: Two men came to Ali, each having married the other's daughter without a dowry, and he rejected it, saying: No, there must be a dowry.

This ruling applies when the contract is made on the basis that each marriage stands as the recompense for the other, the parties binding themselves to that arrangement explicitly. If, however, they contract the marriage as an ordinary marriage without a named dowry — without stipulating what has just been described — then the contract is valid, and each of the two women is entitled to the equivalent of the dowry customary among women of her family, in the manner already described.

The jurists permitted contracting a marriage upon goods that are described and known. It is narrated from Ali that he said, concerning a man who married a woman in return for a young servant: neither falling short nor going to excess. Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: Whoever marries a woman for an unknown dowry has not thereby invalidated the marriage; she is entitled to the equivalent of the dowry customary among women of her peers, and it shall be no more than the dowry of the Sunnah.

The Master was asked about a man who had married a woman in return for a slave girl of his who had been pledged her freedom upon his death, and who then divorced her before the marriage was consummated. He said that the woman was entitled to half the slave girl's service — one day's service belonging to the woman and the next to the master — and that if the master revoked the pledge of freedom or sold the slave girl, the woman was entitled to half her value. It was affirmed that the dowry belongs to the woman.

It is narrated from Ali that he said: Marriage in return for a wage paid to the father is not lawful in Islam, in the manner that Moses hired himself out. The dowry belongs to the wife alone. If a man marries a woman on the condition that he perform some work for her, the marriage is valid, and that wage stands in place of the dowry; he may not consummate the marriage until he has performed the work for which he was engaged, or has given her something in its stead.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said: A woman came to the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, and said: O Messenger of Allah, give me in marriage. He said: Who will take this woman? A man among the people said: I, O Messenger of Allah. He said: What will you give her? He said: I have no wealth. He said: With no wealth at all? The woman turned to go. The Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, repeated his words, yet no one rose but that same man, and the woman turned away again. A third time the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace, addressed the man: Do you know anything of the Quran? He said: Yes. He said: I have given her to you in marriage for what you know of the Quran.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said: If a man marries a woman on the condition that he teach her a chapter from the Book of Allah, he may not consummate the marriage until he has taught her, or has given her something in its stead.

From Ali it is related that once a woman has been brought to her husband, she has no claim to her dowry after she has entered upon him — except by clear proof — meaning, if she claims he gave her nothing and that something of her dowry remains owing.

Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: If a man marries a woman with a portion of the dowry paid immediately and a portion deferred, the immediate portion falls due before consummation. She may lawfully withhold herself from him until he pays it, and he may not consummate the marriage while she does so. The deferred portion runs until death or separation — that is, when no specific time of payment has been stipulated.

If, however, she stipulates that the deferred portion becomes due after consummation, a case has been related from Ali bearing on this: a woman brought before him a man who had married her, consummated the marriage, and named a term for her dowry. Ali said: "There is no term for you in her dowry once you have consummated the marriage; her right has fallen due, so pay her her right."

This ruling — and Allah knows best — applies when he had paid her nothing in advance and had named neither an immediate nor a deferred portion. If, on the other hand, he had named both and had already paid what he obligated upon himself at once, then the deferred remainder runs to the time he stipulated, in accordance with the words of the Messenger of Allah, may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace: "People are bound by their conditions."

Likewise, if he named no term but named a dowry, and she refused to permit consummation until he discharged it, that refusal is her right.

Also related from Ali is a ruling concerning a man who marries a woman and convenes two sets of witnesses — a secret gathering on one dowry and a public gathering on a larger one: the first contract is the binding one, and the matter is settled by it.

From him as well: when the curtains are drawn and the doors are shut, the dowry falls due in full. This is the position of Abu Jafar and Abu Abdullah, and it applies when the wife claims that consummation took place. If, however, she acknowledges that he did not touch her — even though he had drawn the curtain and shut the door upon them — and he then divorces her, she is entitled to no more than half the dowry. She must also observe the waiting period, for her acknowledgment that he did not touch her does not waive the waiting period once he has shut his door and drawn the curtain over her.

It is related from Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abdullah that they ruled a man may take the freeing of his slave woman as her dowry, and that this is permissible. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali clarified the condition: the stipulation must be set before the act of freeing. That is, the man says, "I marry you on the condition that I have made your dowry your freedom," and then he frees her. If, however, he frees her first — saying, "I free you for the sake of Allah on the condition that your freedom is your dowry, and I marry you upon that" — then the choice passes to her. She may marry him if she wishes, or she may refuse, for she has already been freed and has come to own herself independently of him. Should he then marry her, he must do so with a proper dowry.

It is related from Ali that he was asked about a man who steals wealth and uses it either to contract a marriage or to purchase a slave girl. Ali said: The union is lawful, but the liability for the stolen wealth remains upon him. He is a sinner for what he has done, and he must make restitution for what he stole.

**Mentioning the Conditions in Marriage**

The Imams of the household of the Messenger of Allah — may Allah bless him and his family and grant them peace — are reported to have said: every condition that contradicts the Book of Allah is to be rejected.

It is related from Ali that he ruled concerning a man who married a woman and stipulated to her family that if he were to take another wife over her she would be divorced, or if he were to take a concubine over her the concubine would be free. Ali said: The condition of Allah, Mighty and Majestic, comes before their conditions. If he wishes, he fulfills his promise; and if he wishes, he marries another over her or takes a concubine — and no wife is divorced from him should he marry another, nor is any concubine freed should he take one.

The same ruling is related from Abu Jafar and Abu Abdullah.

It is further narrated from Abu Jafar and Abu Abd-Allah (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ), and likewise from Ali, that he gave judgment concerning a man who married a woman and stipulated that she should hold authority over her own affairs. Ali said: This departs from the Sunnah and assigns a right to one who is not its rightful holder. The husband is the guardian; intimacy and divorce rest in his hand. Ali therefore ruled that the dowry was owed by the husband, that intimacy and divorce remained his, and he nullified the condition.

Jafar ibn Muhammad said: A condition that is lawful — one that does not contradict the Book of Allah — is binding upon the man who married the woman on its basis. Among such valid conditions is that she shall remain with her family in a known land, or in a specified dwelling. This is permissible.

It was also narrated from him that he said: Whoever marries a woman on the condition that he will provide her a fixed daily maintenance and not be absent from her during the day — that condition does not invalidate the marriage, but neither is it itself binding. She retains the right to the division of nights and to the maintenance due to wives generally. Yet if a woman fears that her husband may harm her or divorce her, and he agrees with her to forgo some of his rights regarding her maintenance and the division of nights, that arrangement is permissible, in accordance with the words of Allah the Almighty: "If a woman fears discord or desertion from her husband, there is no blame upon them if they come to an agreement between themselves" (al-Nisa 128).

Abu Abd-Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: if a man stipulates that, should he take another wife or a concubine, she shall receive one hundred dinars or whatever sum he has bound himself to, the marriage is permissible. If that sum is drawn from the original dowry, it is binding; if it rests only on the added stipulation, it is not binding. This is the import of what Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said: a man should not make the divorce of one wife a condition for marrying another. The Messenger of Allah (ع and his family) forbade a woman to seek the divorce of her sister wife in order to take her place, for Allah the Almighty is the One who provides for her. And the Messenger of Allah (ع and his family) forbade the marriage of pleasure (mutah).

Concerning the marriage of pleasure, which some had permitted: a man would say to a woman, "Give yourself to me in marriage," naming a sum — a dirham, two dirhams, or whatever was agreed — for a single union, a day, two days, or any other fixed term. Once the parties agreed on the term, those who allowed it held that the union was lawful until that term expired, at which point separation occurred of itself, without divorce. They further claimed that no waiting period (*iddah*) was required of the woman, that neither party inherited from the other, and that such an arrangement was not permissible with a virgin — though some among them held that it was permissible even with women already married.

This is pure fornication. There is no ambiguity in it, and no covering conceals what it is. Allah the Almighty has made intimacy lawful by two paths only: the bond of marriage and the right of possession (*milk al-yamin*). The Almighty said:

"Those who guard their private parts, except with their wives or what their right hands possess, for they are not blameworthy; but whoever seeks beyond that, those are the transgressors." *(al-Muminun 5–7)*

> يَٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّبِىُّ إِذَا طَلَّقْتُمُ ٱلنِّسَآءَ فَطَلِّقُوهُنَّ لِعِدَّتِهِنَّ وَأَحْصُوا۟ ٱلْعِدَّةَ

Were such a union a marriage, the woman could not be parted from the man without divorce and without *iddah*, for Allah the Almighty says: "O Prophet, when you divorce women, divorce them at the beginning of their waiting period" *(al-Talaq 1)*. She would also inherit and be inherited from, as Allah says: "And you shall have half of what your wives leave" *(al-Nisa 12)*, and "They shall have a fourth of what you leave" *(al-Nisa 12)*. The child, too, would be attached to both parents, for the Messenger of Allah (ع and his family) said: "The child belongs to the bed" — meaning to the owner of the bed. Yet in this arrangement there is neither marriage nor right of possession, and what remains is forbidden.

The reports forbidding the marriage of pleasure on the authority of the Messenger of Allah (ع and his family) are numerous, among them his saying: "There is no marriage except with a guardian and two upright witnesses." Those who uphold the marriage of pleasure themselves acknowledge that it is contracted without a guardian and without witnesses — and on that ground alone it cannot stand.

It was narrated from Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abd-Allah that they declared the marriage of pleasure void, forbade it, and prohibited it.

It was narrated from Ali that he gave judgment in a case concerning a slave-woman who had fled from her master and deceived a man by claiming to be free, so that he married her on that basis and she bore him children — until her master established his claim over her. Ali ruled that she be returned to her master, and that the deceived man owed the master the value of the children she had borne him, unless the master chose to grant those children to their father. If the man had purchased her and she bore him a child, and her master then established his claim, she was to be returned to the one whose right was vindicated, and the value of the child was owed by the father, who could in turn recover that amount from the one who had sold her to him. If, however, he had taken her by force, or had known at the time of the marriage that she was owned and that her master had not given her in marriage, then both she and her child belonged to the master.

From Ali it was narrated concerning a free woman whom a male slave had approached, claiming to be free, so that she married him on that basis and then discovered he was owned: they may be separated if the woman wishes. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said that she holds authority over her own decision — if she wishes she may remain with him, and if she wishes she may leave. If she chooses to separate and the marriage has not been consummated, she is owed nothing; but if it has been consummated, she is entitled to her dowry, and the liability falls upon whoever deceived her, whether the slave himself or another. When the slave is eventually freed, if his lord does not then give him in marriage to her, the dowry rests with the slave once he is free; but if the lord had given him in marriage, or had given him leave to marry her, then her dowry is owed by the lord.

It was narrated from Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abd-Allah concerning a man to whom another woman was brought as a bride, so that he consummated the marriage believing her to be his wife and only afterward learned otherwise: he must return that woman, she is entitled to a dowry for what was done to her — claimed against the one who deceived him — and his true wife, the one he had actually married, is to be restored to him.

Concerning a man who is impotent and unable to approach women yet conceals this from his wife: once she learns of it, the choice is hers, and if she exercises that choice after consummation she is entitled to her dowry. They also ruled on a man who marries a woman and discovers in her leprosy, vitiligo, blindness, insanity, a condition of the private parts that prevents intercourse, or a manifest lameness: the choice in that case belongs to the husband. He may keep her if he wishes, or return her if he wishes. If he has had intercourse with her, she is entitled to her dowry, and his claim for it lies against whoever deceived him — the woman herself owes nothing. For defects other than these, she is not to be returned.

It was narrated from Ali concerning a man who marries a woman as a virgin and finds her otherwise: he saw nothing objectionable in this, and said that virginity may be lost through a leap, through ablution, or through the passing of long years.

---

**Mentioning the Forbidden Marriage and the Permissible Marriage**

Allah the Almighty said: "And do not marry those whom your fathers married of women, except what has already passed; it is an indecency and a hateful thing and an evil way. Forbidden to you are your mothers, your daughters..." (al-Nisa 22–23). Allah, Mighty and Majestic, has thus forbidden in the plain text of His Book the marriage of those He named explicitly, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the Imams of his house made clear what required clarification.

> وَرَبَٓئِبُكُمُ ٱلَّتِى فِى حُجُورِكُم مِّن نِّسَآئِكُمُ ٱلَّتِى دَخَلْتُم بِهِنَّ فَإِن لَّمْ تَكُونُوا۟ دَخَلْتُم بِهِنَّ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ

From both Ali and Abu Abd-Allah it is transmitted that the ruling concerning a wife's mother is unrestricted: when a man marries a woman, her mother becomes forbidden to him, whether or not he has consummated the marriage with the daughter.

They said that if a man marries a woman and then divorces her, or if she dies before consummation, her daughter remains lawful for him. This accords with the words of Allah: "And your stepdaughters under your guardianship, born of your wives with whom you have consummated marriage; but if you have not consummated with them — فَإِن لَّمْ تَكُونُوا۟ دَخَلْتُم بِهِنَّ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ — there is no blame upon you" (al-Nisa 23). The word تكونوا۟ fixes the condition on the husband's act; بهن names the wives in question; and جناح, the blame, is what is lifted when consummation has not occurred. The "guardianship" spoken of in the verse is the bond of inviolability. If the marriage with the mother was consummated, however, her daughter becomes forbidden to him; and the same prohibition holds if he has seen of her what other men are not permitted to see — in that case too he may not marry her daughter.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad it was transmitted concerning a man who marries a woman and then dies while she is still his wife, or divorces her before consummation: she is forbidden to his son through every generation that descends from him, and to his fathers however far the line ascends. Likewise, if a man looks upon his bondswoman with desire, or touches her, or looks upon her nakedness, she becomes forbidden to his sons and to his fathers. If, however, one of them owned her without approaching her, without touching her, and without looking upon her with desire, and another then came to own her, she is lawful to him.

The ruling permitted two sisters to be owned together while forbidding their combination in marriage. If a man has approached one of the two, the other becomes forbidden to him; he may not approach the second until the first has left his ownership — whether by manumission, by sale, or by gift. Transferring her to his son does not suffice. If the first sister dies, the other becomes lawful to him. What is forbidden is solely their combination, for God says: *"And that you combine two sisters"* (al-Nisa 23), and that verse draws no distinction between the bondswoman and the free woman.

A man may not marry the sister of a woman he has divorced until her waiting period has elapsed and his right of revocation over her is fully extinguished. For as long as that right remains, he has in effect joined the two sisters together. If the divorce was final and irrevocable, however, he may marry her sister, or any other woman, provided he has no more than three other free wives besides her. It was also transmitted from Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abd-Allah that a woman may not be joined in marriage with her paternal aunt, nor with her maternal aunt.

Ali said: "The Messenger of Allah and his family forbade that, and made it unlawful. The daughter of Hamza was offered to him in marriage, and he said: 'Do you not know that she is the daughter of my brother through suckling, for I was nursed together with Hamza.'"

They saw no harm in joining the daughters of paternal uncles with the daughters of maternal uncles, nor in a man's marrying both his wife and a daughter of his by another woman. Likewise, if a man divorces a woman or dies, and another man then marries her, there is no harm in the son of her first husband — by a different wife — marrying the daughter of her second husband by a different wife.

They held that if a man commits fornication with his wife's mother, her sister, or her daughter, that act does not corrupt the marriage, for the unlawful does not corrupt the lawful. If, however, he commits fornication with a woman and she subsequently bears a child, it is not proper for his son by another wife to marry that woman's daughter. Permission was granted in the case of the woman with whom a man had committed fornication, once both parties had repented.

It was narrated from Ali concerning a woman who commits adultery before her husband has consummated the marriage with her: they are to be separated, she is owed no dowry, and the prescribed punishment — the hadd — is carried out upon her. Her dowry is forfeited because the offense arose from her side. The separation, however, rests upon the husband's will: if he chooses to remain with her, she is still his wife.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, when asked about a sick man who contracts a marriage and then dies, said that the marriage is valid and she inherits from him.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was reported to have ruled on the case of a man who marries two sisters, or five women, in a single contract. The sister whose name was spoken first at the time of the contract has a valid marriage; likewise, the first four of the five women have valid marriages. The marriage of the second sister, and of the fifth woman beyond the four, is annulled. If it cannot be determined which name was mentioned first, the entire contract is void.

Concerning a man who marries a woman during her waiting period, or who marries while either party is in a state of consecration, both knowing the act to be unlawful: they are separated, and she is never again lawful to him. If they were ignorant of the prohibition, they are separated, but may contract a new marriage once she becomes lawful to suitors.

---

**Mentioning the Missing Husband**

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali was reported to have said: if a man is reported dead to his family, and his wife on that basis observes her waiting period and then remarries, and the first husband subsequently returns — the first husband has the greater right to her, regardless of whether the second husband has consummated the marriage. If the second husband has consummated it, she is entitled to her dowry for what was made lawful from her.

Jafar ibn Muhammad said: the wife of a missing man is to remain in her situation for as long as she keeps silent. If she brings her case before the governor, however, he sets for her a waiting period of four years and writes to make inquiries about her husband. If those four years pass with no news of him, the governor summons the missing man's guardian and asks whether the missing man has any wealth. If he does — and the guardian spends upon her from it, or spends upon her from his own means — she has no grounds to remarry. If the guardian will not maintain her and the missing man has no wealth, the governor compels the guardian to pronounce a single divorce at the onset of her waiting period while she is in a state of purity; that divorce by the guardian stands as the husband's own divorce. Should her husband return before her waiting period is complete, he has the greater right to her. If her waiting period has ended, she is lawful to other suitors.

It was said to him: O son of the Messenger of Allah and his family, what is to be done if the guardian does provide for her, yet she says, "I cannot be patient; I want what other women have"? He answered that she has no such recourse, and no claim to it, so long as the guardian provides for her.

The missing man — al-mafqud — is one who has left his home and whose whereabouts are unknown. He may have been seen between two battle lines in time of war, after which the people scattered and he was lost; or he may have been aboard a ship that capsized; or it may simply be that no one from the journey knows where he settled. A man whose location is known, by contrast, does not fall under this ruling. His wife is treated as the wife of an absent man — al-ghaib: she may not remarry unless he dies or divorces her. The Master said: if the whereabouts of the absent man are known, his wife may not remarry.

---

**On Breastfeeding (al-Rida)**

> وَرَبَٓئِبُكُمُ ٱلَّتِى فِى حُجُورِكُم مِّن نِّسَآئِكُمُ ٱلَّتِى دَخَلْتُم بِهِنَّ فَإِن لَّمْ تَكُونُوا۟ دَخَلْتُم بِهِنَّ فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْكُمْ

The saying of God Almighty has already been cited: ﴿وَأُمَّهَاتُكُمُ اللَّاتِي أَرْضَعْنَكُمْ وَأَخَوَاتُكُم مِّنَ الرَّضَاعَةِ﴾ — "and your mothers who have suckled you, and your sisters through breastfeeding." It has been narrated from the Imams of the family of the Messenger of Allah that whatever is forbidden through lineage is forbidden through breastfeeding. The women who are forbidden in marriage have already been set out, and whoever comes, through breastfeeding, to occupy the place of one of them holds the same standing of prohibition.

A man may marry a woman who has breastfed his sons, and he may marry those of her daughters whom she did not nurse alongside him, since such a woman is neither his mother through breastfeeding nor a wife of his father. He may likewise marry her daughter when she is among the daughters of a woman who breastfed his brother or his sister. In the same way, a man may marry the daughters of women who breastfed his son, and their daughters as well, for they did not nurse the son, and no bond — whether through breastfeeding or otherwise — exists between them and him. What is forbidden is marrying the nursing woman herself; but paternal and maternal cousins through breastfeeding are lawful in marriage, just as they are lawful through lineage. A man may marry a woman while his father marries her daughter by another man, and a father and son may each marry one of two sisters.

It was narrated from Ali that he said: breastfeeding creates prohibition whether it is little or much — even a single suckle establishes the prohibition, by the word of Allah Almighty, ﴿وَأُمَّهَاتُكُمُ اللَّاتِي أَرْضَعْنَكُمْ﴾, "and your mothers who have suckled you." The ruling applies equally to a small amount and a large one, for even a small quantity nourishes: from it flesh and blood grow, and bone is strengthened in proportion.

Ali is also reported to have said that the breastfeeding which creates prohibition is that which takes place within the first two years of life, for Allah says: ﴿وَالْوَالِدَاتُ يُرْضِعْنَ أَوْلَادَهُنَّ حَوْلَيْنِ كَامِلَيْنِ لِمَنْ أَرَادَ أَن يُتِمَّ الرَّضَاعَةَ﴾, "and mothers shall suckle their children for two complete years, for whoever wishes to complete the suckling." Whatever occurs after those two years does not constitute breastfeeding and establishes no prohibition. The Messenger of Allah (upon him and his family be peace) said: "لَا رِضَاعَ بَعْدَ فِطَامٍ" — "There is no breastfeeding after weaning."

From Ali, Abu Jafar, and Abu Abd Allah it is narrated concerning a woman who gives her husband her milk to drink — intending by that device to make herself forbidden to him — or who gives her milk to her bondswoman, or nurses her, with the same aim: they said that the man may discipline his wife for such conduct, but that no prohibition arises from it, because the breastfeeding of an adult does not count as breastfeeding. If a man is suckled after two years have elapsed from his birth, or if a wife gives her husband her milk to drink, nothing is made forbidden thereby. Whatever occurs before the two years, however — whether by suckling directly, or by drinking a woman's milk, or by its being administered into the throat (wajur) or the nose (saut) — constitutes breastfeeding and carries the ruling in full.

The milk of the stallion creates prohibition — meaning milk attributed to the man who fathered it. This applies when a man has several wives, or umm-walad mothers, in his household, and one of them nurses a slave boy while another nurses a slave girl: the two become siblings through breastfeeding, even though they did not nurse at the breast of one woman. The one father unites them, and they were nourished by the milk of his wives, so the milk is attributed to him.

Abū Jaʿfar Muḥammad ibn ʿAlī was asked about the wife of a man who had nursed a slave girl: could the man's son by another woman lawfully marry her? He said: No. He was then asked whether the slave girl stood to that son as a sister through breastfeeding. He said: Yes, from the father's side.

He went on to put a case: a man had two wives, each of whom had borne him a son, and one of the two wives nursed a slave girl belonging to other people. He said: the other son may not marry that slave girl, for she was nursed by the milk of the same father — and what lineage forbids, breastfeeding forbids.

When asked about a slave girl belonging to a man whose wife, or the mother of his child, claimed to have nursed her, he said that the woman was not to be believed, since she was drawing a benefit to herself. Regarding a woman who said she had nursed a slave boy and a slave girl and then retracted that claim, he said that her retraction stood. It was put to him: what if she later withdrew her denial and again claimed to have nursed them? He said she was not to be believed. The testimony of a single upright woman is accepted in matters of breastfeeding; but where no upright woman is available, her testimony alone does not suffice.

They forbade seeking a wet-nurse whose milk comes of fornication — as in the case of a woman who commits adultery and bears a child by it. Such a woman was not to be sought as a wet-nurse, nor taken as a foster-nurse (zir), and neither was her daughter born of adultery. They did, however, permit seeking a wet-nurse among polytheist women who were within a marriage, while disapproving of seeking one from the milk of those known for enmity toward the family of Muhammad and his family. Breastfeeding by the milk of fornication makes nothing forbidden. Jafar ibn Muhammad said that unlawful milk does not render the lawful unlawful — as in the case of a woman nursed first by lawful milk and afterward by the milk of fornication. He said that whoever nurses a girl with the milk of fornication does not thereby make it forbidden to marry her, because unlawful milk does not render the lawful forbidden.

A ruling attributed to Ali holds that if a man marries a woman, pays her dowry, and then — before consummating the marriage — a nursing relationship between them comes to light, she must return to him what she received. It was also narrated from the Messenger of Allah and his family that he forbade women from freely nursing boys they do not know.

---

**On the Marriage of Bondswomen (Nikah al-Ima)**

> وَمَن لَّمْ يَسْتَطِعْ مِنكُمْ طَوْلًا أَن يَنكِحَ ٱلْمُحْصَنَتِ ٱلْمُؤْمِنَتِ فَمِن مَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَنُكُم مِّن فَتَيَتِكُمُ ٱلْمُؤْمِنَتِ

Allah Almighty said: ﴿وَمَن لَّمْ يَسْتَطِعْ مِنكُمْ طَوْلًا أَن يَنكِحَ الْمُحْصَنَاتِ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ فَمِن مَّا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُكُم مِّن فَتَيَاتِكُمُ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾, up to His saying ﴿ذَٰلِكَ لِمَنْ خَشِيَ الْعَنَتَ مِنكُمْ ۚ وَأَن تَصْبِرُوا خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ ۗ وَاللَّهُ غَفُورٌ رَّحِيمٌ﴾: "And whoever among you cannot afford to marry free believing women, then from those whom your right hands possess, of your believing bondswomen," up to His saying, "That is for him among you who fears falling into sin; and that you be patient is better for you, and Allah is Forgiving, Merciful."

Ali, commenting on the words of Allah Almighty ﴿ذَٰلِكَ لِمَنْ خَشِيَ الْعَنَتَ مِنكُمْ﴾ — "That is for him among you who fears falling into sin" — said that this means adultery, and nothing else. A free Muslim may not marry a bondswoman unless he fears being overwhelmed by desire and lacks the means to marry a free woman. If he has the means to marry a free woman, he may not marry a bondswoman; and if he does not fear falling into sin, he likewise may not marry her, for Allah Almighty has permitted free men to marry bondswomen only upon these two conditions.

Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad said that a free man may not marry a bondswoman until two conditions are joined in him:

- the fear of sin, and
- the lack of means to marry a free woman.

If both are present, he may marry her.

When a free man marries a bondswoman, the children she bears him belong to her master as slaves — unless he stipulates at the time of marriage that whatever children she bears him shall be free, in which case they are free. The ruling on the child follows the ruling on the mother, in freedom as in bondage. If a slave marries a free woman, their children are free, and his master may not stipulate that the free woman's children be slaves, as he might stipulate regarding the children of a bondswoman. This is because the freeing of a bondswoman's children rests with her master, who may free them if he wishes. A free woman, by contrast, cannot hold ownership of her own children while they are free, nor can anyone else.

A bondswoman may not be given in marriage except with the permission of her master, for Allah says: ﴿فَانكِحُوهُنَّ بِإِذْنِ أَهْلِهِنَّ﴾, "So marry them with the permission of their families." When a bondswoman is jointly owned by two men, she is not lawful to either of them, even if the other permits it, because a person cannot be divided, nor can a divided share be made lawful by gift. If one of the two gives her in marriage without his partner's permission, the marriage is not valid unless the other ratifies it. The husband may not consummate the marriage until the second owner permits it; if he does not permit it, the marriage is dissolved.

Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a bondswoman jointly owned by two men, one of whom gives her in marriage while the other is absent: is the marriage valid? He said: if the absent owner is averse to it, it is not valid.

It was narrated from Ali that he said: it is not lawful for a free Muslim to marry a Jewish or a Christian bondswoman, for Allah Almighty says ﴿مِّن فَتَيَاتِكُمُ الْمُؤْمِنَاتِ﴾, "of your believing bondswomen." Likewise a free man should not marry a Magian or a polytheist bondswoman; for were that lawful, the polytheists would come to enslave the children of the Muslims. If a man wishes to marry a bondswoman, let him free her first, and then marry her if he wishes and she wishes.

The Messenger of Allah ((ع) and his family) married Safiyyah bint Huyayy ibn Akhtab and drew the veil (حِجَاب) over her. Jafar ibn Muhammad said: any man who frees his slave woman and wishes to marry her, let it be with witnesses and an appointed dower; and if he makes her emancipation her dower, that is permitted, as has been explained in the foregoing.

A woman under a contract of emancipation (mukatabah) may be married with the permission of her master. Ali was asked about the marriage of a mukatabah, and he said: she may marry; and whatever child is born to her during her contract of emancipation stands in her own position, so that of that child what is freed in her is freed, and what remains in bondage in her remains in bondage. The reckoning of this is treated in the chapter on those under emancipation contracts, if Allah wills.

Ali is reported to have said that if a man marries a bondswoman while already married to a free wife, the two are to be separated. He is liable for her dower in proportion to what he made lawful of her person, but only if the marriage was consummated; if it was not, she is owed nothing.

Abu Abd Allah Jafar ibn Muhammad said: if a man marries a free woman alongside a bondswoman and the free woman knows of the arrangement, he may divide his time between them — two portions to the free woman and one to the bondswoman. If the free woman did not know at the time of her marriage that he had a bondswoman, and she learns of it afterward, the choice is hers: she may remain with him, or she may leave his bond. If she chooses to leave and the marriage was consummated, she is owed the dower for what he made lawful of her person; if it was not consummated and she parts from him, she is owed nothing.

It was narrated from him that a free man may not lawfully marry a bondswoman on her own. If he marries a free woman and a bondswoman in a single contract, the determining factor is whose name opened the contract: if the free woman's name came first, the bondswoman's marriage is void; if the bondswoman's name came first and the free woman consents to remain alongside her, both marriages stand — provided the man is one for whom marriage to a bondswoman is lawful, as has already been described. A man may contract marriage upon a free woman even when he lacks the means for her dower; but if he does have the means, the bondswoman's marriage is void regardless of whether her name came first or second. Equally, if it cannot be established with which of them the bondswoman's marriage began, that marriage is invalid.

He was then asked about the maintenance (نَفَقَة) owed to a bondswoman wife. He said: when a free man marries a bondswoman, she serves her household by day and comes to her husband by night, and he owes her maintenance so long as this arrangement holds; but if her people bar her from him at night, he owes her no maintenance.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man whose young children own a slave girl: may he lie with her? He said: if he desires her, let him set a fair value on himself for her, so that her price stands against him as a debt owed to his children; he then owns her and may lie with her if he wishes. If the children are grown, however, she is not lawful to him unless they sell her to him, and it is not lawful for him to proceed otherwise. A man has no right to any part of his child's wealth except by the child's own goodwill — save that, if he is driven to it, he may eat of it what sustains him, in the customary measure and without excess, when he is in hardship and the child is wealthy.

It was also narrated from him that he was asked about a man who had a slave girl, and his wife — fearing that he would take her for himself — ordered her son to lie with her, and he did. He said: she has sinned, and her son has sinned, and the son is liable to the prescribed punishment (hadd) if he is an adult. He further disapproved of men approaching her thereafter, even though she is by that act forbidden to the master, because the unlawful does not render the lawful forbidden.

From Ali it was transmitted that he disapproved of a man lying with a bondswoman over whom another person holds a stipulated right. A mudabbarah may be married with her master's permission, and her legal status remains that of a bondswoman until her master dies, at which point she is freed. If a bondswoman is freed while already married: should her husband be a free man, she remains his wife and has no choice in the matter; should he be a slave, she has the choice, upon her emancipation, to remain with him or to leave.

The case of the freed slave woman is settled by what the Messenger of Allah and his family did with Barirah. She was a slave woman married to a slave man, and her situation caused her grief. When she was set free, the Messenger of Allah gave her the choice, and she chose herself over her husband. He then ordered her to observe a waiting period of three menstrual cycles. It was further stated that if a bondswoman's master assists her in fulfilling her emancipation contract — even if she is elderly — she has no right of choice against her husband on account of that assistance.

**The marriage of slaves**

Allah, exalted be He, said: ﴿ عَبْدًا مَمْلُوكًا لَا يَقْدِرُ عَلَىٰ شَيْءٍ ﴾ — "A slave who is owned and has no power over anything" (al-Nahl: 75). The Messenger of Allah and his family forbade a slave to marry without the permission of his master. He said that any free woman who gives herself in marriage to a slave without the permission of her guardian has made her person unlawful and is owed no dower — this being the case when the master denies the marriage. If the master permits his slave to marry, however, the marriage is valid, and the dower falls upon the master when he consents to it.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man who marries his own slave woman to one of his male slaves. He said that the master declares, "I have given her to you in marriage," and gives her some small thing as a dower. The right of separation remains in the master's hand:

- If he wishes, he may part them without a divorce.
- If he sells the male slave, that sale is itself a separation between them.
- If he sells them together, the buyer may part them if he wishes.

Jafar ibn Muhammad held that if a slave woman is sold while she has a free husband, she remains his wife. Her person is not lawful to the buyer until the husband either divorces her or dies and she completes her waiting period. From Ali comes the ruling that if a woman comes to own her husband — or any portion of him — the marriage is dissolved by the ownership itself, and she becomes the owner of her own person. It is not lawful for a woman to marry her own slave unless she first frees him; if she wishes, she may free him and marry him afterward.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad: a slave may buy and sell, and may approach whichever of the slave women his master has permitted him. He may not marry more than two free women. He may, however, marry up to four slave women, and the divorce of any woman he marries rests in his master's hand — the master may divorce them on the slave's behalf whenever he wishes.

**The marriage of polytheists**

**The marriage of polytheists**

The marriages of polytheists among themselves are valid when contracted according to the requirements of their own religion, whether the two parties belong to the same religious community or to different ones, and it is not fitting that such marriages be annulled.

It is narrated from Ali that he said: if a man and his wife are taken among the spoils together, their marriage holds. Even if the husband is captured some days after the wife, they remain as they were — unless one of them is carried off and brought into the House of Islam. Should that occur, the marriage is dissolved, and she is not lawful to him except by a new contract, regardless of which of the two was taken first. So long as either of them remains a captive among the spoils, their marriage stands between them. Once one of them enters the House of Islam, however, the marriage is dissolved.

If the wife embraces Islam and her husband is then captured after her conversion, and she has already passed three menstrual cycles — yet she had not been carried away and her husband had not embraced Islam — they remain upon their marriage. The one who owns them both may separate them if he wishes, as he may with any of his other slaves, unless at the time of their capture they were granted safe conduct on the condition that they not be parted, and that condition was formally contracted for them — in which case their separation is not obligatory.

According to a transmission from Ali, it is not lawful for Muslims to marry polytheist women in the abode of war while the rulings of the polytheists hold sway there. A further transmission from him states that if a woman from the abode of war is granted safe conduct and enters the House of Islam while she still has a polytheist husband, his marital bond to her is severed. She may remarry after her waiting period has cleared her womb. Should her husband then enter under safe conduct as a Muslim, he has no claim upon her except through a new marriage, for the bond was already severed the moment she entered the House of Islam.

If a man embraces Islam while his wife remains a polytheist, she stays his wife. If a woman embraces Islam while her husband remains a polytheist, a separation is made between them. Should her husband embrace Islam before her waiting period expires, they remain upon their marriage; if her waiting period has run its course, she becomes the owner of her own person.

Both Ali and Abu Jafar transmitted a prohibition against marrying Christian women of Arab descent and against eating animals slaughtered by them.

Ali also transmitted a ruling on the apostate who renounces his faith and joins the abode of war: he stands in the position of a dead man. His wealth is distributed among his heirs, his wives observe the waiting period prescribed for widows, and they may then remarry as they wish.

From Jafar ibn Muhammad: if a woman embraces Islam while her husband remains a polytheist, she is separated from him should he fail to embrace Islam, and she retains her full dower. If he had not yet consummated the marriage, she is entitled to half the dower. Where polytheists embrace Islam together, their existing marriages remain intact. The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "Confirm the people of the age of ignorance upon whatever state they entered Islam, whether of marriage, divorce, or inheritance."

From Ali, on the polytheist who embraces Islam while he has two free sisters as wives, or more than four free wives:

- He is left with the first of the two sisters he married, and a separation is made between him and the second.
- A separation is likewise made between him and any wives he took beyond the four free women.

Ali also transmitted that Allah made the women of the People of the Book lawful to Muslims only when Muslim women were few. When Muslim women became many, Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ وَلَا تَنْكِحُوا الْمُشْرِكَاتِ حَتَّى يُؤْمِنَّ ﴾ — "And do not marry polytheist women until they believe" (al-Baqarah: 221). And He said: ﴿ وَلَا تُمْسِكُوا بِعِصَمِ الْكَوَافِرِ ﴾ — "And do not hold to the marriage bonds of disbelieving women" (al-Mumtahanah: 10). The Messenger of Allah and his family forbade a Muslim man to marry a non-Muslim woman while he is able to find a Muslim woman, and forbade a polytheist to marry a Muslim woman.

If a polytheist embraces Islam while his wife is still a polytheist, he may keep her with him if he wishes, in the hope that Allah, mighty and majestic, will guide her, and he may take up to three Muslim women as additional wives, provided she is aware of her standing. If he marries a Muslim woman while the polytheist wife remains in his household, and the Muslim woman does not know of this, and she discovers it after consummation, the matter is placed in her own hand: she may stay if she chooses, or she may go. She is entitled to her dower for what was made lawful of her person, and once her waiting period has elapsed she may marry whomever she wishes, without need of a divorce. If, however, he divorces the polytheist wife before the waiting period — counted from the day the Muslim wife exercised her choice — has elapsed, then he holds the greater right to the Muslim wife.

**The division of turns among co-wives**

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ وَلَنْ تَسْتَطِيعُوا أَنْ تَعْدِلُوا بَيْنَ النِّسَاءِ وَلَوْ حَرَصْتُمْ فَلَا تَمِيلُوا كُلَّ الْمَيْلِ فَتَذَرُوهَا كَالْمُعَلَّقَةِ ﴾ — "You will never be able to deal justly between wives, even though you are eager to do so; yet do not incline altogether away, so as to leave her as one suspended" (al-Nisa: 129). With this, the Exalted made plain that perfect justice between wives in matters of affection, desire, and ardor — setting aside intercourse — lies beyond a man's reach, whereas justice in matters of maintenance, lodging, gifts, and the like can indeed be practiced. It therefore falls upon a man who has several wives to spend time with each of them, by day and by night, in turn.

Jafar ibn Muhammad was asked about a man who has several wives and is intimate with some but not others. He said that the man is obliged to spend each wife's allotted night with her and to remain through her morning. If he feels no stirring toward intercourse, nothing is held against him; but if he is so stirred while with one of his wives, it is not fitting that he turn away from her and withhold himself for another.

From Ali, when he was asked about a man who has wives and then sets out on a journey: he said that on returning the man should begin with the wife whose turn is due. Ali also said that if a man has only one wife, it is not fitting that he leave her without spending the night with her at least one night in four; in the remaining three nights he may do as Allah has made lawful for him.

Jafar ibn Muhammad said that if a man has two wives, he may reserve three nights for himself and assign to one wife her single night, devoting the other night to the second wife. Likewise, if he has three wives, he assigns each her night and devotes the fourth night to whichever of them he wishes. If he has four wives, he may not favor one above another.

From Ali: if a man who already has one wife or several wives takes a new wife, he stays with her seven nights if she is a virgin, and three nights if she has been married before. After that, he divides his nights equally among all his wives.

Ali was also asked about the words of Allah, mighty and majestic: ﴿ وَإِنِ امْرَأَةٌ خَافَتْ مِنْ بَعْلِهَا نُشُوزًا أَوْ إِعْرَاضًا فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا أَنْ يُصْلِحَا بَيْنَهُمَا صُلْحًا وَالصُّلْحُ خَيْرٌ ﴾, "If a woman fears ill treatment or aversion from her husband, there is no blame upon them if they reach a reconciliation between themselves, and reconciliation is best" (al-Nisa: 128). He said that the verse concerns a man who has two wives and becomes unable to fulfill the rights of one of them — or she is a dhimmi woman — so he turns toward the other and wishes to divorce the first, while she is unwilling to be divorced. She therefore reaches a settlement with him on the condition that he visit her from time to time, or that she relinquish to him her allotted share of his nights.

**Maintenance owed to wives**

> قَدْ عَلِمْنَا مَا فَرَضْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِىٓ أَزْوَجِهِمْ وَمَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَنُهُمْ

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ قَدْ عَلِمْنَا مَا فَرَضْنَا عَلَيْهِمْ فِي أَزْوَاجِهِمْ وَمَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَانُهُمْ ﴾, "We have known what We have made obligatory upon them concerning their wives and those whom their right hands possess" (al-Ahzab: 50). And the Blessed and Exalted said: ﴿ وَارْزُقُوهُمْ فِيهَا وَاكْسُوهُمْ وَقُولُوا لَهُمْ قَوْلًا مَعْرُوفًا ﴾, "And provide for them therein and clothe them, and speak to them words of kindness" (al-Nisa: 5).

It is narrated from the family of the Messenger of Allah that he addressed the people during the Farewell Pilgrimage, spoke of women, and enjoined the people to treat them well, saying: "They have over you their sustenance and their clothing in a fitting manner." He forbade — he and his family — that a man eat his fill while his family went hungry, and said: "It is enough sin for a man that he neglect those whom he supports."

It is narrated from him and his family that he said: "There are seven among the foremost of deeds, so keep to them" — and he mentioned among them maintenance for one's dependents.

Further narrations from him and his family record:

- "The severest of trials is many dependents with little wealth, and few dependents is one of the two forms of ease."
- "Whoever is moderate in his livelihood, Allah provides for him, and whoever is wasteful, Allah deprives him."
- "When Allah, mighty and majestic, intends good for a household, He grants them understanding in religion, provides them gentleness in their livelihood, and grants them moderation in their affairs."
- "Gentle moderation is half of livelihood; no man who lives in moderation is ever in want."

From Ali: if a man finds nothing to spend on his wife, he is granted a respite. If he brings her what is sufficient to feed her, they are not separated. If he finds nothing at all, a term is set, and then they are separated. Also from him: a woman brought a complaint against her husband for withholding her maintenance in order to harm her, and he had the husband imprisoned on her account. He further ruled that any woman who leaves her husband's house without his permission is owed no maintenance until she returns.

Also from him, concerning the man who divorces his wife while she is still nursing his child: the mother holds the stronger right to nurse the child, and she receives from him what would be paid to a wet nurse. If her husband dies and leaves with her a child of his whom she is nursing, she is entitled to a nurse's wage drawn from the child's own wealth — whether that wealth comes from inheritance or from another source — and the guardian has no right to remove the child from her care.

> وَٱلَّذِينَ إِذَآ أَنفَقُوا۟ لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا۟ وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا۟ وَكَانَ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ قَوَامًۭا

Maintenance owed to wives and to those relatives for whom it is obligatory is measured according to one's means and capacity. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ لِيُنْفِقْ ذُو سَعَةٍ مِنْ سَعَتِهِ وَمَنْ قُدِرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقُهُ فَلْيُنْفِقْ مِمَّا آتَاهُ اللَّهُ ﴾, "Let a man of ample means spend out of his ampleness, and whoever has his provision straitened, let him spend out of what Allah has given him" (al-Talaq: 7). The ruler therefore imposes upon the one who bears the obligation the maintenance fitting his station — neither extravagant nor stinting. Allah, mighty and majestic, said: ﴿ وَالَّذِينَ إِذَا أَنْفَقُوا لَمْ يُسْرِفُوا وَلَمْ يَقْتُرُوا وَكَانَ بَيْنَ ذَلِكَ قَوَامًا ﴾, "And those who, when they spend, are neither extravagant nor stinting, but hold a just balance between the two" (al-Furqan: 67).

This is a matter well established and not obscure, requiring neither opinion nor independent reasoning, for its measure is known to people by custom in every place and time — varying with need and abundance, with what is available, with cheapness and dearness, and with poverty and wealth.

Every poor person who is unable to manage or to work has his maintenance owed by whoever would inherit from him at his death, in proportion to the share that heir would receive from his estate — with one exception: the wife. Her maintenance falls upon her husband, and he owes her no return beyond it.

If the one upon whom maintenance is obligatory is himself poor and has nothing to spend, his case is like that of a person who has no guardian to provide for him: he seeks his provision from the provision of ٱلله, glorified be His mention.

A man is not bound to provide for a distant relative who would not inherit from him at his death, when his own heir is poor and without means, because maintenance is owed only to those within that circle of inheritance. Allah, mighty and majestic, has excused him from what lies beyond his capacity, in His words: ﴿ لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا ﴾, "Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity" (al-Baqarah: 286), and in His words: ﴿ لَا يُكَلِّفُ اللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا مَا آتَاهَا ﴾, "Allah does not burden a soul except with what He has given it" (al-Talaq: 7).

Should he afterward come into ease, he provides for those in his charge from that point onward. He cannot be held to account for the period already past.

> لَا يُكَلِّفُ ٱللَّهُ نَفْسًا إِلَّا وُسْعَهَا

A man of the Ansar once invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and his household to a meal, and the Messenger accepted. In the Ansari's home there was a pregnant slave woman moving back and forth as she served the food. The Messenger of Allah said to him: "What is this?" The man replied: "A slave woman of mine whom I purchased some days ago — she is with child." The Messenger said: "Have you been with her?" He answered: "Yes, O Messenger of Allah, I have." The Messenger of Allah then said to him: "Were it not for the sanctity of your food, I would have called down upon you a curse that would follow you into your grave. Free what is in her womb — your seed has already nourished its hearing, its sight, its flesh, its blood, its hair, and its skin."

Ali said: it is not lawful for a man to approach a woman who carries another man's child until she has delivered and become pure. If he purchases a pregnant slave woman, he must likewise not approach her until she gives birth and becomes pure. From the Messenger of Allah and his household: when a man has been with a slave woman, she is to be cleared by one menstrual cycle.

---

*On istibrāʾ*

Ali said: whoever buys a young slave girl who has not yet reached puberty, shows no sign of it, and presents no risk of pregnancy, may approach her if he wishes and is under no obligation to perform istibrāʾ upon her.

He said: whoever buys a slave girl who has despaired of menstruation should set her apart for two months before approaching her, if he wishes. This applies where there remains some doubt that she may still menstruate, even though her menses appear to have ceased.

Abū ʿAbdullāh Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad, the prayers of Allah be upon him, said: whoever buys an old woman and knows with certainty that she does not menstruate — there being no doubt in her case — may approach her if he wishes and need not perform istibrāʾ.

He said: whoever buys a slave girl from a woman may approach her before performing istibrāʾ, and there is no harm in that. If he performs istibrāʾ as a safeguard for himself, that is better. The obligation of istibrāʾ falls on the seller: if he has approached the slave woman and then wishes to sell her, he must not do so until he has performed istibrāʾ upon her by one menstrual cycle, lest she be carrying his child and his offspring be sold along with her.

It was narrated from ʿAlī, the prayers of Allah be upon him, that he said: if a man buys a slave woman who does not menstruate, or one who has reached puberty without having menstruated, he must observe istibrāʾ upon her for forty-five nights.

ʿAlī, the prayers of Allah be upon him, was asked about a man who bought a slave girl who had reached the age of discernment but had not menstruated and was a virgin, whose seller had taken her back and then sold her. He said that her case was grave: the buyer must perform istibrāʾ upon her for nine months, and may approach her afterward only if no pregnancy has appeared — that being the cautious course.

It was also related from him concerning a man who buys a slave girl while she is in a state of purity, and whose seller informs him that he has not approached her since her last menstruation, nor during the present purity in which she is. He said that if the seller is trustworthy in the buyer's eyes, the buyer may approach her if he wishes; and if he performs istibrāʾ, that is the more cautious course for him. He further said that whoever buys a slave girl who has had no husband, and whose master has not approached her, must nonetheless perform istibrāʾ upon her by one menstrual cycle.

He was asked about a man who bought a slave girl, then freed her and married her, and whether he might approach her. He said that the man must perform istibrāʾ of her womb by one menstrual cycle; and if he approaches her before doing so, there is no harm in it.

It was narrated from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad that he was asked about a man who had lain with his slave woman and then wished to give her in marriage before performing istibrāʾ. He said: No. He was then asked by how much the istibrāʾ should be performed. He said: by one menstrual cycle, though two are more beloved to him. A man must likewise perform istibrāʾ of a slave woman when he wishes to sell her, just as he performs it when he buys her.

It was narrated from ʿAlī, may the prayers of Allah be upon him, that he said: when a man buys a slave woman, there is no harm in his enjoying of her what falls short of intercourse before he performs istibrāʾ — meaning fondling, kissing, and approach short of the private part. It was further narrated from him that he was asked about a man who bought a slave woman and feared she might be pregnant; he said that the man must perform istibrāʾ upon her for forty-five nights.

He was asked about a slave woman who had committed adultery, whether her master might approach her. He said that the master does not approach her until he has performed istibrāʾ upon her. Likewise, if a man commits adultery with a slave woman and then buys her, he ought not to approach her until he has performed istibrāʾ upon her. Should she have conceived by him through that adultery, the child is not attributed to him, for the Messenger of Allah said: "الْوَلَدُ لِلْفِرَاشِ وَالْعَاهِرُ الْحَجَرُ" — meaning the child belongs to the marriage bed, and for the fornicator is the stone.

It was narrated from Jaʿfar ibn Muḥammad that he said: whoever buys a slave girl while she is menstruating, once she becomes pure he may approach her if he wishes. It was further narrated from ʿAlī that he said concerning a woman taken captive who has a husband: she performs istibrāʾ by one menstrual cycle, and once she is pure her master may approach her. And if a woman is coerced and violated, her husband does not approach her until she has performed istibrāʾ by one menstrual cycle.
