He is liable for them, because they become a loan. If, however, he borrows something identified as a particular item — a specific dirham, for instance — it cannot rightly be treated as a loan. Whoever borrows a piece of property and then mortgages or sells it is subject to this rule: if the owner is at hand, the owner may recover it, and the buyer may seek restitution from the seller for the price paid. Whoever pledges borrowed property is liable for an equivalent pledge, or for whatever that pledge was worth, unless the owner of the borrowed item had given permission to pledge or sell it. If the property remains in his possession, no obligation falls upon him.

Whoever receives a deposit must preserve and safeguard it as a person of comparable standing would. If it is destroyed or lost through no act of wrongdoing on his part, after he has taken proper care of it, no liability falls upon him. If, however, he loses it through negligence, misuse, or transgression, he is liable for it. If the owner of the deposit instructs him to deliver it to a certain man, and he claims to have done so, but that man denies receiving it and the owner does not accept his word, then he must pay for it after all of them have sworn oaths.

A holder of a deposit may draw upon it if he carries a corresponding debt and can attest to that; the deposit then becomes his responsibility. If a child or an insane person entrusts a deposit and it is lost, no recourse falls against the one who held it, for he was misled through no fault of his own. If a slave receives a deposit without his master's permission and the deposit is lost, the slave bears responsibility for it — though the claim is made against him only once he is freed, not against his master. If two men jointly entrust something to a third party and one of them comes to claim it while the other is absent, the holder should release only half, since it was deposited jointly; he may not hand the whole to one without the other being present. Nor may the one present take any portion until his companion arrives — unless the absent party has died and his heirs come in his stead, in which case the deposit may be released to them. This is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, (عَلَيْهِمُ السَّلَامُ).

---

**On Found Property, the Foundling, and Related Matters**

Whoever finds lost property within the Haram of Makkah, or in any place where he is confident of its safety and does not fear it will be taken, should announce it and leave it where it lies until its owner returns for it. If the property is not within the Haram and he fears for its safety, he should take it up if he is able, for he cannot simply abandon it — the Messenger of Allah, (ع), forbade the wasting of wealth. Once he takes it, he announces it publicly. If the owner comes forward and can testify to it or describe it, it is returned to him.

If no claimant appears within the period specified in the Sunnah, during which he has continued to make his announcement, he places it in the treasury of the Muslims if a means of doing so is available. If none is available, he has two options:

- He may give the property in charity on the owner's behalf, on the understanding that should the owner later come forward, he restores its value to him.
- He may keep it with him, given his inability to deposit it in the treasury of the Muslims.

Picking up a stray camel found in a safe place is disliked, because such animals can endure thirst and hunger long enough to reach their owners. If time passes and the finder fears for the animal's safety, however, he may take it in and care for it, spending on its upkeep, to be reimbursed by the owners when they come to reclaim it. Should no claimant appear after a prolonged period, the matter is referred to the governing authority, who sells the animal, retains the proceeds, and treats the price as found property is treated — whether the animal in question is a sheep, cattle, a slave, or any other beast. No stray animal is simply left where it was found; the procedure described above applies in every case. If a claimant does come forward and demands a fee from the finder, that fee is not obligatory, for God Almighty has made the safeguarding of believers' wealth a duty that believers owe one another. The finder receives a reward when his intention was righteous, and whatever he spent in caring for the animal is to be repaid to him.

Whoever finds perishable property that would spoil if left in place should sell it and handle the proceeds as he would handle found property. Whoever finds property buried inside someone's home: that property belongs to the people of that home, provided they claim it — even if the structure is a ruin that people pass through, in which case the standard procedure for found property applies. If what is found was buried and bears the appearance of wealth from a prior age, it is conveyed to the treasury of the Muslims. What is obligatory for the finder in such cases has already been set out.

A foundling whose parents are unknown is considered free. His inheritance passes to the treasury of the Muslims; no relative inherits from him by lineage, and he neither inherits nor is inherited from except through the bond of marriage. When he reaches adulthood and his circumstances improve, and the person who took him in and raised him seeks repayment of the costs of that upbringing, the foundling is obliged to make it good. Whoever offers a reward for the return of a runaway slave or a stray animal, and the search is carried out, is bound to pay that reward as he himself stipulated. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt.

**On Division and Property Structures**

Whatever lies between dwelling walls, and whatever wealth is held between partners that admits of division without being ruined by it, is to be divided among them if any or all of the partners request it. If the thing is of a kind that division would ruin, or that would harm one or more of the partners when divided, it is sold and the proceeds distributed. There is no objection to dividing a house so that its lower portion belongs to some partners and its upper portion to others. The roof of the lower level and its walls are the responsibility of the owner of the lower portion; what lies above belongs to the owner of the upper level, and the ground beneath that upper level is likewise the upper owner's. If the lower portion falls into disrepair through no fault of the upper owner, the lower owner is responsible for its repair, as he is for the lower walls upon which the upper level rests. Whoever causes damage to any part of the structure is bound to repair what he has damaged. Everything belonging to the lower level is the lower owner's responsibility to repair, because it is his property — even though the upper level is borne upon it and rests upon it — and on that basis the house is valued at the time of division.

When a wall stands between two men and it falls, both are obliged to rebuild it. If one of them rebuilds it alone, the other may not benefit from it until he pays half the cost. If the wall belongs to one of them alone and it falls, that owner is obliged to rebuild it; and if he abandons it and the other man rebuilds it in his place, the one who abandoned it retains no right in it.

No one may open an aperture in his wall through which he can look into his neighbor's private quarters. If, however, he opens it for light and air, and it affords no view into those quarters, he is entitled to do so — and his neighbor, in turn, is entitled to build a wall within his own property to block it, should he wish.

No one may be prevented from building within his own property in a way that screens a neighbor's view, provided he acts within his right.

Whoever opens a door onto a thoroughfare, or digs a well within the bounds of his own wall, is not to be prevented from doing so when the street in question is a passable, through-running public road. If it gives onto a dead-end lane, he may not do so except with the permission of those whose path runs through it. If it stands at the very end of the lane, where none of them has a path past it, he may do as he wishes in the portion adjoining him through which no one else passes.

No one should divert a public, through-running road from its course. If, however, the road belongs to him and lies entirely at his disposal, the diversion is his to make.

All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt.

**On Testimony**

> رِّجَالِكُمْ ۖ فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌۭ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ

Allah Almighty said, "Establish the testimony for the sake of Allah" (Al-Talaq: 2), and "Call to witness two witnesses from among your men; and if there are not two men, then one man and two women from among those whom you approve as witnesses" (Al-Baqarah: 282), and "Let two just men from among you bear witness" (Al-Talaq: 2). He also said, "Do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful" (Al-Baqarah: 283), and "That is nearer to their bearing witness in its proper form" (Al-Maidah: 108), and "And shun the word of falsehood" (Al-Hajj: 30).

The Messenger of Allah said that whoever conceals knowledge he possesses will come on the Day of Resurrection bridled with a bridle of fire. He, (ع), also said that the false witness will be raised on the Day of Resurrection lapping at his tongue in the Fire as a dog laps its tongue in a vessel. And he said that the false witness is among the reviled. Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali, (ع), said that the witness must deliver what he was asked to witness and must fear Allah his Lord, for it is among the forms of false witness that a man bears witness to what he does not know and denies what he does know. Whoever bears false witness, and this becomes known of him, is given a painful flogging, is paraded about, and his deed is made public — and he is liable for whatever was lost through his testimony.

The testimony of a just believer is admissible on behalf of anyone, whether near of kin or distant. A just slave's testimony is likewise admissible, except in favor of his masters or in any matter that would result in his manumission; once he has been freed from that bond, however, his testimony in such a matter becomes admissible. The testimony of boys in a bloodshed case carries the weight of a presumption upon which the qasama oath may be administered, but it is not admissible in any other matter until they reach maturity.

The following testimony is inadmissible:

- Two suspect persons testifying together
- One who is himself under accusation
- A child of adultery
- A partner testifying against his partner in a matter that lies between the two of them — though his testimony is admissible in matters outside their shared dealings, provided he is just

A follower, a hired man, or a servant who is just may testify on behalf of the one he serves, works for, or follows, except in any matter that would draw a benefit to himself or in which he is suspect. A neighbor may not testify in his own favor. The testimony of an adversary against his opponent is inadmissible, as is the testimony of people of deviant inclinations against the believers.

If a slanderer repents, his testimony becomes admissible. If a witness's testimony has been established and the one testified against then challenges him — bringing forward just witnesses who discredit him on grounds of something objectionable, of suspicion, or of conduct unbecoming of just people — that testimony is set aside.

Whoever prays at the congregational mosque, presents himself well, and has no known fault to his name is an admissible witness, unless grounds for discrediting him are established.

The testimony of a Muslim is admissible against the people of shirk, but the testimony of a polytheist is not admissible against Muslims. The one exception concerns a bequest made during travel when no other witness is available — in that case, the polytheist's testimony stands, provided he swears an oath alongside it. The testimony of non-Muslims against one another is admissible when it is sound within their own religion and nothing discrediting is known of them.

If a person gives testimony while still in a state of disbelief, or while still a minor, and thereafter the disbeliever embraces Islam and the minor reaches maturity, their testimony is admissible — provided they are just at the time they deliver it. The exception is when that testimony was already given earlier and was at that time rejected: in such a case, it must be given afresh.

The testimony of women is admissible in matters of marriage and wealth, but not in divorce, prescribed punishments, or anything that falls between those categories. If three men and two women testify to adultery, stoning becomes obligatory; but if there are two men and four women, their testimony to adultery is not admissible. Women's testimony is admissible in the matter of istihlal — the cry of the newborn — and the testimony of a single midwife is accepted if she is just and no other woman is present. When a newborn cries and then dies, that cry establishes that it was born alive. Women's testimony is not admissible for sighting the crescent of Ramadan, and so cannot initiate or end the fast; it is, however, admissible in matters of the waiting period, the postpartum period, and those things concerning women that men are not permitted to witness.

No testimony may be given upon another's testimony in cases involving a prescribed punishment, killing, or retaliation. Testimony relayed on behalf of a single original witness requires two men to carry it, and it is only admissible under specific conditions:

- The original witness is absent in a place distant enough to permit shortening the prayer and breaking the fast while traveling.
- The original witness is ill or infirm and unable to attend the judge's session.
- The original witness has died after entrusting his testimony to others.

If the original witness is present and in sound health, no one may testify in his place — he must appear and testify in person. A witness may only testify to what he himself knows.

> إِلَّا مَن شَهِدَ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ

If the witnesses disagree over a divorce — one testifying that he divorced her in accordance with the prescribed waiting period and the other testifying otherwise — their testimony is inadmissible. If they disagree over the dowry, one testifying to the lesser amount and the other to the greater, the woman has a choice: she may swear an oath alongside the witness who testified to the greater amount and claim it, or she may take the lesser amount without an oath — unless her adversary wishes to swear against her in that case. A man may swear an oath together with his two witnesses, just as such an oath is admissible on behalf of one for whom two witnesses have already testified, for rights are sometimes forfeited in ways unknown both to the witnesses and to the one against whom testimony is given. No one may bear witness upon a written document unless he can establish his own testimony to it and knows it for certain. Allah, the most truthful of all speakers, said:

> إِلَّا مَن شَهِدَ بِٱلْحَقِّ وَهُمْ يَعْلَمُونَ
>
> "Except for those who bear witness to the truth while they know." (Al-Zukhruf: 86)

> رِّجَالِكُمْ ۖ فَإِن لَّمْ يَكُونَا رَجُلَيْنِ فَرَجُلٌۭ وَٱمْرَأَتَانِ مِمَّن تَرْضَوْنَ مِنَ ٱلشُّهَدَآءِ

If witnesses give their testimony and then seek to retract it before judgment is issued, the retraction is accepted and no ruling is made upon their testimony. If they seek to retract after judgment has been issued, the retraction is not accepted, and they are liable for whatever was lost as a result of their testimony.

Whoever is summoned to give testimony may not refuse, for Allah, exalted be He, declared: "And let not the witnesses refuse when they are called" (Al-Baqarah: 282). Whoever has witnessed something and is called upon to testify must do so, in keeping with the words of Allah Almighty: "Do not conceal testimony; whoever conceals it, his heart is sinful" (Al-Baqarah: 283).

As for one who happens to overhear people settling their accounts, or hears one man acknowledge a debt to another, without having been asked to witness the exchange — if the one who made the acknowledgment later calls upon him to testify to what he heard, the choice is his: if he wishes, he may bear witness to what he heard.

When asked to testify to what he heard, a man must do so truthfully; if he declines, no fault attaches to him, since he was never formally summoned as a witness. In matters of death, lineage, ancestral standing, and long-established possession, testimony on the basis of report and common knowledge is admissible — knowledge that has spread widely among the people. Through such report, people come to know one another. They testify to the death of one who has died, and to a man's attribution to his father, though most of them never witnessed these things with their own eyes and never heard the acknowledgment firsthand; in such matters, the reported acknowledgment is accepted. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, may Allah's blessings be upon them.

### The Case and the Evidence

> وَلَا تَأْكُلُوٓا۟ أَمْوَلَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِٱلْبَطِلِ وَتُدْلُوا۟ بِهَآ إِلَى ٱلْحُكَّامِ لِتَأْكُلُوا۟ فَرِيقًۭا مِّنْ أَمْوَلِ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْإِثْمِ وَأَنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ

Allah, exalted is He, said: "And do not consume one another's wealth unjustly, nor proffer it to the judges that you may sinfully consume a portion of the people's wealth while you know" ﴿وَلَا تَأْكُلُوا أَمْوَالَكُم بَيْنَكُم بِالْبَاطِلِ وَتُدْلُوا بِهَا إِلَى الْحُكَّامِ لِتَأْكُلُوا فَرِيقًا مِّنْ أَمْوَالِ النَّاسِ بِالْإِثْمِ وَأَنتُمْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ (Al-Baqarah: 188).

And He said: "Indeed, Allah commands you to render trusts to their rightful owners, and when you judge between people to judge with justice" ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَأْمُرُكُمْ أَن تُؤَدُّوا الْأَمَانَاتِ إِلَىٰ أَهْلِهَا وَإِذَا حَكَمْتُم بَيْنَ النَّاسِ أَن تَحْكُمُوا بِالْعَدْلِ﴾ (Al-Nisa: 58).

The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "I judge between you only by evidence and oaths. Some of you may be more persuasive in his plea than others; so whoever I award something out of his brother's wealth, I have only cut off for him a piece of the Fire." He and his family likewise forbade the seizing of a Muslim's wealth by a false oath. The ruling of a judge does not make lawful what is otherwise unlawful for the one in whose favor it is given. Whoever is awarded what is not rightfully his may not lawfully take it, for the judge rules by what is outwardly apparent, while Allah knows the unseen and the hidden.

The burden of evidence in claims over wealth lies upon the claimant, and the oath lies upon the one against whom the claim is made. That oath is sworn by Allah, mighty and majestic, and by none other. The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "Whoever swears, let him swear by Allah; and whoever has an oath sworn to him by Allah, let him accept it; and whoever does not do so is not a Muslim."

If the claimant presses his claim and the defendant denies it, the judge asks the defendant to swear. Should the defendant refer the oath back to the claimant — saying, "Let him swear to what he claims against me, and I will give it to him" — that is his right, for had the claimant wished to swear alongside his evidence, that too would have been his right. If the claimant then swears, judgment is given in his favor on the strength of his claim together with his oath. If, however, he declines to swear, the defendant is relieved of the obligation, nothing is awarded to the claimant, and nothing further lies against the defendant beyond this.

Once evidence has been established, the defendant has the right to ask the claimant to swear that his claim against him remains exactly as the testimony showed — that nothing of it, great or small, has lapsed. This right exists because rights, as has been noted, may lapse in ways the witnesses have no knowledge of. If the defendant stands to incur no liability unless the claimant swears, and the claimant has not requested that oath, a judge who is aware of this right should bring it to the claimant's attention, since most people do not know what they are entitled to. Once informed, if the claimant asks for the oath it is administered; if he does not ask, the matter rests as it stands. Where the testimony concerns a minor or an absent party, the judge does not rule in the claimant's favor until the claimant has sworn alongside the evidence. And if the claimant swears and judgment is given for him, but the defendant afterward produces upright witnesses, the judge grants the defendant his right and sets aside any weight that the claimant's earlier oath might have carried.

Judgment on the testimony of a single witness together with the claimant's oath is valid in matters of wealth alone; it does not apply to anything other than wealth.

When the proofs are evenly matched over a single object — whether the object is in the hand of one of the two adversaries, in the hands of both together, or in neither's hand — and each party brings upright witnesses, both adversaries are required to swear. If one declines the oath, the object is awarded to the one who swore, on the strength of his evidence. If both swear, the matter is settled by lot, and whichever party's lot is drawn receives the object. The same applies when the object is in both their hands and both have sworn: the lot is cast between them. If the object is in the hand of a third party and both decline the oath, it is awarded to neither. Likewise, if the object is in the hand of one of them and the other declines the oath, it is not awarded to that other party but remains with the one who holds it; and if the holder also declines the oath, it still remains in his hand, and if he swears it is left with him in the same way.

Where the testimony of one party establishes that the object originated with him — that it was bred or produced in his possession — while the testimony of the other asserts only that the object is his, without establishing its origin, the object is awarded to the party whose evidence accounts for both its origin and its increase.

Whoever willingly acknowledges that he is a slave is held to be a slave. Should he afterward claim his freedom, or should freedom be claimed on his behalf, that claim is not accepted without evidence. If, however, he made the acknowledgment of servitude under compulsion and then asserts that he is free, the burden of proof falls on whoever claims his servitude.

When a man receives dinars or dirhams from another and then returns to him alleging that some of the coin was defective — while the giver denies this — the giver must swear that he handed over only sound coin and that he knows of no defect in what he gave. Should the giver decline that oath, the recipient swears that the defect was indeed present in what was given to him, and the giver must then replace it.

When a man and a woman dispute over the furnishings of a household — or their heirs dispute, or one of the original parties disputes with the heirs of the other — whoever among them produces evidence for what he or she claims is awarded it. If neither party has evidence, they swear against each other; whoever declines the oath is ruled against on the opponent's claim in the matter disputed. If both decline to swear, or both swear, and neither has evidence, then the man receives what custom recognizes as belonging to men, and the woman receives what custom recognizes as belonging to women.

When two men, or a group, lie with one woman within a single term — whether they are free men, slaves, or free polytheists — and she conceives, and each man claims the child, lots are cast; whoever's lot is drawn is awarded the child, and paternity is attributed to him. If the lot falls to a polytheist while the child's mother is a Muslim, the child is Muslim, and the polytheist holds no claim over the child of a Muslim woman. If the mother is herself a polytheist and the lot falls to the polytheist, the child follows the religion of them both. If the lot falls to a Muslim or to a freed slave, the child is a free Muslim.

When someone sends an item with a bearer to a third party, and the bearer says he delivered it while the intended recipient denies receiving it, the bearer's word is not accepted without evidence. If, however, the item was delivered and the sender then instructed the bearer to give it as charity, and the bearer says he has already done so, his word is accepted along with his oath — provided he is under suspicion. All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt, may.

### The Etiquette of Judges

> يَدَاوُۥدُ إِنَّا جَعَلْنَكَ خَلِيفَةًۭ فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ فَٱحْكُم بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ بِٱلْحَقِّ

Allah, mighty and majestic, said: "O David, We have made you a vicegerent upon the earth, so judge between the people in truth" ﴿يَا دَاوُودُ إِنَّا جَعَلْنَاكَ خَلِيفَةً فِي الْأَرْضِ فَاحْكُم بَيْنَ النَّاسِ بِالْحَقِّ﴾ (Sad: 26). And He said: "And judge between them by what Allah has revealed" ﴿وَأَنِ احْكُم بَيْنَهُم بِمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ﴾ (Al-Maidah: 49).

And He said: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the disbelievers" ﴿وَمَن لَّمْ يَحْكُم بِمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْكَافِرُونَ﴾ (Al-Maidah: 44). And He said: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the wrongdoers" ﴿وَمَن لَّمْ يَحْكُم بِمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الظَّالِمُونَ﴾ (Al-Maidah: 45).

And He said: "And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, those are the defiantly disobedient" ﴿وَمَن لَّمْ يَحْكُم بِمَا أَنزَلَ اللَّهُ فَأُولَٰئِكَ هُمُ الْفَاسِقُونَ﴾ (Al-Maidah: 47).

And He said: "Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what was revealed to you and what was revealed before you, yet wish to take their disputes to the Taghut, though they were commanded to reject it; and Satan wishes to lead them far astray" ﴿أَلَمْ تَرَ إِلَى الَّذِينَ يَزْعُمُونَ أَنَّهُمْ آمَنُوا بِمَا أُنزِلَ إِلَيْكَ وَمَا أُنزِلَ مِن قَبْلِكَ يُرِيدُونَ أَن يَتَحَاكَمُوا إِلَى الطَّاغُوتِ وَقَدْ أُمِرُوا أَن يَكْفُرُوا بِهِ وَيُرِيدُ الشَّيْطَانُ أَن يُضِلَّهُمْ ضَلَالًا بَعِيدًا﴾ (Al-Nisa: 60).

The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "Do not ask for command, for whoever asks for it is left to it, and whoever is given it without asking is helped in it." He forbade anyone from putting himself forward for the office of judge. Yet for one whom a just imam has summoned to it, and who is competent in it, the proper course is not to hold back. It is not permitted to him to judge for a tyrannical imam, nor to judge while he has no knowledge of the science of judgment.

> كُنتُ مُتَّخِذَ ٱلْمُضِلِّينَ عَضُدًۭا

The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "Whoever gives a legal ruling without knowledge is cursed by the angels of heaven and the angels of the earth; and whoever judges and errs will come on the Day of Resurrection with his hands shackled to his neck." He forbade, and his family forbade, that one who has no knowledge be appointed to judge. And Ali, may the blessings of Allah be upon him, wrote to Rifaa: "Do not employ anyone whose word concerning us you cannot trust; otherwise Allah will be your adversary and will demand from you." When it was said to him concerning Muawiyah, "Were you to employ him, then once he has affirmed your authority you could dismiss him," he replied: "Where then is the word of Allah, mighty and majestic: And I would not take the misleaders as helpers ﴿وَمَا كُنتُ مُتَّخِذَ الْمُضِلِّينَ عَضُدًا﴾ (Al-Kahf: 51)?"

He delivered a sermon, and within it he said: "As for what follows: my pledge is held in surety, and I stand answerable for it. For one who takes warning, godliness keeps watch, so that no people's crop of piety is left to wither, and no rooted stock that rests upon piety is left to thirst. Truth and good belong to the one who knows his own measure, and it is ignorance enough in a man that he does not know his own measure.

"Among the most hateful of creatures to Allah, mighty and majestic, are two men. One is a man whom Allah has abandoned to himself: he has swerved from the straight path, enamored of an innovation, given over to fasting and prayer within it, so that he becomes a trial for whoever is dazzled by his worship. He has strayed from the guidance of those who came before him and leads astray those who follow him after, bearing the weight of sins belonging to others whom he misled by his error.

"The other is a man who has heaped up ignorance and moves among the rabble of the people, plunging into the murk of discord. The ignorant have named him a scholar, though he has not passed even a single sound day in knowledge. He hoards much of that whose little is better than its much, until he has drunk his fill from stagnant water and amassed what is of no worth.

He sits among the people as a judge, appointing himself to resolve what has confounded others. When he differs from a judge who came before him, he offers no surety in his own ruling. When a difficult case is brought before him, he stuffs it with padding drawn from his own opinion and then cuts the matter short. He stands upon a web of doubts as a spider stands upon its own spinning, never knowing whether he has struck the mark or missed it entirely. When he is right, he fears he has erred; when he errs, he hopes he was right. He does not reckon with knowledge in anything he has rejected, and he cannot see that beyond what he has reached there may be further doctrine. When he measures one thing by another, he does not consider his own view false; and when a matter darkens over him, he conceals his ignorance, lest it be said that he does not know — and then he sits and delivers judgment. He is a key to obscurities, a rider of doubts, a man who flounders through ignorance. He does not excuse himself from what he does not know, that he might at least be safe; nor does he bite down with a firm tooth upon knowledge, that he might gain something from it. He scatters narrations as the wind scatters dry chaff. Inheritances weep on his account, and blood cries out on his account, and through his judgment what is lawful in marriage is made forbidden. By Allah, he is not competent to rule on what is brought before him, nor is he fit for what has been entrusted to him.

"O people, look closely at the flaw of these veins of injustice, and hold fast to the obedience of one whose ignorance you cannot excuse; for the knowledge with which Adam, (ع), came down, and all that with which the prophets were favored, is found in the Seal of the Prophets, Muhammad and his family, and in his pure progeny. If you are led astray, then where are you going?"

He said: "When the Messenger of Allah, (ع) and his family, sent me to Yemen, I said: O Messenger of Allah, you send me to judge between them while I am a young man and there are men of years among them, and I have no knowledge of judgment. He struck me upon my chest and said: O Allah, guide his heart and make his tongue firm. By the One who splits the seed and creates the soul, never after that did I doubt in judging between two parties."

He said: "Discords arise only from passions that are followed and rulings that are newly invented, in which the judgment of Allah is opposed and men give their loyalty to other men. Were truth pure and unmixed, there would be no disagreement; and were falsehood pure and unmixed, it would not be hidden from those of discernment. But a handful is taken from this and a handful from that, and the two are mingled together — and there it is that Satan masters his followers, while those for whom the best reward has already been decreed are saved."

The Master said: "The Muslims should not be placed under one who is greedy, lest he covet their wealth; nor under the ignorant, who would ruin them through his ignorance; nor under the miser, who would withhold their rights from them; nor under the harsh man, whose harshness would drive them to harshness in return; nor under one who betrays his trust over the public funds, taking from one people and giving to another; nor under one who takes bribes in judgment, so that the rights of the people are lost; nor under one who suspends the Sunnah, for he would destroy the community."

The Messenger of Allah and his family said: "Whoever acts wrongfully as a judge, whether deliberately or in error, is in the Fire." And Ali (ع) wrote to Rifaa, his judge over Ahvaz: "Know that this office of command is a trust; so whoever turns it into a betrayal, upon him is the curse of Allah until the Day of Resurrection."

The Messenger of Allah and his family forbade the judge from favoring either party by giving one more of his attention and presence of mind than the other, and forbade him from speaking before he had heard the statements of both adversaries.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said: "Whoever among you knows anything of our rulings, let him be a judge among you, for I have made him a judge; so bring your disputes before him." And he said: "Whoever consumes unlawful gain consumes the bribe given in judgment."

The judge should deal equitably between the two adversaries in his ruling, treating them alike in his speech, his attention, and his regard, and he should not speak until he has heard the statements of both. He should not give judgment in the mosque, nor carry out a prescribed punishment within it, though there is no harm in his administering correction there to one who deserves it. He should possess dignity, deliberateness, and care in examining the condition of those he relies upon and admits near him. He should restrain himself from mixing with common traders and from personally engaging in buying and selling, entrusting that instead to one in whose faith and trustworthiness he has confidence, and warning him against any breach of it.

As for the one entrusted to judge between the Muslims, he keeps himself apart from mingling with the market folk and from engaging personally in buying and selling. He delegates such matters to those he trusts in their religion and honesty, and he warns them against underestimating or neglecting their duties.

He rules according to the Book of Allah the Almighty. What he does not find there, he seeks in what is authentically established from the Messenger of Allah and his family, and from the Imams of his lineage. If the ruling remains unknown to him, he refers the matter to the Imam of his time and asks him. He rules neither by his own opinion nor by his own desire, neither by analogy nor by approbation. He accepts no intercession, nor does the party on whose behalf intercession is made receive the intercessor with favor in a way that would draw the judge toward him. Before him, the noble and the humble, the virtuous and the questionable, the strong and the weak stand as equals. He does not hear one party in the absence of the other, nor does he coach one side in its argument, assist it, or lean toward either party in any matter whatsoever.

If he decides a case and it afterward becomes clear to him that his ruling has violated the right, he overturns it and rules by the truth. He does the same with cases brought before him in the past upon which he had already ruled.

Abu Jafar Muhammad ibn Ali said: Among the Children of Israel there was a judge who judged them with truth. When death came upon him, his wife began to weep at his side. He said to her: Why do you weep for me, when I am passing, Allah willing, to what is good? For I know that I once judged unjustly. She asked: And what is the sign of that? He said: When I am laid in my grave, come down to me and uncover my face, and you will see the sign of it.

She did so, and she saw a great worm crossing within his nostril. Frightened, she covered him again and left.

When night came she saw him in a dream, and he said to her: Did what you saw of me alarm you? She said: Yes, I was indeed alarmed. He said: What you saw befell me only on account of you. Your brother once brought a dispute against a man, and I wished that you might be the one in the right, so that I would rule in your favor; and so it was. That affliction reached me because of my desire that the right should be yours.

The account of the judge's dream closes there. Elsewhere, Abu Abdullah Jafar ibn Muhammad (ع) was asked about the words of Allah the Almighty and Exalted: ﴿And do not consume your wealth among yourselves unjustly, and offer it as a bribe to the rulers so that you may consume a portion of the wealth of the people in sin, while you know﴾ (al-Baqarah 188). He said: "Allah, mighty and exalted, knew that there would be rulers in this nation who act unjustly. He did not intend by this verse the rulers among the people of justice; He intended the rulers among the people of injustice. If a man holds a right against another, summons him before the rulers of the people of justice, and that other man refuses — instead bringing the matter before the rulers of the people of injustice — then he is among those who have sought judgment from al-Taghut (اَلطَّاغُوت). That is the meaning of Allah the Almighty's words: ﴿Have you not seen those who claim to believe in what has been revealed to you and what has been revealed before you, yet they wish to take their disputes to al-Taghut﴾ (al-Nisa 60).

"The people of injustice are those who oppose you in your affair. Beware, therefore, of carrying your disputes against one another to the people of injustice. Instead, look among yourselves for a man who knows something of our rulings and appoint him as an arbitrator, for I have made him a judge. Bring your disputes to him. As for whatever was decreed against the households of the wrongdoers by those who ruled against them in the days of their power — leave it, and do not pursue it."

The judge does not rule in a way that allows one party to profit from the arguments used against the party convicted. He may accept what comes to him from the public treasury, but he may not take anything for himself in the matter he is deciding between the parties. He may inspect the markets of the Muslims, their measures and their weights, and he may delegate this oversight to someone he trusts. He does not imprison anyone on mere suspicion, except in a matter of blood. He strikes with the durrah in cases of slander, in discretionary punishment, and in discipline; when the prescribed punishments fall due, the flogging is carried out with the whip. He does not imprison a man who is in straitened circumstances over a debt.

If, however, the debtor is found to be solvent and possesses the means to satisfy what has been ruled against him, and that wealth is in his hands, the judge orders him to hand it over. If he refuses, he is beaten until he discharges what has been adjudged against him. If the debtor is absent, he is detained until he produces what is owed, and the judgment is then carried out against him. If, after his return, he persists in withholding it, his property is sold on his behalf and his debt is settled from the proceeds.

A judge does not accept a written ruling sent from another judge in matters involving a prescribed punishment, nor in divorce. He does not accept testimony upon testimony, and he takes no guarantor in a matter of a prescribed punishment. He carries out the judgment of a just judge, but he will not act on another judge's letter unless someone he trusts bears witness to its authenticity.

If testimony against a defendant had been established in a prior judge's court but never carried into effect, and the witnesses against the defendant subsequently deny it, the sitting judge has the defendant take an oath in favor of the claimant — provided the claimant requests it. If the defendant swears that the claim was never discharged against him, the judge asks the claimant to produce his evidence.

The judge accepts the appointment of an agent, and testimony in such matters is heard whether the litigant is present or absent. He rules against the absent party and holds him to presenting his argument upon his return. He likewise judges between the People of the Book with truth when they bring their dispute before him.

All of this is the position of the Ahl al-Bayt.
